Moreover, we find that this interplay lies at the heart of what we call the ``dominant frequency bias'', where linear CNNs arrive at these discoveries using only the dominant frequencies of the different structural parts present in the dataset. We furthermore provide experiments that show how our theory relates to deep, non-linear CNNs used in practice. Our findings shed new light on the inner working of CNNs, and can help explain their shortcut learning and their tendency to rely on texture instead of shape.

papers.title: Enhancing the Extraction of Interpretable Information for Ischemic Stroke Imaging from Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we improve the interpretability of deep neural networks for medical image segmentation by modifying Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) to extract more sensible visual explanations and link signal amplitude to information content?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces modifications to Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) to improve interpretability for medical image segmentation, showing that filtering high-amplitude noise reveals more sensible saliency maps, and proposes a mathematical framework (filter calculus) for analyzing function approximation.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents an LRP implementation for medical image segmentation, showing that filtering high-amplitude noise can improve interpretability, and introduces a filter calculus framework for function approximation. However, good accuracy does not guarantee correct reasoning, and medical knowledge is needed to constrain LRP outputs.
papers.key_findings:
Raw LRP outputs for 3D U-Net lesion segmentation are noisy and highlight irrelevant regions, undermining interpretability.
Applying fraction-pass and fraction-clamp filters to LRP signals removes high-amplitude noise and reveals heatmaps that better match the lesion region.
Low-amplitude signals in LRP contain significant information, while high-amplitude spikes are often noise.
The proposed inclusivity coefficients (input-inclusivity and ground-truth inclusivity) can quantify the interpretability of LRP outputs.
A mathematical framework (filter calculus) is introduced to analyze function approximation and interpretability.
papers.limitation:
The small dataset (ISLES 2017) may limit the optimality of LRP output.
More robust medical knowledge is required to constrain LRP output.
The training procedure is basic without data augmentation, which might affect results.
future_direction: Study the evolution of interpretability signals during training to provide an independent evaluation metric for DNNs.
Investigate normalized signals and their correlation with network performance.
Further develop the filter calculus for function approximation and interpretability.
papers.abstract: We implement a visual interpretability method Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) on top of 3D U-Net trained to perform lesion segmentation on the small dataset of multi-modal images provided by ISLES 2017 competition. We demonstrate that LRP modifications could provide more sensible visual explanations to an otherwise highly noise-skewed saliency map. We also link amplitude of modified signals to useful information content. High amplitude localized signals appear to constitute the noise that undermines the interpretability capacity of LRP. Furthermore, mathematical framework for possible analysis of function approximation is developed by analogy.

papers.title: Knowledge Circuits in Pretrained Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative circuits of components such as attention heads and MLPs, and how can these circuits be used to analyze model behaviors and knowledge editing?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces knowledge circuits as a method to uncover how transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative components, and demonstrates their utility in analyzing knowledge editing and model behaviors like hallucinations and in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge circuits provide a valuable framework for understanding how transformers store and express knowledge, and can inform the design of better knowledge editing methods.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge circuits effectively capture knowledge representations, maintaining over 70% of original performance with less than 10% of the graph.
Knowledge is aggregated in early-to-middle layers and enhanced in later layers.
Special components like mover heads and relation heads are critical for information transfer and relational capture.
ROME editing incorporates information at the edited layer, while fine-tuning directly writes knowledge and dominates predictions.
Hallucinations occur when the circuit lacks effective mover heads or they select incorrect information.
papers.limitation:
Coarse granularity of circuits, not capturing fine-grained neuron-level behavior.
Logit lens method may have discrepancies between middle layers and output unembedding matrix.
future_direction: Finer-grained circuit analysis at the neuron level.
Developing more robust techniques to map intermediate representations to outputs (e.g., Attention Lens).
Investigating activation mechanisms of reused heads and polysemanticity.
papers.abstract: The remarkable capabilities of modern large language models are rooted in their vast repositories of knowledge encoded within their parameters, enabling them to perceive the world and engage in reasoning. The inner workings of how these models store knowledge have long been a subject of intense interest and investigation among researchers. To date, most studies have concentrated on isolated components within these models, such as the Multilayer Perceptrons and attention head. In this paper, we delve into the computation graph of the language model to uncover the knowledge circuits that are instrumental in articulating specific knowledge. The experiments, conducted with GPT2 and TinyLLAMA, have allowed us to observe how certain information heads, relation heads, and Multilayer Perceptrons collaboratively encode knowledge within the model. Moreover, we evaluate the impact of current knowledge editing techniques on these knowledge circuits, providing deeper insights into the functioning and constraints of these editing methodologies. Finally, we utilize knowledge circuits to analyze and interpret language model behaviors such as hallucinations and in-context learning. We believe the knowledge circuits hold potential for advancing our understanding of Transformers and guiding the improved design of knowledge editing. Code and data are available in https://github.com/zjunlp/KnowledgeCircuits.

papers.title: Deeply Explainable Artificial Neural Network
papers.research_question: How to create a deep learning architecture that embeds explainability ante hoc, providing per-sample, per-feature explanations while maintaining high accuracy.
papers.core_contribution: DxANN is a novel deep learning architecture that provides intrinsic explainability through ante hoc design, using Explainability Contribution Score (ECS) to generate per-feature explanations while achieving accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art models.
papers.conclusion: DxANN offers a practical solution for intrinsically interpretable deep learning, matching the performance of foundation models while providing clinically aligned explanations without post hoc methods.
papers.key_findings:
DxANN achieves high classification accuracy on medical image tasks, with 97.1% for DME diagnosis and 97.2% for OA diagnosis, comparable to fine-tuned foundation models.
The Explainability Contribution Score (ECS) provides per-sample, per-feature explanations via heatmaps that highlight clinically relevant regions in images.
DxANN's explanations are generated natively during inference without external tools, offering consistent and transparent decision-making.
future_direction: Extending DxANN to other data modalities, multimodal inputs, and other model architectures such as MLP, transformers, and RNNs.
papers.abstract: While deep learning models have demonstrated remarkable success in numerous domains, their black-box nature remains a significant limitation, especially in critical fields such as medical image analysis and inference. Existing explainability methods, such as SHAP, LIME, and Grad-CAM, are typically applied post hoc, adding computational overhead and sometimes producing inconsistent or ambiguous results. In this paper, we present the Deeply Explainable Artificial Neural Network (DxANN), a novel deep learning architecture that embeds explainability ante hoc, directly into the training process. Unlike conventional models that require external interpretation methods, DxANN is designed to produce per-sample, per-feature explanations as part of the forward pass. Built on a flow-based framework, it enables both accurate predictions and transparent decision-making, and is particularly well-suited for image-based tasks. While our focus is on medical imaging, the DxANN architecture is readily adaptable to other data modalities, including tabular and sequential data. DxANN marks a step forward toward intrinsically interpretable deep learning, offering a practical solution for applications where trust and accountability are essential.

papers.title: Signal Strength and Noise Drive Feature Preference in CNN Image Classifiers
papers.research_question: What factors drive feature preference in CNN image classifiers? Specifically, how do signal strength (pixel count) and noise (deviation, overlap, predictivity) affect which features (shape, texture, color) are preferred by CNNs?
papers.core_contribution: CNNs prefer features with stronger signal (more pixels) and lower noise (less deviation, overlap, and higher predictivity), and show no inherent preference for color, shape, or texture when signal and noise are controlled. The paper proposes a predictive model for feature preference: F(pr) = Signal - Noise.
papers.conclusion: Signal strength and noise are key drivers of feature preference in CNNs, and careful control of these factors can avoid biases and align machine and human feature preferences more closely.
papers.key_findings:
CNNs prefer task-relevant features with larger signal (pixel count) over those with smaller signal.
CNNs prefer task-relevant features with lower noise, including lower deviation, lower overlap, and higher predictivity.
CNNs show no strong preference between color, shape, or texture when signal and noise are carefully controlled (feature equivalency).
Texture bias in ImageNet-trained CNNs can be shifted to shape bias by controlling signal in test images, without retraining the model.
Decreasing deviation in MNIST digits increases the model's reliance on those digits over a simple pixel feature, as shown in the Binary shiftMNIST experiment.
future_direction: Test the extensibility of the results across other tasks (including unsupervised objectives), datasets, data augmentation strategies, and architectures.
Conduct follow-up experiments with full control over signal, deviation, overlap, and predictivity in test images across all classes to accurately quantify texture bias in ImageNet-trained CNNs.
The results may inform DNN learning theory.
papers.abstract: Feature preference in Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) image classifiers is integral to their decision making process, and while the topic has been well studied, it is still not understood at a fundamental level. We test a range of task relevant feature attributes (including shape, texture, and color) with varying degrees of signal and noise in highly controlled CNN image classification experiments using synthetic datasets to determine feature preferences. We find that CNNs will prefer features with stronger signal strength and lower noise irrespective of whether the feature is texture, shape, or color. This provides guidance for a predictive model for task relevant feature preferences, demonstrates pathways for bias in machine models that can be avoided with careful controls on experimental setup, and suggests that comparisons between how humans and machines prefer task relevant features in vision classification tasks should be revisited. Code to reproduce experiments in this paper can be found at \url{https://github.com/mwolff31/signal_preference}.

papers.title: A Combination of Integrated Gradients and SRFAMap for Explaining Neural Networks Trained with High-Order Statistical Radiomic Features
papers.research_question: To what extent can the application of additive mapping to convert statistical radiomic feature attributions into an interpretable saliency map achieve the same explanation faithfulness as a radiomic feature activation map?
papers.core_contribution: This paper proposes a novel approach to generate explanatory saliency maps for neural network models trained with high-order statistical radiomic features by combining Integrated Gradients and SRFAMap, demonstrating improved faithfulness metrics compared to baseline methods.
papers.conclusion: The research addresses the explainability of high-order statistical radiomic features by proposing a method that provides a single saliency map for all features, showing better faithfulness than existing methods.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method (SRFAMap + Integrated Gradients) yields higher insertion and deletion correlation metrics for saliency maps than the baseline Radiomic Feature Activation Maps method.
Classification performance (Accuracy and MCC) is similar across models using different texture statistics matrices (GLCM, GLRLM, GLSZM, GLDM, NGTDM).
Saliency maps generated by SRFAMap are visually less scattered and more densely localized than those produced by RFAM.
The faithfulness metrics (Insertion and Deletion Correlation) can be affected by out-of-distribution images, leading to unpredictable model behavior.
The approach is limited to differentiable models like neural networks and cannot be used with non-differentiable architectures like Decision Trees or Support Vector Machines.
papers.limitation:
The proposed approach can only be used with models learnt by training a neural network, not other architectures such as Decision trees or Support Vector Machines.
Insertion and Deletion correlation methods modify input images by removing or inserting pixels, creating out-of-distribution inputs that may lead to unpredictable model outputs.
future_direction: Evaluate the proposed approach with different datasets, considering other medical image modalities like MRI and Ultrasound.
Develop a new metric to assess saliency maps’ faithfulness without using model predictions on out-of-distribution inputs.
Extend the additivity mechanism to form saliency scores for individual pixels with other properties, such as multiplicativity.
papers.abstract: Abstract This research tackles the problem of high-order statistical radiomic features’ visual explainability. While methods like Radiomic Features Activation Maps exist to solve this problem, they have important limitations. This includes the inability to produce a single explanation for all features and a lack of direct connection between classification results and generated explanations. This study contributes to the body of knowledge with a new explanatory saliency map generation approach for models trained with high-order statistical radiomic features. It extends the existing SRFAMap method using the Integrated Gradients method from Explainable AI. In detail, it exploits the integrated gradients of high-order statistical radiomic feature functions. Results with the tuberculosis classification dataset demonstrated better insertion and deletion correlation faithfulness metrics for saliency maps generated with the proposed approach than Radiomic Features Activation Maps.

papers.title: Insights into a radiology-specialised multimodal large language model with sparse autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders be applied to interpret the internal representations of a radiology-specialised multimodal large language model (MAIRA-2) and steer its generations?
papers.core_contribution: This work applies Matryoshka-SAE to the radiology MLLM MAIRA-2, identifying a subset of interpretable clinical concepts within its representations and demonstrating the feasibility and challenges of steering model generations using these features.
papers.conclusion: The study provides initial insights into the internal concepts of MAIRA-2 using SAEs, marking a step toward mechanistic interpretability, while highlighting practical and methodological challenges in automated interpretability and steering.
papers.key_findings:
A small subset (1.8%) of SAE features are highly interpretable (F1 > 0.75), corresponding to clinically relevant concepts like medical devices, pathologies, and textual features.
Nearly half (46%) of SAE features are not interpretable by the automated pipeline (F1 < 0.5).
Steering model generations using SAE features is possible but produces more off-target changes than on-target changes, with success highly dependent on the specific feature.
There is a strong correlation between the on-target effects of positive and negative steering coefficients.
The trained SAEs and their automated interpretations are publicly released to foster further research.
papers.limitation:
Many SAE features (46%) are not interpretable by the automated pipeline.
Steering often produces more off-target changes than on-target changes.
The study reveals practical and methodological challenges across the SAE training, automated concept discovery, and steering pipeline.
papers.abstract: Interpretability can improve the safety, transparency and trust of AI models, which is especially important in healthcare applications where decisions often carry significant consequences. Mechanistic interpretability, particularly through the use of sparse autoencoders (SAEs), offers a promising approach for uncovering human-interpretable features within large transformer-based models. In this study, we apply Matryoshka-SAE to the radiology-specialised multimodal large language model, MAIRA-2, to interpret its internal representations. Using large-scale automated interpretability of the SAE features, we identify a range of clinically relevant concepts - including medical devices (e.g., line and tube placements, pacemaker presence), pathologies such as pleural effusion and cardiomegaly, longitudinal changes and textual features. We further examine the influence of these features on model behaviour through steering, demonstrating directional control over generations with mixed success. Our results reveal practical and methodological challenges, yet they offer initial insights into the internal concepts learned by MAIRA-2 - marking a step toward deeper mechanistic understanding and interpretability of a radiology-adapted multimodal large language model, and paving the way for improved model transparency. We release the trained SAEs and interpretations: https://huggingface.co/microsoft/maira-2-sae.

papers.title: Explainable Transformer Prototypes for Medical Diagnoses
papers.research_question: How can we improve explainability in transformer-based models for medical image diagnosis by focusing on region-to-region attention rather than pixel-to-pixel?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an interpretable self-attention mechanism using prototype learning for medical image diagnosis, providing region-to-region attention for better visual explanations.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method offers a promising direction for explainability in medical diagnostics, with both quantitative and qualitative results supporting its effectiveness.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed interpretable self-attention mechanism achieves a mean AUC of 0.798 on the NIH Chest X-Ray dataset without pre-training, competitive with state-of-the-art methods.
The region-to-region attention more accurately identifies lesion locations in chest X-rays compared to ad-hoc explanation methods like Grad-CAM.
The method provides visual explanations at multiple resolution levels by replacing all self-attention layers in CvT.
The use of parametric prototype vectors for keys and values allows learning canonical representations for important patterns.
papers.limitation: The performance gap compared to some state-of-the-art methods might be closed by pre-training on large datasets.
future_direction: Explore the robustness of the proposed algorithm in medical and non-medical domains.
papers.abstract: Deployments of artificial intelligence in medical diagnostics mandate not just accuracy and efficacy but also trust, emphasizing the need for explainability in machine decisions. The recent trend in automated medical image diagnostics leans towards the deployment of Transformer-based architectures, credited to their impressive capabilities. Since the self-attention feature of transformers contributes towards identifying crucial regions during the classification process, they enhance the trustability of the methods. However, the complex intricacies of these attention mechanisms may fall short of effectively pinpointing the regions of interest directly influencing AI decisions. Our research endeavors to innovate a unique attention block that underscores the correlation between 'regions' rather than 'pixels'. To address this challenge, we introduce an innovative system grounded in prototype learning, featuring an advanced self-attention mechanism that goes beyond conventional ad-hoc visual explanation techniques by offering comprehensible visual insights. A combined quantitative and qualitative methodological approach was used to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method on the large-scale NIH chest X-ray dataset. Experimental results showed that our proposed method offers a promising direction for explainability, which can lead to the development of more trustable systems, which can facilitate easier and rapid adoption of such technology into routine clinics. The code is available at www.github.com/NUBagcilab/r2r_proto.

papers.title: Exemplary Natural Images Explain CNN Activations Better than State-of-the-Art Feature Visualization
papers.research_question: How informative are synthetic feature visualizations (from Olah et al. 2017) for helping humans predict CNN activations, and how do they compare to a baseline of natural images?
papers.core_contribution: Natural images that strongly activate a CNN feature map are more informative for helping humans predict the feature map's activations than state-of-the-art synthetic feature visualizations.
papers.conclusion: Synthetic feature visualizations are significantly less informative than natural images for assessing CNN activations, and visualization methods should improve over this simple baseline.
papers.key_findings:
Synthetic feature visualizations provide helpful information (82% accuracy), but natural images are significantly more helpful (92% accuracy).
The superiority of natural images holds across network layers, for both expert and lay participants, and for both hand-picked and randomly selected feature maps.
Participants are faster and more confident when using natural images as references compared to synthetic visualizations.
Subjective impressions of the interpretability of synthetic feature visualizations vary greatly between participants.
papers.abstract: Feature visualizations such as synthetic maximally activating images are a widely used explanation method to better understand the information processing of convolutional neural networks (CNNs). At the same time, there are concerns that these visualizations might not accurately represent CNNs' inner workings. Here, we measure how much extremely activating images help humans to predict CNN activations. Using a well-controlled psychophysical paradigm, we compare the informativeness of synthetic images by Olah et al. (2017) with a simple baseline visualization, namely exemplary natural images that also strongly activate a specific feature map. Given either synthetic or natural reference images, human participants choose which of two query images leads to strong positive activation. The experiments are designed to maximize participants' performance, and are the first to probe intermediate instead of final layer representations. We find that synthetic images indeed provide helpful information about feature map activations ($82\pm4\%$ accuracy; chance would be $50\%$). However, natural images - originally intended as a baseline - outperform synthetic images by a wide margin ($92\pm2\%$). Additionally, participants are faster and more confident for natural images, whereas subjective impressions about the interpretability of the feature visualizations are mixed. The higher informativeness of natural images holds across most layers, for both expert and lay participants as well as for hand- and randomly-picked feature visualizations. Even if only a single reference image is given, synthetic images provide less information than natural images ($65\pm5\%$ vs. $73\pm4\%$). In summary, synthetic images from a popular feature visualization method are significantly less informative for assessing CNN activations than natural images. We argue that visualization methods should improve over this baseline.

papers.title: COMIX: Compositional Explanations using Prototypes
papers.research_question: How can we design an interpretable image classification method that provides faithful explanations by decomposing images into concepts and matching them to training prototypes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces COMiX, a novel interpretable-by-design image classification method that decomposes test images into learned concepts (class-defining features) and matches each region to corresponding regions in training images, providing faithful explanations that reflect the actual decision-making process.
papers.conclusion: COMiX offers a novel interpretable machine learning approach that performs decision-making through concept similarity to training data, with favorable properties of fidelity, sparsity, necessity, and sufficiency, while maintaining competitive accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
COMiX provides faithful explanations by design, linking test images to training prototypes, and demonstrates competitive accuracy with state-of-the-art interpretable models.
The method shows a 48.82% improvement in the C-insertion score on ImageNet over the best baseline, indicating superior fidelity.
COMiX exhibits favorable sparsity properties, with higher PQ-index scores than a standard ViT baseline across multiple datasets.
The method can provide both factual (why a class was predicted) and counterfactual (how an alternative class would be explained) interpretations.
COMiX demonstrates surprisingly good finetuning-free generalization to new datasets using a nearest-neighbor approach.
papers.limitation: Use of pseudo-labels for preliminary selection of features is a limitation, as feature selection necessitates pre-selection of the proposal class for subsequent refinement.
future_direction: Expand COMiX to segmentation scenarios.
Investigate the reasons for COMiX's good finetuning-free performance.
papers.abstract: Aligning machine representations with human understanding is key to improving interpretability of machine learning (ML) models. When classifying a new image, humans often explain their decisions by decomposing the image into concepts and pointing to corresponding regions in familiar images. Current ML explanation techniques typically either trace decision-making processes to reference prototypes, generate attribution maps highlighting feature importance, or incorporate intermediate bottlenecks designed to align with human-interpretable concepts. The proposed method, named COMIX, classifies an image by decomposing it into regions based on learned concepts and tracing each region to corresponding ones in images from the training dataset, assuring that explanations fully represent the actual decision-making process. We dissect the test image into selected internal representations of a neural network to derive prototypical parts (primitives) and match them with the corresponding primitives derived from the training data. In a series of qualitative and quantitative experiments, we theoretically prove and demonstrate that our method, in contrast to post hoc analysis, provides fidelity of explanations and shows that the efficiency is competitive with other inherently interpretable architectures. Notably, it shows substantial improvements in fidelity and sparsity metrics, including 48.82% improvement in the C-insertion score on the ImageNet dataset over the best state-of-the-art baseline.

papers.title: The Mind’s Eye: Visualizing Class-Agnostic Features of CNNS
papers.research_question: How can we visually interpret the class-agnostic features of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) by creating images that depict the most informative features of a specific layer?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a class-agnostic feature visualization method for CNNs that uses a dual-objective loss (activation maximization and distance minimization) to create images representing the most informative features of a given layer, without modifying the original model.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method provides visual explanations for the top features extracted by CNN layers, which can improve the understanding of trained CNNs and the polysemantic (entangled) features associated with specific images or sets of images.
papers.key_findings:
The method visualizes the top k descriptive features from a set of images, revealing the most informative features for a specific CNN layer.
Visualizations from deeper layers show more complex and entangled features compared to earlier layers, which capture more basic patterns.
The method can handle variations in input images (e.g., number of objects, orientation) without detrimental effects on the overall feature combination.
The optimization process shows how feature-inclusive regions change over iterations, converging to a representation of the object's general appearance.
The approach does not require a generator network, limiting computational cost to the FLOPs of the original network.
papers.abstract: Visual interpretability of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) has gained significant popularity because of the great challenges that CNN complexity imposes to understanding their inner workings. Although many techniques have been proposed to visualize class features of CNNs, most of them do not provide a correspondence between inputs and the extracted features in specific layers. This prevents the discovery of stimuli that each layer responds better to. We propose an approach to visually interpret CNN features given a set of images by creating corresponding images that depict the most informative features of a specific layer. Exploring features in this class-agnostic manner allows for a greater focus on the feature extractor of CNNs. Our method uses a dual-objective activation maximization and distance minimization loss, without requiring a generator network nor modifications to the original model. This limits the number of FLOPs to that of the original network. We demonstrate the visualization quality on widely-used architectures. <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1</sup> <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1</sup> Code is available at https://git.io/JL9Wg and our demo video: https://youtu.be/Au3jaUdnPKM

papers.title: Multi-Granular Node Pruning for Circuit Discovery
papers.research_question: How can we perform circuit discovery at multiple granularities (down to neurons) in a scalable way, overcoming the limitations of existing edge-pruning methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a node-level pruning framework for circuit discovery that operates at multiple granularities (from blocks to neurons) in a single optimization step, achieving higher efficiency and finer granularity than existing edge-pruning methods.
papers.conclusion: The node pruning approach is efficient and effective for circuit discovery, achieving substantial reductions in circuit size and number of retained attention heads, and suggests future work combining edge and node pruning for even more minimal circuits.
papers.key_findings:
The structure of discovered circuits depends on the task; for example, all MLP blocks are essential for the IOI task, while for the GT task, most MLPs can be removed.
Different component granularities exhibit varying susceptibility to compression; for instance, the outputs of MLP1 (Keys) can be sparsified to a much greater extent than those of MLP2 (Values).
The method identifies circuits that are smaller in nodes than those discovered by prior methods while maintaining task performance.
The method reveals that many neurons within components deemed important by coarse methods are actually irrelevant.
The method has a significantly lower memory footprint (5-10x) compared to baselines, as it does not require storing intermediate activations.
papers.limitation: The framework discovers node-level circuits but does not explicitly recover the interaction structure between nodes, such as which active nodes exchange information and the directionality of those interactions.
future_direction: Combining edge and node pruning in a hierarchical fashion
Developing a hybrid node and edge procedure to infer interaction structure
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery aims to identify minimal subnetworks that are responsible for specific behaviors in large language models (LLMs). Existing approaches primarily rely on iterative edge pruning, which is computationally expensive and limited to coarse-grained units such as attention heads or MLP blocks, overlooking finer structures like individual neurons. We propose a node-level pruning framework for circuit discovery that addresses both scalability and granularity limitations. Our method introduces learnable masks across multiple levels of granularity, from entire blocks to individual neurons, within a unified optimization objective. Granularity-specific sparsity penalties guide the pruning process, allowing a comprehensive compression in a single fine-tuning run. Empirically, our approach identifies circuits that are smaller in nodes than those discovered by prior methods; moreover, we demonstrate that many neurons deemed important by coarse methods are actually irrelevant, while still maintaining task performance. Furthermore, our method has a significantly lower memory footprint, 5-10x, as it does not require keeping intermediate activations in the memory to work.

papers.title: Exemplary Natural Images Explain CNN Activations Better than\n State-of-the-Art Feature Visualization
papers.research_question: How informative are synthetic feature visualizations for understanding CNN activations, and how do they compare to natural images as a baseline?
papers.core_contribution: Natural images are more informative than synthetic feature visualizations for helping humans predict CNN activations, suggesting that current visualization methods should improve over this simple baseline.
papers.conclusion: Synthetic feature visualizations are less informative than natural images for understanding CNN activations, and visualization methods should improve over this simple baseline.
papers.key_findings:
Synthetic feature visualizations provide helpful information (82% accuracy) but natural images are more helpful (92% accuracy).
The superiority of natural images holds across most layers and branches of the network.
Both expert and lay participants perform similarly, and both benefit more from natural images.
Even hand-picked feature visualizations do not outperform natural images.
Presenting both maximally and minimally activating images and multiple examples improves performance, especially for natural images.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to one network architecture (Inception V1) and one feature visualization method (Olah et al., 2017).
The design choices aim at an upper bound on the informativeness of the visualizations, which may not reflect real-world usage.
future_direction: Improve visualization methods to outperform the natural image baseline.
Extend the evaluation to other network architectures and visualization methods.
Investigate other tasks beyond activation prediction.
papers.abstract:

Here, we measure how much extremely activating images help humans to predict

images, human participants choose which of two query images leads to strong
positive activation. The experiments are designed to maximize participants'

papers.title: On the Biology of a Large Language Model
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform computations, and can we reverse engineer their mechanisms using attribution graphs?
papers.core_contribution: This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The model performs genuine two-hop reasoning with intermediate steps, such as representing 'Texas' when answering about the capital of the state containing Dallas.
In poetry generation, the model plans ahead by pre-selecting rhyming words before writing each line.
Multilingual circuits use a mix of language-specific and abstract, language-independent components, with more abstraction in larger models.
Entity recognition circuits distinguish known and unknown entities, influencing when the model answers or refuses, with circuit misfires causing hallucinations.
Refusal mechanisms involve harmful request features aggregated from pretraining and trigger refusal during fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
tools provide satisfying insight for about a quarter of prompts
replacement model incompletely and imperfectly captures the original model
future_direction: Developing more effective unsupervised exploration tools for increasingly capable models
papers.abstract: How do large language models internally perform computations, and can we reverse engineer their mechanisms using attribution graphs? This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability. Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.

papers.title: Using Causal Analysis for Conceptual Deep Learning Explanation
papers.research_question: How to provide clinically relevant explanations for deep learning models in healthcare by associating hidden units with concepts and using causal analysis to ensure influence.
papers.core_contribution: A framework for explaining black-box models using clinically relevant concepts and causal mediation analysis to ensure concepts causally influence the model's decisions.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework provides global explanations for black-box models in terms of clinically relevant concepts that are causally influencing the model's decisions.
papers.key_findings:
Concept classifiers using sparse logistic regression achieve high recall, indicating effective association of hidden units with concepts.
Hidden units act as visual concept detectors, localizing radiographic features without explicit concept supervision during training.
Causal mediation analysis via counterfactual interventions ranks concepts based on indirect effect, with top-ranked concepts being clinically consistent.
The indirect effect is highest in middle layers (dense-block 3), showing their role in mediating decisions.
A decision tree surrogate function provides interpretable global explanations using the top-ranked concepts.
future_direction: Extend concept definition to include a broader set of clinical metrics.

papers.title: Building Interpretable Models for Moral Decision-Making
papers.research_question: How do neural networks make moral decisions on trolley-style dilemmas, and where do moral biases originate within their architectures?
papers.core_contribution: Designs a 2-layer transformer optimized for moral reasoning tasks, achieving 77% accuracy on Moral Machine data, and combines interpretability methods to map internal mechanisms of moral judgment.
papers.conclusion: Demonstrates that small, custom transformers can achieve moral competence and be transparently analyzed, enabling targeted interventions for bias mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
The model learns a moral hierarchy where characters like Pregnant and Stroller have positive causal effects, while Criminal has negative effects.
Moral biases localize to distinct computational stages: legality bias in Layer 0 and species bias in Layer 1.
Circuit probing identifies sparse subnetworks in the MLP block that causally implement moral scoring.
The model shows functional specialization with different attention heads specializing in different bias dimensions.
Small, custom transformers can achieve moral competence while remaining interpretable, enabling targeted bias interventions.
papers.limitation: Training on aggregate human preferences inherits cultural biases.
future_direction: Extend the approach to traditional large language models on moral questions.
papers.abstract: We build a custom transformer model to study how neural networks make moral decisions on trolley-style dilemmas. The model processes structured scenarios using embeddings that encode who is affected, how many people, and which outcome they belong to. Our 2-layer architecture achieves 77% accuracy on Moral Machine data while remaining small enough for detailed analysis. We use different interpretability techniques to uncover how moral reasoning distributes across the network, demonstrating that biases localize to distinct computational stages among other findings.

papers.title: INSightR-Net: Interpretable Neural Network for Regression using Similarity-based Comparisons to Prototypical Examples
papers.research_question: How to create an interpretable convolutional neural network for regression tasks without compromising performance?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an inherently interpretable CNN for regression (INSightR-Net) that uses similarity-based comparisons to prototypical examples, achieving competitive performance with a ResNet baseline while providing intuitive explanations.
papers.conclusion: INSightR-Net provides an intuitive explanation for regression tasks while maintaining baseline prediction performance, and can be applied to any feedforward regression CNN.
papers.key_findings:
INSightR-Net achieves competitive prediction performance (MAE and accuracy) compared to a ResNet-18 baseline.
The new similarity function improves explanation sparsity while preserving model diversity.
The prototype sample distance loss (LP_SD) is necessary for good sparsity and diversity.
The cluster loss (L_Clst) helps in clustering samples around prototypes in the latent space.
Removing the min-k averaging in L_Clst reduces both sparsity and diversity, indicating the importance of using multiple closest prototypes.
papers.abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have shown exceptional performance for a range of medical imaging tasks. However, conventional CNNs are not able to explain their reasoning process, therefore limiting their adoption in clinical practice. In this work, we propose an inherently interpretable CNN for regression using similarity-based comparisons (INSightR-Net) and demonstrate our methods on the task of diabetic retinopathy grading. A prototype layer incorporated into the architecture enables visualization of the areas in the image that are most similar to learned prototypes. The final prediction is then intuitively modeled as a mean of prototype labels, weighted by the similarities. We achieved competitive prediction performance with our INSightR-Net compared to a ResNet baseline, showing that it is not necessary to compromise performance for interpretability. Furthermore, we quantified the quality of our explanations using sparsity and diversity, two concepts considered important for a good explanation, and demonstrated the effect of several parameters on the latent space embeddings.

papers.title: Understanding and Mitigating Gender Bias in LLMs via Interpretable Neuron Editing
papers.research_question: How can we understand the neuron-level mechanisms of gender bias in LLMs and mitigate this bias through targeted neuron editing without compromising the model's core capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an interpretable neuron editing method that effectively reduces gender bias in LLMs while preserving their original capabilities, supported by a new dataset and a detailed analysis of bias mechanisms at the neuron level.
papers.conclusion: The proposed interpretable neuron editing method successfully addresses the challenges of understanding and mitigating gender bias in LLMs, achieving a strong balance between fairness and functionality without compromising the models' original capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Gender bias is pervasive across multiple LLMs, as evidenced by non-zero entropy differences and skewed proportions in the CommonWords dataset.
Specific neuron circuits, including 'gender neurons' activated by stereotypical words and 'general neurons' activated by the <start> token, are responsible for gender bias.
Editing even a small number of general neurons can significantly degrade the model's performance on common tasks due to hierarchical neuron interactions.
The proposed interpretable neuron editing method, combining logit-based and causal-based strategies, effectively reduces gender bias (e.g., improving ICAT scores) while maintaining performance on tasks like reading comprehension and arithmetic.
The method outperforms existing fine-tuning and neuron editing approaches in balancing bias reduction with capability preservation.
papers.limitation:
The method relies on the CommonWords dataset for neuron selection, and results may vary for tasks or datasets not covered in the study.
Experiments are conducted on five decoder-only LLMs, requiring potential adaptations for other architectures.
The evaluation metrics (ICAT, entropy difference, accuracy) may not fully capture fairness or real-world performance.
The interpretability insights guiding neuron selection rely on assumptions (e.g., projecting neurons into vocabulary space) that may only be approximations.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit gender bias, posing challenges for their safe deployment. Existing methods to mitigate bias lack a comprehensive understanding of its mechanisms or compromise the model's core capabilities. To address these issues, we propose the CommonWords dataset, to systematically evaluate gender bias in LLMs. Our analysis reveals pervasive bias across models and identifies specific neuron circuits, including gender neurons and general neurons, responsible for this behavior. Notably, editing even a small number of general neurons can disrupt the model's overall capabilities due to hierarchical neuron interactions. Based on these insights, we propose an interpretable neuron editing method that combines logit-based and causal-based strategies to selectively target biased neurons. Experiments on five LLMs demonstrate that our method effectively reduces gender bias while preserving the model's original capabilities, outperforming existing fine-tuning and editing approaches. Our findings contribute a novel dataset, a detailed analysis of bias mechanisms, and a practical solution for mitigating gender bias in LLMs.

papers.title: Deep Image Segmentation Using Explainable Attention Mechanisms: Applications in Biomedical Imaging
papers.research_question: How can we overcome the lack of interpretability in deep learning models for medical image segmentation by introducing an explainable framework that combines CNNs and transformers with attention mechanisms and XAI tools?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces an explainable hybrid deep learning model for biomedical image segmentation that combines a CNN encoder with a Transformer decoder, integrates CBAM attention modules, and embeds XAI tools (Grad-CAM++ and SHAP) to achieve high segmentation accuracy and interpretability in a unified architecture.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework successfully improves segmentation accuracy and provides inherent interpretability, addressing the trust gap and forming a solid basis for clinical adoption of AI-aided diagnostic tools.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed model outperforms baseline models (U-Net, Attention U-Net, TransUNet) on ISIC 2018 and BraTS 2021 datasets, achieving Dice scores of 0.902 and 0.895 respectively.
The integrated explainability tools (Grad-CAM++ and SHAP) produce visual explanations that align with clinical landmarks, validated by expert assessments with over 85% clinical relevance.
Ablation studies confirm the importance of attention modules (CBAM) and explainability components for both performance and clinical trust.
papers.limitation:
The computational cost is significantly larger than lightweight CNN models due to transformer modules and attention methods, which may hinder real-time deployment in resource-limited clinical settings.
The model requires detailed preprocessing and augmentation optimization for best performance and assumes clean and annotated datasets, which may not align with noisy or incomplete real-world clinical data.
Explainability methods like SHAP are computationally expensive and may not be fitting to all use cases.
future_direction: Applying the same pipeline to other medical imaging modalities (e.g., chest X-rays, CT scans, retinal fundus images) with domain-specific adjustments.
Addressing task-specific problems like modality-dependent noise, data scarcity, or label variability via transfer learning, weak supervision, or synthetic data generation.
Meeting emerging ethical and regulatory requirements for AI-driven diagnostic systems, focusing on accountability, fairness, and decision-making transparency.
papers.abstract: Correct and discernible segmentation of an image is an important part of biomedical imaging, especially when anatomical structures and pathological regions are identified. Although deep learning architectures, like U-Net and its variants, have performed well, their lack of interpretability, transparency and contextual reasoning has limited their clinical adoption. This research helps to overcome the most important issue of high-performance medical segmentation by introducing a new explainable framework that combines convolutional encoders with transformer-based decoders and dual attention mechanisms. There are three aspects of this work, based on the following objectives. (1) To boost the performance of segmentation by means of hybrid local-global feature modelling; (2) To bring about clarity through visual explanation tools; and (3) To conduct clinical viability checks through expert assessments. The architecture proposed includes CBAM for fine spatial and channel attention and combines Grad-CAM++ and SHAP for local and global explainability. Such modules make it possible for clinicians to view the decision paths of models and establish trust in automated outputs. Experiments in two datasets, which were publicly available, were performed: ISIC 2018 for skin lesion segmentation and BraTS 2021 for brain tumor segmentation. The quantitative results show that the suggested method is better than several strong baseline models, such as U-Net, Attention U-Net, and TransUNet, delivering Dice scores of 0.902 and 0.895 on ISIC and BraTS datasets, respectively. Visual comparisons and expert confirmation validate the clinical plausibility of the predicted masks and demonstrate the potential worth of the explainability in high-stakes healthcare conditions. On the whole, this work provides a prudent, precise and explainable deep learning approach toward medical image segmentation and offers ample room for scientific integration and trust-conscious implementation in diagnostics workflows.

papers.title: Interpreting Arithmetic Mechanism in Large Language Models through Comparative Neuron Analysis
papers.research_question: How is arithmetic ability implemented in large language models, specifically the role of attention heads and FFN neurons, and what is the internal logic chain from input to prediction? Additionally, how does the LoRA fine-tuning method work?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Comparative Neuron Analysis (CNA) method to interpret arithmetic mechanisms in LLMs, identifying an internal logic chain of four stages, and applies it to understand LoRA and for model pruning and bias reduction.
papers.conclusion: The paper identifies important attention heads and FFN neurons for arithmetic, proposes the CNA method to construct the internal logic chain, finds LoRA amplifies important FFN neurons, and applies CNA to model pruning and editing.
papers.key_findings:
Arithmetic ability is localized in a few attention heads (arithmetic heads), each specializing in distinct operations.
The internal logic chain from input to prediction consists of four stages: feature enhancing, feature transferring, feature predicting, and prediction enhancing.
LoRA enhances prediction probabilities by amplifying the coefficient scores of important FFN neurons related to the final prediction.
Model pruning retaining only 5% of deep FFN neurons identified by CNA maintains performance on arithmetic tasks.
Model editing by zeroing 18 FFN neurons identified by CNA reduces gender bias by 35.7%.
papers.limitation:
The case studies rely on projecting vectors in vocabulary space, which is empirically interpretable but lacks complete theoretical foundation.
There is a lack of standardization across various studies regarding attribution methods (e.g., different intervention methods).
A potential risk is that attackers can identify and edit important neurons to change model behavior maliciously.
future_direction: Further investigation of the multiplication heads which do not significantly impact accuracy.
Explorations on different datasets for gender bias reduction.
Distinguishing whether a model has been edited to prevent malicious use.

papers.title: LLM Circuit Analyses Are Consistent Across Training and Scale
papers.research_question: Do circuit analyses of LLMs generalize across training time and model scale?
papers.core_contribution: Circuit analyses are consistent across training and scale: task abilities and supporting functional components emerge at similar token counts across model sizes, and the overarching algorithms implemented by circuits remain stable even when individual components change.
papers.conclusion: Circuit analyses generalize well over both training and scale, suggesting that studies on small models at the end of pre-training can inform understanding of larger models and models with longer training.
papers.key_findings:
Task abilities and functional components (e.g., induction heads, name-mover heads) emerge consistently at similar token counts across different model scales.
The algorithm implemented by a circuit remains stable over training even when the specific attention heads implementing it change.
Circuit size correlates with model size and can fluctuate over time while the algorithm remains the same.
Components like induction heads emerge around 2B tokens across scales, paralleling task learning curves.
Circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training provide insights that generalize to larger models and longer training runs.
papers.limitation:
The study does not include fine-tuning or other post-training techniques.
Circuit completeness is challenging to verify.
The findings need validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
future_direction: Validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
Investigating the load-balancing mechanism that maintains task performance when components change.
papers.abstract: Most currently deployed large language models (LLMs) undergo continuous training or additional finetuning. By contrast, most research into LLMs' internal mechanisms focuses on models at one snapshot in time (the end of pre-training), raising the question of whether their results generalize to real-world settings. Existing studies of mechanisms over time focus on encoder-only or toy models, which differ significantly from most deployed models. In this study, we track how model mechanisms, operationalized as circuits, emerge and evolve across 300 billion tokens of training in decoder-only LLMs, in models ranging from 70 million to 2.8 billion parameters. We find that task abilities and the functional components that support them emerge consistently at similar token counts across scale. Moreover, although such components may be implemented by different attention heads over time, the overarching algorithm that they implement remains. Surprisingly, both these algorithms and the types of components involved therein can replicate across model scale. These results suggest that circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training can provide insights that still apply after additional pre-training and over model scale.

papers.title: An Interpretable CNN for the Segmentation of the Left Ventricle in Cardiac MRI by Real-Time Visualization
papers.research_question: How can an interpretable convolutional neural network be created for left ventricle segmentation in cardiac MRI, balancing accuracy and interpretability without relying on transfer learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel interpretable CNN for left ventricle segmentation in cardiac MRI, trained from scratch without transfer learning, using global average pooling for interpretability and real-time visualization of gradient changes and layer features.
papers.conclusion: The proposed interpretable CNN method is feasible and efficient for left ventricle segmentation in cardiac MRI, providing a balance of accuracy and interpretability without the need for transfer learning.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed model achieved a Dice coefficient of 94.48% and an accuracy of 99.7% on the Sunnybrook dataset.
The model, trained from scratch, performed comparably to standard ImageNet transfer learning models for the medical imaging task.
The use of global average pooling improved interpretability and reduced parameters, helping avoid overfitting.
Real-time visualization of gradient changes and layer features allowed for monitoring and analysis during training.
The model is lightweight and suitable for deployment on mobile devices.
papers.abstract: The interpretability of deep learning models has emerged as a compelling area in artificial intelligence research. The safety criteria for medical imaging are highly stringent, and models are required for an explanation. However, existing convolutional neural network solutions for left ventricular segmentation are viewed in terms of inputs and outputs. Thus, the interpretability of CNNs has come into the spotlight. Since medical imaging data are limited, many methods to fine-tune medical imaging models that are popular in transfer models have been built using massive public ImageNet datasets by the transfer learning method. Unfortunately, this generates many unreliable parameters and makes it difficult to generate plausible explanations from these models. In this study, we trained from scratch rather than relying on transfer learning, creating a novel interpretable approach for autonomously segmenting the left ventricle with a cardiac MRI. Our enhanced GPU training system implemented interpretable global average pooling for graphics using deep learning. The deep learning tasks were simplified. Simplification included data management, neural network architecture, and training. Our system monitored and analyzed the gradient changes of different layers with dynamic visualizations in real-time and selected the optimal deployment model. Our results demonstrated that the proposed method was feasible and efficient: the Dice coefficient reached 94.48%, and the accuracy reached 99.7%. It was found that no current transfer learning models could perform comparably to the ImageNet transfer learning architectures. This model is lightweight and more convenient to deploy on mobile devices than transfer learning models.

papers.title: Towards interpretable-by-design deep learning algorithms
papers.research_question: How can deep learning models be made interpretable by design using prototypes, and how does this approach perform in terms of accuracy, computational efficiency, and resistance to confounding without requiring finetuning of the backbone model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the IDEAL framework, which transforms standard deep learning models into interpretable, prototype-based models without necessarily requiring finetuning, achieving competitive performance, especially with Vision Transformer backbones, while offering inherent interpretability and robustness to confounding.
papers.conclusion: The IDEAL framework offers an interpretable-by-design alternative to standard deep learning that can match the performance of opaque models, especially when using modern architectures like ViT, without the need for computationally expensive finetuning, and is effective for lifelong learning and mitigating confounding biases.
papers.key_findings:
The IDEAL framework without finetuning achieves performance competitive with finetuned models, with the gap being especially small for Vision Transformer (ViT) architectures.
The framework provides interpretability through real-image prototypes, allowing users to see which training examples a prediction is based on.
IDEAL circumvents catastrophic forgetting and enables efficient class-incremental learning, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines on benchmarks like iCIFAR-100.
Without finetuning, IDEAL improves performance on confounded data compared to finetuned counterparts by avoiding overfitting to spurious correlations.
The choice of prototype selection method (e.g., k-means) is crucial for performance when the backbone is not finetuned, but becomes less significant when the backbone is finetuned.
papers.abstract: The proposed framework named IDEAL (Interpretable-by-design DEep learning ALgorithms) recasts the standard supervised classification problem into a function of similarity to a set of prototypes derived from the training data, while taking advantage of existing latent spaces of large neural networks forming so-called Foundation Models (FM). This addresses the issue of explainability (stage B) while retaining the benefits from the tremendous achievements offered by DL models (e.g., visual transformers, ViT) pre-trained on huge data sets such as IG-3.6B + ImageNet-1K or LVD-142M (stage A). We show that one can turn such DL models into conceptually simpler, explainable-through-prototypes ones. The key findings can be summarized as follows: (1) the proposed models are interpretable through prototypes, mitigating the issue of confounded interpretations, (2) the proposed IDEAL framework circumvents the issue of catastrophic forgetting allowing efficient class-incremental learning, and (3) the proposed IDEAL approach demonstrates that ViT architectures narrow the gap between finetuned and non-finetuned models allowing for transfer learning in a fraction of time \textbf{without} finetuning of the feature space on a target dataset with iterative supervised methods.

papers.title: Have Faith in Faithfulness: Going Beyond Circuit Overlap When Finding Model Mechanisms
papers.research_question: How faithful are circuits found by edge attribution patching (EAP), and what is the relationship between overlap and faithfulness? The paper also introduces a new method, EAP-IG, to improve faithfulness.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces EAP-IG, a gradient-based circuit finding method that produces more faithful circuits than EAP, and shows that overlap metrics are insufficient for evaluating circuit faithfulness.
papers.conclusion: When comparing circuits, measuring overlap is no substitute for measuring faithfulness; EAP-IG provides a more faithful alternative to EAP for circuit finding.
papers.key_findings:
EAP-IG circuits are more faithful than EAP circuits on many tasks, though activation patching circuits sometimes outperform both.
Overlap (node or edge) does not always imply faithfulness; moderate overlap does not predict faithfulness well.
EAP-IG scores have higher correlation with activation patching scores for important edges, leading to more faithful circuits.
EAP-IG requires few steps (e.g., m=5) to achieve high faithfulness, making it efficient.
Cross-task faithfulness analysis reveals that circuit mechanisms can be shared across related tasks (e.g., Greater-Than variants) but not always.
papers.limitation:
Testing circuit completeness is challenging, and manually-found 'ground-truth' circuits may be unreliable.
EAP-IG does not always match the performance of activation patching (e.g., on the IOI task).
future_direction: Developing more efficient algorithms for computing faithfulness.
Investigating weighted graph edit distance as a metric that accounts for edge importance.
Exploring methods to ensure circuit completeness in addition to faithfulness.
papers.abstract: Many recent language model (LM) interpretability studies have adopted the circuits framework, which aims to find the minimal computational subgraph, or circuit, that explains LM behavior on a given task. Most studies determine which edges belong in a LM's circuit by performing causal interventions on each edge independently, but this scales poorly with model size. Edge attribution patching (EAP), gradient-based approximation to interventions, has emerged as a scalable but imperfect solution to this problem. In this paper, we introduce a new method - EAP with integrated gradients (EAP-IG) - that aims to better maintain a core property of circuits: faithfulness. A circuit is faithful if all model edges outside the circuit can be ablated without changing the model's performance on the task; faithfulness is what justifies studying circuits, rather than the full model. Our experiments demonstrate that circuits found using EAP are less faithful than those found using EAP-IG, even though both have high node overlap with circuits found previously using causal interventions. We conclude more generally that when using circuits to compare the mechanisms models use to solve tasks, faithfulness, not overlap, is what should be measured.

papers.title: X-VMamba: Explainable Vision Mamba
papers.research_question: How can we understand what State Space Models (SSMs) have learned and how they process information, given the lack of transparent attention mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a controllability-based interpretability framework for State Space Models (SSMs) that quantifies how input patches influence internal state dynamics, with two formulations (Jacobian-based and Gramian-based) that operate in a single forward pass with linear complexity.
papers.conclusion: Controllability analysis establishes a principled, mathematically rigorous interpretability paradigm for SSMs, providing unprecedented visibility into their internal dynamics and hierarchical processing across domains.
papers.key_findings:
SSMs naturally implement hierarchical feature refinement, with early layers capturing diffuse low-level textures and deeper layers focusing on semantically meaningful, clinically relevant patterns.
Influence scores become progressively more focused in deeper layers, with fewer patches having high influence, indicating a hierarchical filtering mechanism.
The choice of image scanning strategy (e.g., forward, backward, transposed) substantially modulates the distribution of influence scores across patches.
The proposed controllability framework provides domain-specific signatures aligned with diagnostic criteria, such as lesion boundaries in dermatology and high-density areas in mammography.
papers.limitation:
The Gramian formulation assumes local linearity of the SSM dynamics and does not account for non-linearities between layers (e.g., activation functions, normalization).
The current analysis computes controllability independently at each layer and does not provide an end-to-end attribution map from raw inputs to final outputs.
For sequential data, the method provides static, per-time-step influence scores and does not capture temporal causal influence (how inputs at time t affect outputs at future times t+τ).
future_direction: Extending the controllability framework to account for non-linear transformations between SSM layers.
Developing methods for end-to-end attribution by propagating influence scores through the entire network depth.
Enabling temporal causal analysis for sequential data to capture how inputs influence future outputs over finite horizons.
papers.abstract: State Space Models (SSMs), particularly the Mamba architecture, have recently emerged as powerful alternatives to Transformers for sequence modeling, offering linear computational complexity while achieving competitive performance. Yet, despite their effectiveness, understanding how these Vision SSMs process spatial information remains challenging due to the lack of transparent, attention-like mechanisms. To address this gap, we introduce a controllability-based interpretability framework that quantifies how different parts of the input sequence (tokens or patches) influence the internal state dynamics of SSMs. We propose two complementary formulations: a Jacobian-based method applicable to any SSM architecture that measures influence through the full chain of state propagation, and a Gramian-based approach for diagonal SSMs that achieves superior speed through closed-form analytical solutions. Both methods operate in a single forward pass with linear complexity, requiring no architectural modifications or hyperparameter tuning. We validate our framework through experiments on three diverse medical imaging modalities, demonstrating that SSMs naturally implement hierarchical feature refinement from diffuse low-level textures in early layers to focused, clinically meaningful patterns in deeper layers. Our analysis reveals domain-specific controllability signatures aligned with diagnostic criteria, progressive spatial selectivity across the network hierarchy, and the substantial influence of scanning strategies on attention patterns. Beyond medical imaging, we articulate applications spanning computer vision, natural language processing, and cross-domain tasks. Our framework establishes controllability analysis as a unified, foundational interpretability paradigm for SSMs across all domains. Code and analysis tools will be made available upon publication

papers.title: Contrastive Integrated Gradients: A Feature Attribution-Based Method for Explaining Whole Slide Image Classification
papers.research_question: How to improve feature attribution for whole slide image classification to better highlight class-discriminative regions and provide more interpretable explanations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Contrastive Integrated Gradients (CIG), a feature attribution method that computes contrastive gradients in logit space to highlight class-discriminative regions, and proposes two new metrics (MIL-AIC and MIL-SIC) for evaluating attribution in weakly supervised settings.
papers.conclusion: CIG consistently produces more informative and stable attributions than existing methods, both quantitatively and qualitatively, improving interpretability and supporting more explainable AI systems in computational pathology.
papers.key_findings:
CIG achieves higher MIL-AIC and MIL-SIC scores than baseline attribution methods (Vanilla Gradient, IG, EG, IDG) across multiple cancer datasets and model architectures.
CIG produces more focused and accurate attributions that align closely with tumor regions, as shown in qualitative visualizations.
CIG satisfies the axioms of integrated attribution methods (completeness, sensitivity, implementation invariance).
CIG works reliably across different cancer subtypes (breast, renal, lung) and model types (MLP, CLAM).
The proposed evaluation metrics (MIL-AIC, MIL-SIC) are adapted for weakly supervised WSI classification and capture how model predictions evolve as salient regions are introduced.
papers.limitation:
The evaluation is best suited for tumor-positive slides and may be less meaningful for normal slides.
Lack of human-subject evaluation.
future_direction: Incorporate rigorous human-subject evaluations of interpretability.
papers.abstract: Interpretability is essential in Whole Slide Image (WSI) analysis for computational pathology, where understanding model predictions helps build trust in AI-assisted diagnostics. While Integrated Gradients (IG) and related attribution methods have shown promise, applying them directly to WSIs introduces challenges due to their high-resolution nature. These methods capture model decision patterns but may overlook class-discriminative signals that are crucial for distinguishing between tumor subtypes. In this work, we introduce Contrastive Integrated Gradients (CIG), a novel attribution method that enhances interpretability by computing contrastive gradients in logit space. First, CIG highlights class-discriminative regions by comparing feature importance relative to a reference class, offering sharper differentiation between tumor and non-tumor areas. Second, CIG satisfies the axioms of integrated attribution, ensuring consistency and theoretical soundness. Third, we propose two attribution quality metrics, MIL-AIC and MIL-SIC, which measure how predictive information and model confidence evolve with access to salient regions, particularly under weak supervision. We validate CIG across three datasets spanning distinct cancer types: CAMELYON16 (breast cancer metastasis in lymph nodes), TCGA-RCC (renal cell carcinoma), and TCGA-Lung (lung cancer). Experimental results demonstrate that CIG yields more informative attributions both quantitatively, using MIL-AIC and MIL-SIC, and qualitatively, through visualizations that align closely with ground truth tumor regions, underscoring its potential for interpretable and trustworthy WSI-based diagnostics

papers.title: High resolution weakly supervised localization architectures for medical images
papers.research_question: How can the localization accuracy of Class-Activation Maps (CAM) be improved for weakly-supervised medical image analysis by designing a network architecture that avoids components harmful to shift-equivariance?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes PYLON, a high-resolution weakly-supervised localization network that avoids Global Average Pooling and Group Normalization to preserve shift-equivariance, achieving state-of-the-art point localization accuracy on the Chest X-Ray 14 dataset without sacrificing classification performance.
papers.conclusion: Shift-equivariance is crucial for accurate weakly-supervised localization, and avoiding GAP and Group Normalization leads to better performance. PYLON demonstrates high localization accuracy without compromising classification ability.
papers.key_findings:
Segmentation models (e.g., DeeplabV3+, FPN, PAN) perform poorly for weakly-supervised localization due to task mismatch.
Global Average Pooling (GAP) and Group Normalization are identified as components that significantly degrade localization accuracy in weakly-supervised settings.
Removing GAP and replacing Group Normalization with Batch Normalization improves localization accuracy in segmentation models.
PYLON, which removes GAP and uses a redesigned decoder, achieves the highest point localization accuracy, especially for small objects like nodules.
Higher resolution feature maps improve localization accuracy, with diminishing returns beyond a certain point.
papers.limitation: The reason why Group Normalization hinders localization accuracy is not determined, leaving an open question for future work.
future_direction: Investigate why Group Normalization hinders localization in weakly-supervised settings.
papers.abstract: In medical imaging, Class-Activation Map (CAM) serves as the main explainability tool by pointing to the region of interest. Since the localization accuracy from CAM is constrained by the resolution of the model's feature map, one may expect that segmentation models, which generally have large feature maps, would produce more accurate CAMs. However, we have found that this is not the case due to task mismatch. While segmentation models are developed for datasets with pixel-level annotation, only image-level annotation is available in most medical imaging datasets. Our experiments suggest that Global Average Pooling (GAP) and Group Normalization are the main culprits that worsen the localization accuracy of CAM. To address this issue, we propose Pyramid Localization Network (PYLON), a model for high-accuracy weakly-supervised localization that achieved 0.62 average point localization accuracy on NIH's Chest X-Ray 14 dataset, compared to 0.45 for a traditional CAM model. Source code and extended results are available at https://github.com/cmb-chula/pylon.

papers.title: Mask-Free Neuron Concept Annotation for Interpreting Neural Networks in Medical Domain
papers.research_question: How can neural networks be interpreted in medical domains without requiring pixel-wise annotated datasets for neuron concept annotation?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes MAMMI, a mask-free neuron concept annotation method for medical image models that uses vision-language models and adaptive selection to handle class imbalance, outperforming previous methods.
papers.conclusion: MAMMI is an effective mask-free method for neuron concept annotation in medical vision models, addressing limitations of previous approaches and demonstrating superior performance.
papers.key_findings:
MAMMI achieves superior performance in neuron concept annotation compared to mask-based and other vision-language methods in medical settings.
Using a medical-specific concept set extracted from MIMIC-CXR reports significantly improves interpretability over general concept sets.
Adaptive neuron representative image selection effectively handles class-imbalanced data distributions and improves concept matching.
MedCLIP outperforms other CLIP models for medical concept annotation in MAMMI.
MAMMI accurately identifies neuron concepts at penultimate layers, whereas baselines like TSI and CLIP Dissect fail to do so.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in deep neural networks have shown promise in aiding disease diagnosis and medical decision-making. However, ensuring transparent decision-making processes of AI models in compliance with regulations requires a comprehensive understanding of the model's internal workings.
