By selectively retaining only the most relevant parts of each layer, our method enables targeted compression that maintains clinically meaningful representations. Experiments across multiple medical image classification benchmarks demonstrate that this approach achieves high compression rates with minimal loss in accuracy, paving the way for lightweight, interpretable models suited for real-world deployment in healthcare settings.

papers.title: Comparing Computational Pathology Foundation Models using Representational Similarity Analysis
papers.research_question: What are the similarities and differences in the representational structures of computational pathology foundation models, and how do training paradigms affect these representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically analyzes the representational spaces of six computational pathology foundation models using representational similarity analysis, revealing differences in representational structures, slide- and disease-dependence, and intrinsic dimensionality, and showing that stain normalization reduces slide-dependence.
papers.conclusion: The analytical approach presented can be extended to other medical imaging domains, and gaining insight into the structure of learned representations can inform algorithmic refinement and support safe, effective deployment in clinical settings.
papers.key_findings:
UNI2 and Virchow2 have the most distinct representational structures, while Prov-GigaPath has the highest average similarity across models.
Having the same training paradigm (vision-only vs. vision-language) did not guarantee higher representational similarity.
All models show high slide-dependence but relatively low disease-dependence in their representations.
Stain normalization decreases slide-dependence for all models by a range of 5.5% (CONCH) to 20.5% (PLIP).
Vision-language models have relatively compact representations (lower intrinsic dimensionality) compared to the more distributed representations of vision-only models.
papers.limitation:
The study only used TCGA data, so the results may quantitatively differ in different datasets.
RSA has high CPU memory demand, scaling quadratically with the number of samples, which constrains sample size and requires high-memory computing nodes.
future_direction: Explicitly assess generalizability across different institutions, staining protocols, and scanner hardware, including how the studied representational metrics relate to downstream performance.
Systematically analyze how variations in training datasets and hyperparameters affect representational structure.
papers.abstract: Foundation models are increasingly developed in computational pathology (CPath) given their promise in facilitating many downstream tasks. While recent studies have evaluated task performance across models, less is known about the structure and variability of their learned representations. Here, we systematically analyze the representational spaces of six CPath foundation models using techniques popularized in computational neuroscience. The models analyzed span vision-language contrastive learning (CONCH, PLIP, KEEP) and self-distillation (UNI (v2), Virchow (v2), Prov-GigaPath) approaches. Through representational similarity analysis using H&E image patches from TCGA, we find that UNI2 and Virchow2 have the most distinct representational structures, whereas Prov-Gigapath has the highest average similarity across models. Having the same training paradigm (vision-only vs. vision-language) did not guarantee higher representational similarity. The representations of all models showed a high slide-dependence, but relatively low disease-dependence. Stain normalization decreased slide-dependence for all models by a range of 5.5% (CONCH) to 20.5% (PLIP). In terms of intrinsic dimensionality, vision-language models demonstrated relatively compact representations, compared to the more distributed representations of vision-only models. These findings highlight opportunities to improve robustness to slide-specific features, inform model ensembling strategies, and provide insights into how training paradigms shape model representations. Our framework is extendable across medical imaging domains, where probing the internal representations of foundation models can support their effective development and deployment.

papers.title: Network Dissection: Quantifying Interpretability of Deep Visual Representations
papers.research_question: How can we quantify the interpretability of latent representations in CNNs by measuring the alignment between individual hidden units and semantic concepts, and what factors affect this interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Network Dissection, a framework for quantifying the interpretability of CNN representations by evaluating the alignment between individual convolutional units and a broad set of semantic concepts, and uses it to show interpretability is an axis-aligned property affected by architecture, training data, and regularization.
papers.conclusion: Network Dissection provides a method to quantify interpretability in CNNs, revealing that interpretability is an axis-aligned property indicative of partially disentangled representations, and is influenced by network architecture, training data, and training techniques.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability of units is not axis-independent; random rotations of the representation significantly reduce the number of unique concept detectors, indicating interpretability is a special alignment learned by the network.
Deeper network architectures (ResNet > VGG > GoogLeNet > AlexNet) and training on scene-centric data (Places) lead to more interpretable units (more unique concept detectors).
Self-supervised training tasks produce fewer object detectors and more texture detectors compared to supervised training, and the form of self-supervision (e.g., colorization) affects which concepts emerge.
Batch normalization significantly reduces interpretability, while dropout and different random initializations have less impact on the final level of interpretability.
Widening a convolutional layer (increasing the number of units) can increase the number of unique concept detectors without significantly harming classification accuracy.
papers.limitation: Network dissection works only as well as the underlying dataset; if a unit matches a human-understandable concept that is absent in Broden, it will not score well for interpretability.
future_direction: Expanding the Broden dataset to include more kinds of visual concepts.
Finding ways to capture the benefits of batch normalization without destroying interpretability.
papers.abstract: We propose a general framework called Network Dissection for quantifying the interpretability of latent representations of CNNs by evaluating the alignment between individual hidden units and a set of semantic concepts. Given any CNN model, the proposed method draws on a data set of concepts to score the semantics of hidden units at each intermediate convolutional layer. The units with semantics are labeled across a broad range of visual concepts including objects, parts, scenes, textures, materials, and colors. We use the proposed method to test the hypothesis that interpretability is an axis-independent property of the representation space, then we apply the method to compare the latent representations of various networks when trained to solve different classification problems. We further analyze the effect of training iterations, compare networks trained with different initializations, and measure the effect of dropout and batch normalization on the interpretability of deep visual representations. We demonstrate that the proposed method can shed light on characteristics of CNN models and training methods that go beyond measurements of their discriminative power.

papers.title: DeepMiner: Discovering Interpretable Representations for Mammogram Classification and Explanation
papers.research_question: How to discover interpretable representations in deep neural networks and build explanations for medical predictions, specifically for mammogram classification.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DeepMiner, a human-in-the-loop framework for discovering interpretable representations in CNNs and generating explanations for medical predictions, specifically for mammogram classification.
papers.conclusion: DeepMiner is a framework that uncovers interpretable representations in deep neural networks and builds explanations for deep network predictions, and it is applicable to many other domains.
papers.key_findings:
Many individual units in the final convolutional layer of a CNN respond strongly to diseased tissue concepts specified by the BI-RADS lexicon.
DeepMiner can generate explanations for CNN mammogram classification that are consistent with ground truth radiology reports.
DeepMiner enables better understanding of the nuances of CNN classification decisions and possibly discovers new visual knowledge relevant to medical diagnosis.
future_direction: Generalization to other medical image classification tasks.
Incorporation of auxiliary features such as genetic information.
Potential for discovering unknown discriminative visual features for diseases less well understood than breast cancer.
papers.abstract: We propose DeepMiner, a framework to discover interpretable representations in deep neural networks and to build explanations for medical predictions. By probing convolutional neural networks (CNNs) trained to classify cancer in mammograms, we show that many individual units in the final convolutional layer of a CNN respond strongly to diseased tissue concepts specified by the Breast Imaging-Reporting and Data System (BI-RADS) lexicon. After expert annotation of the interpretable units, our proposed method is able to generate explanations for CNN mammogram classification that are consistent with ground truth radiology reports on the Digital Database for Screening Mammography. We show that DeepMiner not only enables better understanding of the nuances of CNN classification decisions but also possibly discovers new visual knowledge relevant to medical diagnosis.

papers.title: Improving Interpretability in Medical Imaging Diagnosis using\n Adversarial Training
papers.research_question: Can adversarial training improve the interpretability (specifically, the sharpness and visual coherence of saliency maps) of convolutional neural networks for medical image diagnosis, such as skin cancer detection?
papers.core_contribution: Adversarial training of CNNs on medical images leads to sharper and more visually coherent gradient-based saliency maps, which better highlight diagnostically relevant features like color variation within lesions, and fine-tuning these robust networks can further improve saliency map quality.
papers.conclusion: Adversarial training can improve the interpretability of CNNs in medical imaging by yielding sharper, more visually coherent saliency maps that focus on diagnostically relevant regions, offering a promising direction for building more transparent diagnostic models.
papers.key_findings:
Adversarially trained models produce significantly sharper and more visually coherent gradient-based saliency maps (using Gradient and Integrated Gradients) compared to standard models.
Saliency maps from adversarially trained models highlight regions with significant color variation within skin lesions, a common characteristic of melanoma.
The maximum perturbation size (epsilon) used during adversarial training greatly influences the resulting saliency maps, suggesting a potential image-specific optimal value.
Fine-tuning an adversarially trained (robust) model with a small learning rate further sharpens the saliency maps and reduces noise.
Robustifying the first layers of a CNN to extract robust low-level features, then fine-tuning later layers, can combine the benefits of robust features (for interpretability) and standard features (for higher accuracy).
papers.limitation:
Saliency maps of robust models can highlight image artifacts (e.g., dark regions, hairs) or be noisy.
The choice of the maximum perturbation size (epsilon) during adversarial training significantly affects the saliency maps, and an inappropriate choice can lead to poor explanations.
The study is preliminary and its claims need validation on other types of medical images (e.g., X-rays, MRI scans), datasets, and network architectures.
future_direction: Investigating which layers are important to 'robustify' to obtain visually coherent explanations.
Understanding why saliency methods are brittle to training noise and can capture artifacts.
Generalizing the findings to other medical imaging datasets and network architectures.
papers.abstract:
We investigate the influence of adversarial training on the interpretability
of convolutional neural networks (CNNs), specifically applied to diagnosing
skin cancer. We show that gradient-based saliency maps of adversarially trained
CNNs are significantly sharper and more visually coherent than those of
standardly trained CNNs. Furthermore, we show that adversarially trained
networks highlight regions with significant color variation within the lesion,
a common characteristic of melanoma. We find that fine-tuning a robust network
with a small learning rate further improves saliency maps' sharpness. Lastly,
we provide preliminary work suggesting that robustifying the first layers to
extract robust low-level features leads to visually coherent explanations.

papers.title: Mammo-SAE: Interpreting Breast Cancer Concept Learning with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be used to interpret breast cancer concept learning in a vision-language foundation model, specifically to identify latent neurons associated with clinically relevant concepts and understand the model's decision-making process?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Mammo-SAE, a sparse autoencoder framework for interpreting breast cancer concept learning in the Mammo-CLIP foundation model, demonstrating that it can identify clinically relevant latent neurons and that finetuning improves concept separation and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Mammo-SAE provides a valuable tool for understanding the causal mechanisms within foundation models for medical imaging and opens new avenues for inference-time interventions to improve interpretability and performance in breast cancer detection.
papers.key_findings:
Top-activated class-level latent neurons often align with ground-truth regions of interest, but some neurons respond to confounding background features.
Finetuning Mammo-CLIP leads to larger concept separation in the latent space, improving both interpretability and predictive performance.
SAE-reconstructed features retain most of the original information, with a drop in AUC-ROC of less than 2%.
A small subset of latent neurons (as few as 10) captures most of the task-relevant signal, as shown by intervention experiments.
The model sometimes relies on spurious or task-irrelevant background regions when making predictions, especially in the pretrained variant.
papers.limitation:
Focus exclusively on the final layer of the Mammo-CLIP model, leaving earlier layers unexplored.
Evaluation limited to only two breast cancer-related concepts (mass and suspicious calcification), not extending to other clinically relevant findings.
Analysis confined to Mammo-CLIP; applying the framework to other vision-language models in medical imaging remains for future work.
Visual probing restricted to the top-10 class-level latent neurons per class, which may overlook other relevant neurons.
future_direction: Applying the interpretability framework to other vision-language models in medical imaging, such as MedCLIP or GLoRIA.
Understanding and controlling for background-sensitive neurons to build more robust and interpretable breast cancer detection models.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Interpretability is critical in high-stakes domains such as medical imaging, where understanding model decisions is essential for clinical adoption. In this work, we introduce Sparse Autoencoder (SAE)-based interpretability to breast imaging by analyzing {Mammo-CLIP}, a vision--language foundation model pretrained on large-scale mammogram image--radiology report pairs. We train a patch-level \texttt{Mammo-SAE} on Mammo-CLIP visual features to identify and probe latent neurons associated with clinically relevant breast concepts such as \textit{mass} and \textit{suspicious calcification}. We show that top-activated class-level latent neurons often tend to align with ground-truth regions, and also uncover several confounding factors influencing the model’s decision-making process. Furthermore, we demonstrate that finetuning Mammo-CLIP leads to larger concept separation in the latent space, improving interpretability and predictive performance. Our findings suggest that sparse latent representations offer a powerful lens into the internal behavior of breast foundation models. The code will be released at https://krishnakanthnakka.github.io/MammoSAE/.

papers.title: Expert identification of visual primitives used by CNNs during mammogram classification
papers.research_question: Can we create networks that explain their decision making? We seek to produce relevant and informative descriptions of the predictions made by a CNN in a format familiar to radiologists.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an expert-in-the-loop interpretation method to label the behavior of internal units in CNNs trained for mammogram classification, showing that many units detect visual patterns correlated with meaningful medical phenomena.
papers.conclusion: This exploratory study is an important first step towards interpreting the decisions made by CNNs in classification of diseased tissue, demonstrating that many CNN units identify meaningful medical phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
Many CNN units identify recognizable medical phenomena used by radiologists, showing significant overlap with the BI-RADS lexicon.
Some units had no identified connection with breast cancer, and other units identified entangled events.
Networks trained to recognize cancer end up using many BI-RADS categories even though training labels were only positive/negative for cancer.
Units identify advanced cancers, large benign masses, calcifications, and important associated features such as spiculation, breast density, architectural distortions, and tissue near the nipple.
The network behavior could provide a new computational perspective on the relationship between breast density, tissue characteristics, and cancer risk.
papers.limitation: Some units had no identified connection with breast cancer, and yet other units identified entangled events.
papers.abstract: This work interprets the internal representations of deep neural networks trained for classification of diseased tissue in 2D mammograms. We propose an expert-in-the-loop inter- pretation method to label the behavior of internal units in convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Expert radiologists identify that the visual patterns detected by the units are correlated with meaningful medical phenomena such as mass tissue and calcificated vessels. We demonstrate that several trained CNN models are able to produce explanatory descriptions to support the final classification decisions. We view this as an important first step toward interpreting the internal representations of medical classification CNNs and explaining their predictions.

papers.title: Explaining Chest X-ray Pathology Models using Textual Concepts
papers.research_question: How can we explain black-box medical image classifiers using textual concepts without requiring manually annotated concept datasets?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes CoCoX, a method that leverages a vision-language model's joint embedding space to generate conceptual counterfactual explanations for chest X-ray pathology classifiers without needing annotated concept data.
papers.conclusion: CoCoX provides clinically relevant conceptual explanations for chest X-ray pathology classifiers and can be extended to other medical imaging domains with domain-specific concept banks.
papers.key_findings:
CoCoX generates top concepts that align with clinically relevant features for pathologies like Cardiomegaly, Pleural Effusion, and Atelectasis.
The method achieves high recall for primary clinical findings but lower recall for secondary findings, which are more numerous and include non-visual attributes.
CoCoX generates explanations faster than the baseline method CheXplaining in Style.
The approach works across different classifier architectures (DenseNet121, ResNet34, VLM+Linear).
The concept bank can be easily augmented with new textual concepts without requiring annotated images.
papers.limitation: Concepts such as 'Older patients' in the secondary list for Cardiomegaly and Atelectasis are non-visual attributes and challenging to generate conceptual counterfactuals for.
future_direction: Extending the method to other medical imaging domains (e.g., MRI or CT scans) with tailored concept banks.
Exploring ways to improve concept bank creation.
Exploring standardized metrics like expert consensus scores and counterfactual faithfulness in future iterations.
papers.abstract: Deep learning models have revolutionized medical imaging and diagnostics, yet their opaque nature poses challenges for clinical adoption and trust. Amongst approaches to improve model interpretability, concept-based explanations aim to provide concise and human-understandable explanations of any arbitrary classifier. However, such methods usually require a large amount of manually collected data with concept annotation, which is often scarce in the medical domain. In this paper, we propose Conceptual Counterfactual Explanations for Chest X-ray (CoCoX), which leverages the joint embedding space of an existing vision-language model (VLM) to explain black-box classifier outcomes without the need for annotated datasets. Specifically, we utilize textual concepts derived from chest radiography reports and a pre-trained chest radiography-based VLM to explain three common cardiothoracic pathologies. We demonstrate that the explanations generated by our method are semantically meaningful and faithful to underlying pathologies.

papers.title: Network Dissection: Quantifying Interpretability of Deep Visual\n Representations
papers.research_question: How can interpretability of deep visual representations be quantified, and what factors affect the emergence of interpretable units in CNNs?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework called Network Dissection for quantifying the interpretability of latent representations in CNNs by evaluating the alignment between individual hidden units and a broad set of semantic concepts.
papers.conclusion: Network dissection provides a method to quantify interpretability in CNNs, revealing that interpretability is not an inevitable result of discriminative power and is affected by network architecture, training data, and training techniques.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability is not axis-independent; random rotations of the representation destroy interpretability, indicating it is a property of the learned basis.
Interpretability varies with network architecture and depth, with ResNet showing the highest number of unique concept detectors.
Supervised training on scene-centric data (Places) yields more object detectors than object-centric data (ImageNet), while self-supervised models produce more texture detectors.
Batch normalization significantly decreases interpretability, while dropout removal increases texture detectors but decreases object detectors.
Widening the convolutional layer (increasing units) can increase the number of interpretable concept detectors without significantly harming classification accuracy.
papers.limitation: Network dissection works only as well as the underlying dataset; if a unit matches a human-understandable concept that is absent in Broden, then it will not score well for interpretability.
future_direction: Finding ways to capture the benefits of batch normalization without destroying interpretability.
Expanding Broden to include more kinds of visual concepts.
papers.abstract:
We propose a general framework called Network Dissection for quantifying the
interpretability of latent representations of CNNs by evaluating the alignment
between individual hidden units and a set of semantic concepts. Given any CNN
model, the proposed method draws on a broad data set of visual concepts to
score the semantics of hidden units at each intermediate convolutional layer.
The units with semantics are given labels across a range of objects, parts,
scenes, textures, materials, and colors. We use the proposed method to test the
hypothesis that interpretability of units is equivalent to random linear
combinations of units, then we apply our method to compare the latent
representations of various networks when trained to solve different supervised
and self-supervised training tasks. We further analyze the effect of training
iterations, compare networks trained with different initializations, examine
the impact of network depth and width, and measure the effect of dropout and
batch normalization on the interpretability of deep visual representations. We
demonstrate that the proposed method can shed light on characteristics of CNN
models and training methods that go beyond measurements of their discriminative
power.

papers.title: An X-Ray Is Worth 15 Features: Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretable Radiology Report Generation
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders be used to extract interpretable features from radiology images and generate accurate radiology reports without fine-tuning large vision-language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAE-Rad, a framework that uses sparse autoencoders to decompose latent representations from a pre-trained vision transformer into interpretable features for radiology report generation, eliminating the need for fine-tuning large models.
papers.conclusion: SAEs can enhance multimodal reasoning in healthcare, providing a more interpretable alternative to existing VLMs.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-Rad achieves competitive radiology-specific metrics on the MIMIC-CXR dataset compared to state-of-the-art models while using significantly fewer computational resources.
SAE-Rad learns meaningful visual concepts and generates reports aligning closely with expert interpretations.
The hybrid SAE architecture achieves accurate latent reconstructions with comparable sparsity to state-of-the-art techniques.
SAE-Rad requires fewer edits and has lower significant clinical impact error rates in a radiologist reader study compared to baseline methods.
The framework demonstrates the utility of mechanistic interpretability for downstream tasks in healthcare.
papers.abstract: Radiological services are experiencing unprecedented demand, leading to increased interest in automating radiology report generation. Existing Vision-Language Models (VLMs) suffer from hallucinations, lack interpretability, and require expensive fine-tuning. We introduce SAE-Rad, which uses sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to decompose latent representations from a pre-trained vision transformer into human-interpretable features. Our hybrid architecture combines state-of-the-art SAE advancements, achieving accurate latent reconstructions while maintaining sparsity. Using an off-the-shelf language model, we distil ground-truth reports into radiological descriptions for each SAE feature, which we then compile into a full report for each image, eliminating the need for fine-tuning large models for this task. To the best of our knowledge, SAE-Rad represents the first instance of using mechanistic interpretability techniques explicitly for a downstream multi-modal reasoning task. On the MIMIC-CXR dataset, SAE-Rad achieves competitive radiology-specific metrics compared to state-of-the-art models while using significantly fewer computational resources for training. Qualitative analysis reveals that SAE-Rad learns meaningful visual concepts and generates reports aligning closely with expert interpretations. Our results suggest that SAEs can enhance multimodal reasoning in healthcare, providing a more interpretable alternative to existing VLMs.

papers.title: Interpretability Beyond Feature Attribution: Quantitative Testing with\n Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV)
papers.research_question: How can we interpret neural networks using human-defined concepts and quantify the sensitivity of predictions to these concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) to represent human-friendly concepts in a model's activation space, and a method (TCAV) to quantify the importance of these concepts to model predictions using directional derivatives.
papers.conclusion: TCAV provides a human-friendly linear interpretation of neural networks, allowing analysts to quantify the importance of user-defined concepts to model predictions, and has been shown to be a useful technique in various applications including bias detection and medical image analysis.
papers.key_findings:
CAVs align with intended concepts, validated by sorting images and activation maximization (deep dream).
TCAV can reveal biases in models, such as gender and race biases in image classifiers.
TCAV quantifies the importance of specific concepts to model classes (e.g., stripes for zebras, red for fire engines).
TCAV can help interpret model errors in medical applications, such as diabetic retinopathy grading.
In a controlled experiment, TCAV more accurately communicated concept importance to humans compared to saliency maps.
future_direction: Applying TCAV to other types of data (audio, video, sequences).
Using TCAV to identify adversarial examples.
Automatically identifying concepts.
papers.abstract:
The interpretation of deep learning models is a challenge due to their size,
complexity, and often opaque internal state. In addition, many systems, such as
image classifiers, operate on low-level features rather than high-level
concepts. To address these challenges, we introduce Concept Activation Vectors
(CAVs), which provide an interpretation of a neural net's internal state in
terms of human-friendly concepts. The key idea is to view the high-dimensional
internal state of a neural net as an aid, not an obstacle. We show how to use
CAVs as part of a technique, Testing with CAVs (TCAV), that uses directional
derivatives to quantify the degree to which a user-defined concept is important
to a classification result--for example, how sensitive a prediction of "zebra"
is to the presence of stripes. Using the domain of image classification as a
testing ground, we describe how CAVs may be used to explore hypotheses and
generate insights for a standard image classification network as well as a
medical application.

papers.title: MATEX: Multi-scale Attention and Text-guided Explainability of Medical Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How can interpretability in medical vision-language models be improved by incorporating anatomically informed spatial reasoning and text guidance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MATEX, a framework that enhances interpretability in medical VLMs by combining multi-scale attention rollout, text-guided spatial priors, and layer consistency for precise and clinically meaningful attribution maps.
papers.conclusion: MATEX produces high-fidelity, anatomically grounded explanations for CLIP-based models, outperforming existing methods in spatial precision and diagnostic relevance.
papers.key_findings:
MATEX achieves the best confidence increase (47.55%) and lowest drop (0.51%) in image modality, outperforming baselines like M2IB.
MATEX ranks second in image ROAR+ (37.9%) just below M2IB (38.7%) but ahead of other methods.
In text-based evaluations, MATEX maintains strong performance with ROAR+ of 16.98%, low drop of 1.91%, and high gain of 50.07%.
Qualitatively, MATEX provides sharper localization and better anatomical alignment than M2IB, with reduced noise activation.
MATEX captures multi-region pathologies without spatial drift and maintains clear boundaries around relevant findings.
papers.limitation:
MATEX adds ~40% overhead from multi-layer backpropagation.
Its priors are currently specific to chest X-rays and require adaptation for other modalities.
Attribution quality is sensitive to parameter tuning and the reliability of CLIP attention.
papers.abstract: We introduce MATEX (Multi-scale Attention and Text-guided Explainability), a novel framework that advances interpretability in medical vision-language models by incorporating anatomically informed spatial reasoning. MATEX synergistically combines multi-layer attention rollout, text-guided spatial priors, and layer consistency analysis to produce precise, stable, and clinically meaningful gradient attribution maps. By addressing key limitations of prior methods, such as spatial imprecision, lack of anatomical grounding, and limited attention granularity, MATEX enables more faithful and interpretable model explanations. Evaluated on the MS-CXR dataset, MATEX outperforms the state-of-the-art M2IB approach in both spatial precision and alignment with expert-annotated findings. These results highlight MATEX's potential to enhance trust and transparency in radiological AI applications.

papers.title: On Interpretability of CNNs for Multimodal Medical Image Segmentation
papers.research_question: How to extend the Multilayer Convolutional Sparse Coding (ML-CSC) framework for multimodal medical image segmentation to improve interpretability and performance?
papers.core_contribution: Extends the ML-CSC framework to multimodal medical image segmentation, proposing a merged joint feature extraction model that improves segmentation performance while maintaining interpretability through sparse coding theory.
papers.conclusion: The proposed multimodal ML-CSC model and merged joint feature extraction approach improve segmentation performance on the BraTS dataset and offer interpretability through sparse coding theory and algorithm unrolling.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed merged JF-ML-ISTA CNN model achieves higher Dice scores for all tumor classes compared to the previous JF-ML-ISTA model.
The learned thresholds and step sizes are mostly consistent with sparse coding theory, but some thresholds become negative during end-to-end training, indicating inconsistencies.
The model can decompose MRI modalities into segmentation class-specific components, but decomposition quality varies and can be unsatisfactory for some samples.
papers.limitation: The end-to-end supervised training procedure may lead to inconsistent sparse coding parameters, such as negative thresholds, and unsatisfactory decomposition for some samples.
future_direction: Theoretical analysis and convergence guarantees for the proposed sparse coding algorithms.
papers.abstract: Despite their huge potential, deep learning-based models are still not trustful enough to warrant their adoption in clinical practice. The research on the interpretability and explainability of deep learning is currently attracting huge attention. Multilayer Convolutional Sparse Coding (ML-CSC) data model, provides a model-based explanation of convolutional neural networks (CNNs). In this article, we extend the ML-CSC framework towards multimodal data for medical image segmentation, and propose a merged joint feature extraction ML-CSC model. This work generalizes and improves upon our previous model, by deriving a more elegant approach that merges feature extraction and convolutional sparse coding in a unified framework. A segmentation study on a multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) dataset confirms the effectiveness of the proposed approach. We also supply an interpretability study regarding the involved model parameters.

papers.title: CXR-LanIC: Language-Grounded Interpretable Classifier for Chest X-Ray Diagnosis
papers.research_question: How to make chest X-ray diagnosis models interpretable for clinical adoption by providing transparent, verifiable explanations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CXR-LanIC, a framework for interpretable chest X-ray diagnosis through task-aligned pattern discovery using transcoder-based sparse autoencoders on a BiomedCLIP classifier.
papers.conclusion: CXR-LanIC addresses the black-box problem in medical AI by providing interpretable patterns, achieving competitive accuracy, and supporting safer clinical deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Discovers approximately 5,000 monosemantic visual patterns spanning clinical categories through transcoder ensembles.
Achieves competitive diagnostic accuracy on five key findings while providing interpretable explanations.
Demonstrates that task-aligned pattern discovery from classifier embeddings yields clinically relevant features.
papers.limitation: Patterns currently lack natural language descriptions, requiring future LMM-based annotation.
future_direction: Complete LMM-based annotation of patterns to generate natural language explanations.
Validate explanation quality through LMM verification and radiologist evaluation.
papers.abstract: Deep learning models have achieved remarkable accuracy in chest X-ray diagnosis, yet their widespread clinical adoption remains limited by the black-box nature of their predictions. Clinicians require transparent, verifiable explanations to trust automated diagnoses and identify potential failure modes. We introduce CXR-LanIC (Language-Grounded Interpretable Classifier for Chest X-rays), a novel framework that addresses this interpretability challenge through task-aligned pattern discovery. Our approach trains transcoder-based sparse autoencoders on a BiomedCLIP diagnostic classifier to decompose medical image representations into interpretable visual patterns. By training an ensemble of 100 transcoders on multimodal embeddings from the MIMIC-CXR dataset, we discover approximately 5,000 monosemantic patterns spanning cardiac, pulmonary, pleural, structural, device, and artifact categories. Each pattern exhibits consistent activation behavior across images sharing specific radiological features, enabling transparent attribution where predictions decompose into 20-50 interpretable patterns with verifiable activation galleries. CXR-LanIC achieves competitive diagnostic accuracy on five key findings while providing the foundation for natural language explanations through planned large multimodal model annotation. Our key innovation lies in extracting interpretable features from a classifier trained on specific diagnostic objectives rather than general-purpose embeddings, ensuring discovered patterns are directly relevant to clinical decision-making, demonstrating that medical AI systems can be both accurate and interpretable, supporting safer clinical deployment through transparent, clinically grounded explanations.

papers.title: Mammo-CLIP Dissect: A Framework for Analysing Mammography Concepts in Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: The paper investigates: (1) how concept learning differs between DL vision models trained on general image datasets versus mammography-specific datasets; (2) how fine-tuning for downstream mammography tasks affects concept specialisation; and (3) which mammography-relevant concepts remain under-represented.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Mammo-CLIP Dissect, a concept-based explainability framework for dissecting deep learning vision models in mammography, and uses it to analyze how domain-specific training and fine-tuning affect concept learning.
papers.conclusion: Mammo-CLIP Dissect provides concept-level insights into how CNNs capture mammography-specific knowledge, moving beyond pixel-level interpretability toward an understanding aligned with radiologists' reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Models trained on mammography data capture more clinically relevant concepts and align more closely with radiologists' workflows.
Fine-tuning for task-specific classification enhances capture of certain concept categories (e.g., benign calcifications) but reduces coverage of others (e.g., density-related features).
Neurons show selective responsiveness to distinct mammography features such as implants and calcifications.
Mammo-CLIP Dissect reveals that domain-specific training leads to stronger and more stable alignment with mammography concepts.
The framework identifies under-represented concepts, including architectural distortion and modality-inappropriate terms.
papers.limitation: The concept set includes overlaps and modality-inappropriate concepts (e.g., from ultrasound or MRI) which may confound evaluation.
future_direction: Refining concept sets to reduce ambiguity.
Addressing subtle underrepresented findings.
Developing fine-tuning strategies that preserve general conceptual breadth while enhancing task-relevant features.
papers.abstract: Understanding what deep learning (DL) models learn is essential for the safe deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) in clinical settings. While previous work has focused on pixel-based explainability methods, less attention has been paid to the textual concepts learned by these models, which may better reflect the reasoning used by clinicians. We introduce Mammo-CLIP Dissect, the first concept-based explainability framework for systematically dissecting DL vision models trained for mammography. Leveraging a mammography-specific vision-language model (Mammo-CLIP) as a "dissector," our approach labels neurons at specified layers with human-interpretable textual concepts and quantifies their alignment to domain knowledge. Using Mammo-CLIP Dissect, we investigate three key questions: (1) how concept learning differs between DL vision models trained on general image datasets versus mammography-specific datasets; (2) how fine-tuning for downstream mammography tasks affects concept specialisation; and (3) which mammography-relevant concepts remain underrepresented. We show that models trained on mammography data capture more clinically relevant concepts and align more closely with radiologists' workflows than models not trained on mammography data. Fine-tuning for task-specific classification enhances the capture of certain concept categories (e.g., benign calcifications) but can reduce coverage of others (e.g., density-related features), indicating a trade-off between specialisation and generalisation. Our findings show that Mammo-CLIP Dissect provides insights into how convolutional neural networks (CNNs) capture mammography-specific knowledge. By comparing models across training data and fine-tuning regimes, we reveal how domain-specific training and task-specific adaptation shape concept learning. Code and concept set are available: https://github.com/Suaiba/Mammo-CLIP-Dissect.

papers.title: Pre-processing and Compression: Understanding Hidden Representation Refinement Across Imaging Domains via Intrinsic Dimension
papers.research_question: How does the intrinsic dimension (ID) of a neural network's hidden representations change through its layers, and how does this behavior differ between natural and medical image domains?
papers.core_contribution: The progression of intrinsic dimension through network layers differs between natural and medical image models, with medical image models peaking earlier, and there is a strong correlation between the peak representation ID and the ID of the input data.
papers.conclusion: There are notable discrepancies in network behavior between natural and medical imaging domains regarding hidden representation information content, and the information content of a model's learned representations is guided by that of its training data.
papers.key_findings:
The intrinsic dimension of hidden representations typically first increases then decreases through network depth.
The peak of intrinsic dimension occurs earlier in medical image models (average relative depth 0.35) compared to natural image models (average relative depth 0.57).
There is a strong correlation (Pearson r=0.89) between the peak representation intrinsic dimension (dmax_repr) and the intrinsic dimension of the input data (ddata).
future_direction: Further probing the proposed connections between learned feature 'abstractness' and peak representation ID, such as by seeing if training for classification tasks with increasingly abstract super-classes results in an increased peak ID depth.
Attempting to disentangle the effects of dataset ID and feature 'abstractness' on peak representation ID using experiments that can control the precise ID of training data.
papers.abstract: In recent years, there has been interest in how geometric properties such as intrinsic dimension (ID) of a neural network's hidden representations change through its layers, and how such properties are predictive of important model behavior such as generalization ability. However, evidence has begun to emerge that such behavior can change significantly depending on the domain of the network's training data, such as natural versus medical images. Here, we further this inquiry by exploring how the ID of a network's learned representations changes through its layers, in essence, characterizing how the network successively refines the information content of input data to be used for predictions. Analyzing eleven natural and medical image datasets across six network architectures, we find that how ID changes through the network differs noticeably between natural and medical image models. Specifically, medical image models peak in representation ID earlier in the network, implying a difference in the image features and their abstractness that are typically used for downstream tasks in these domains. Additionally, we discover a strong correlation of this peak representation ID with the ID of the data in its input space, implying that the intrinsic information content of a model's learned representations is guided by that of the data it was trained on. Overall, our findings emphasize notable discrepancies in network behavior between natural and non-natural imaging domains regarding hidden representation information content, and provide further insights into how a network's learned features are shaped by its training data.

papers.title: Feature visualization for convolutional neural network models trained on neuroimaging data
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates, for the first time, the application of feature visualization to CNNs trained on neuroimaging data, showing that it can reveal learned concepts such as lesion shapes and hierarchical features similar to natural image CNNs, with implications for model interpretability and validation.
papers.conclusion: Feature visualization is a promising method for interpreting CNNs in neuroimaging, capable of revealing learned patterns and aiding in model validation, though interpretability for abstract features like sex classification remains limited.
papers.key_findings:
Lower-level patterns in neuroimaging CNNs are similar to those found in natural image studies, supporting the idea of transfer learning across domains.
Feature visualization reveals the shapes of artificial lesions in higher layers, with square lesions showing sharp edges and Gaussian lesions showing smoother patterns.
Abstract patterns for the sex classification task remain difficult to interpret, indicating challenges for complex real-world tasks.
Different regularization strategies (e.g., jitter, rotation, total variation denoising) affect the quality and interpretability of generated images.
Generated images can serve as a validation tool, with uniform distributions potentially indicating model overparameterization.
papers.limitation:
Abstract features in the sex classification task are hard to interpret.
Generated images with almost uniform distributions are a potential sign of overparameterization of the model.
future_direction: Training on larger data sets of clinical tasks.
Assessment of further regularization methods.
Involving scenarios where neuropathological indicators can be clearly described, such as the hummingbird sign in progressive supranuclear palsy.
papers.abstract: A major prerequisite for the application of machine learning models in clinical decision making is trust and interpretability. Current explainability studies in the neuroimaging community have mostly focused on explaining individual decisions of trained models, e.g. obtained by a convolutional neural network (CNN). Using attribution methods such as layer-wise relevance propagation or SHAP heatmaps can be created that highlight which regions of an input are more relevant for the decision than others. While this allows the detection of potential data set biases and can be used as a guide for a human expert, it does not allow an understanding of the underlying principles the model has learned. In this study, we instead show, to the best of our knowledge, for the first time results using feature visualization of neuroimaging CNNs. Particularly, we have trained CNNs for different tasks including sex classification and artificial lesion classification based on structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data. We have then iteratively generated images that maximally activate specific neurons, in order to visualize the patterns they respond to. To improve the visualizations we compared several regularization strategies. The resulting images reveal the learned concepts of the artificial lesions, including their shapes, but remain hard to interpret for abstract features in the sex classification task.

papers.title: Pixel Ablation-CAM: A New Paradigm in CNN Interpretability for Feature Map Visual Explanations
papers.research_question: How can pixel-wise ablation provide finer-grained visual explanations for CNN decisions compared to channel-wise ablation methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Pixel Ablation-CAM, a pixel-wise ablation method that provides more precise and detailed visual explanations for CNN decisions by treating each pixel in the final convolutional layer as a 1D vector, improving interpretability and localization over gradient-based and channel-wise ablation methods.
papers.conclusion: Pixel Ablation-CAM is a new pixel-wise ablation technique that enhances the interpretability of CNN-based models by providing more precise and detailed visual explanations, effectively addressing the limitations of existing gradient-based and channel-wise ablation methods.
papers.key_findings:
Pixel Ablation-CAM produces more precise and targeted explanation maps compared to Grad-CAM, Ablation-CAM, and Ablation-CAM++.
The method achieves lower average drop in confidence and activation scores and higher percent increase in these scores, indicating better localization and explanatory power.
In human evaluations, Pixel Ablation-CAM explanations were preferred over Grad-CAM and Ablation-CAM, indicating higher human interpretability and trust.
Pixel Ablation-CAM can distinguish between models, generating more reliable visualizations for better-performing models like ResNet-50 compared to VGG-16.
The method addresses limitations of gradient saturation in gradient-based methods and spatial information loss in channel-wise ablation by operating at the pixel level.
papers.limitation: The method requires n×m forward passes per image for a feature map of size n×m, leading to computational complexity.
future_direction: Refining the computational efficacy of the proposed methodology.
Investigating its possible integration in increasingly intricate and varied CNN structures and assignments.
papers.abstract: Many cutting-edge computer vision systems now rely heavily on convolutional neural networks, or CNNs. However, conventional interpretation techniques frequently concentrate on 2D feature maps, ignoring the intricate contributions of individual pixels. This work aims to produce “visual explanations” that improve the explainability and transparency of decisions made by various CNN-based algorithms. We provide Pixel Ablation-CAM, a new method that builds on the ideas of Ablation-CAM by using pixel-wise ablation, which enables a finer-grained comprehension of model choices. With this method, activation maps are reinterpreted as arrays of one-dimensional vectors that represent channel-specific pixel activations. We show that, as compared to other approaches such as Grad-CAM, Pixel Ablation-CAM offers better resolution and accuracy in class-discriminative localisation maps by methodically ablating these vectors and monitoring changes in class activation scores. Our extensive testing demonstrates that Pixel Ablation-CAM improves model trust and interpretability, providing fresh perspectives on CNN behavior and propelling the field of explainable AI forward.

papers.title: Clinical Interpretability of Deep Learning Segmentation Through Shapley-Derived Agreement and Uncertainty Metrics
papers.research_question: How can contrast-level Shapley values provide clinically interpretable explanations for deep learning segmentation models in medical imaging?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Shapley-derived agreement and uncertainty metrics to provide clinically interpretable explanations for deep learning segmentation models, correlating with performance.
papers.conclusion: Shapley-derived explanations can serve as indicators of automated segmentation performance, bridging the gap between opaque model reasoning and clinically-aligned explanations.
papers.key_findings:
Subjects with higher Dice scores show significantly greater agreement between model Shapley rankings and clinical rankings.
Increased Shapley ranking variance correlates with decreased Dice score performance across all models.
U-Net and Seg-Resnet models show stronger negative correlations between variance and performance compared to Swin-UNETR and UNETR.
Agreement metrics can indicate model reliability by aligning with clinical protocols.
Uncertainty metrics derived from Shapley ranking variance help predict model performance degradation.
papers.limitation: lack of an agreement consensus sourced from radiologists
future_direction: use of Monte Carlo dropout to quantify prediction uncertainty across multiple stochastic forward passes
papers.abstract: Segmentation is the identification of anatomical regions of interest, such as organs, tissue, and lesions, serving as a fundamental task in computer-aided diagnosis in medical imaging. Although deep learning models have achieved remarkable performance in medical image segmentation, the need for explainability remains critical for ensuring their acceptance and integration in clinical practice, despite the growing research attention in this area. Our approach explored the use of contrast-level Shapley values, a systematic perturbation of model inputs to assess feature importance. While other studies have investigated gradient-based techniques through identifying influential regions in imaging inputs, Shapley values offer a broader, clinically aligned approach, explaining how model performance is fairly attributed to certain imaging contrasts over others. Using the BraTS 2024 dataset, we generated rankings for Shapley values for four MRI contrasts across four model architectures. Two metrics were proposed from the Shapley ranking: agreement between model and ``clinician" imaging ranking, and uncertainty quantified through Shapley ranking variance across cross-validation folds. Higher-performing cases (Dice \textgreater0.6) showed significantly greater agreement with clinical rankings. Increased Shapley ranking variance correlated with decreased performance (U-Net: $r=-0.581$). These metrics provide clinically interpretable proxies for model reliability, helping clinicians better understand state-of-the-art segmentation models.

papers.title: MedSAE: Dissecting MedCLIP Representations with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be used to improve interpretability of medical vision-language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces Medical Sparse Autoencoders (MedSAEs) to extract interpretable, monosemantic features from MedCLIP embeddings, advancing mechanistic interpretability in medical vision.
papers.conclusion: This work presents a first step toward mechanistic interpretability in medical vision-language models, highlighting sparse autoencoders as a promising direction for building transparent, robust, and trustworthy medical AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
MedSAE neurons achieve lower entropy (2.25) than raw MedCLIP features (2.38), indicating higher monosemanticity.
21 medically meaningful features are identified with MedGEMMA-based automated naming, with detection accuracy above 70%.
MedSAE features show stronger alignment with clinical concepts compared to raw embeddings.
papers.limitation:
presence of inactive neurons and the need for more expressive SAE architectures
computational cost and dataset sensitivity of automated naming
limited validation across modalities and institutions
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence in healthcare requires models that are accurate and interpretable. We advance mechanistic interpretability in medical vision by applying Medical Sparse Autoencoders (MedSAEs) to the latent space of MedCLIP, a vision-language model trained on chest radiographs and reports. To quantify interpretability, we propose an evaluation framework that combines correlation metrics, entropy analyzes, and automated neuron naming via the MedGEMMA foundation model. Experiments on the CheXpert dataset show that MedSAE neurons achieve higher monosemanticity and interpretability than raw MedCLIP features. Our findings bridge high-performing medical AI and transparency, offering a scalable step toward clinically reliable representations.

papers.title: Localization-Guided Supervision for Robust Medical Image Classification by Vision Transformers
papers.research_question: How can explanation supervision (using foreground masks) be used to improve the generalization and robustness of Vision Transformers for medical image classification?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework (LGM-ViT) that uses explanation supervision (foreground masks) to regularize attribution maps during training of Vision Transformer models, improving performance and robustness in medical image classification.
papers.conclusion: LGM-ViT enhances the performance and robustness of Vision Transformers in medical image classification, offering improved interpretability and reliability for healthcare applications.
papers.key_findings:
LGM-ViT outperforms baseline and competing methods on two medical imaging datasets (BraTS2020 and LiTS17) across multiple metrics.
The framework encourages the model to focus on relevant image regions, leading to more robust predictions.
The proposed EAFEM method for generating attribution maps is effective.
Localization supervision can improve performance even when applied to a limited subset of the training data.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to binary classification within the medical domain.
future_direction: Extend validation to multiclass classification and apply the method to additional datasets from various domains.
Utilize the EAFEM method for spatial localization in applications beyond classification.
papers.abstract: Abstract A major challenge in developing data-driven algorithms for medical imaging is the limited size of available datasets. Furthermore, these datasets often suffer from inter-site heterogeneity caused by the use of different scanners and scanning protocols. These factors may contribute to overfitting, which undermines the generalization ability and robustness of deep learning classification models in the medical domain, leading to inadequate performance in real-world applications. To address these challenges and mitigate overfitting, we propose a framework which incorporates explanation supervision during training of Vision Transformer (ViT) models for image classification. Our approach leverages foreground masks of the class object during training to regularize attribution maps extracted from ViT, encouraging the model to focus on relevant image regions and make predictions based on pertinent features. We introduce a new method for generating explanatory attribution maps from ViT-based models and construct a dual-loss function that combines a conventional classification loss with a term that regularizes attribution maps. Our approach demonstrates superior performance over existing methods on two challenging medical imaging datasets, highlighting its effectiveness in the medical domain and its potential for application in other fields. Source code is available at: https://github.com/sagibe/LGMViT .

papers.title: A Comprehensive Review of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) in Computer Vision
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ImageNet, a large-scale, clean, and diverse image database organized according to the WordNet hierarchy, providing a valuable resource for computer vision research.
papers.conclusion: ImageNet, with its scale, accuracy, diversity, and hierarchical structure, offers unparalleled opportunities for researchers in computer vision and beyond, and is expected to become a central resource for vision-related research.
papers.key_findings:
ImageNet is significantly larger, more diverse, and more accurate than existing image datasets like TinyImage, ESP, Caltech101, and LabelMe.
The construction method using Amazon Mechanical Turk with a confidence-based voting scheme achieves an average labeling precision of 99.7% across different tree depths.
Exploiting the hierarchical structure of ImageNet with a simple tree-max classifier improves image classification performance compared to independent classifiers.
Using clean, full-resolution images from ImageNet with advanced feature representations (e.g., NBNN) leads to better object recognition performance compared to using noisy, low-resolution images.
ImageNet enables object localization and reveals intra-category diversity through clustering, showing variations in viewpoints and poses.
papers.limitation:
ImageNet currently does not provide segmentation annotations.
About 20% of synsets have very few images due to lack of web images or difficulty in illustration.
future_direction: Complete ImageNet to cover approximately 50,000 synsets with 50 million images.
Extend ImageNet to include more information such as localization, segmentation, cross-synset referencing, and expert annotation.
Use ImageNet as a training resource, benchmark dataset, and for introducing new semantic relations for visual modeling.
papers.abstract: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) is increasingly important in computer vision, aiming to connect complex model outputs with human understanding. This review provides a focused comparative analysis of representative XAI methods in four main categories, attribution-based, activation-based, perturbation-based, and transformer-based approaches, selected from a broader literature landscape. Attribution-based methods like Grad-CAM highlight key input regions using gradients and feature activation. Activation-based methods analyze the responses of internal neurons or feature maps to identify which parts of the input activate specific layers or units, helping to reveal hierarchical feature representations. Perturbation-based techniques, such as RISE, assess feature importance through input modifications without accessing internal model details. Transformer-based methods, which use self-attention, offer global interpretability by tracing information flow across layers. We evaluate these methods using metrics such as faithfulness, localization accuracy, efficiency, and overlap with medical annotations. We also propose a hierarchical taxonomy to classify these methods, reflecting the diversity of XAI techniques. Results show that RISE has the highest faithfulness but is computationally expensive, limiting its use in real-time scenarios. Transformer-based methods perform well in medical imaging, with high IoU scores, though interpreting attention maps requires care. These findings emphasize the need for context-aware evaluation and hybrid XAI methods balancing interpretability and efficiency. The review ends by discussing ethical and practical challenges, stressing the need for standard benchmarks and domain-specific tuning.

papers.title: Weight Space Correlation Analysis: Quantifying Feature Utilization in Deep Learning Models
papers.research_question: Does a deep learning model actively utilize encoded confounding metadata (e.g., scanner model) for its final prediction, or is it merely present in the embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Weight Space Correlation (WSC) analysis, an interpretable method to quantify feature utilization by measuring alignment between classification heads of primary and auxiliary tasks, enabling detection of shortcut learning.
papers.conclusion: Weight Space Correlation analysis is a simple, interpretable method that moves beyond identifying confounding information to quantifying its utilization. Applied to SA-SonoNet, it confirms the model uses clinically relevant features and not spurious correlations, enhancing trustworthiness.
papers.key_findings:
WSC analysis successfully detects artificially induced shortcut learning in controlled experiments.
Applied to SA-SonoNet for sPTB prediction, WSC shows the model's decision boundary aligns with clinically relevant factors (e.g., cervical length) but is decoupled from irrelevant acquisition factors (e.g., scanner).
Metadata information is often encoded in embeddings but not necessarily utilized by the primary classifier.
WSC provides a tool for verifying model trustworthiness by inspecting whether it uses features unrelated to the genuine clinical signal.
The method is validated on both balanced and biased datasets, showing increased correlation when shortcuts are present.
papers.limitation:
Assumes a linear relationship between the embedding space and class predictions.
May not capture non-linear combinations of multiple confounding factors.
Does not prove the direction of the shortcut, only that feature utilization is coupled.
Cannot distinguish performance drops due to data quality or feature shift from shortcut learning.
future_direction: Extend WSC analysis to higher-order interactions between multiple metadata dimensions.
papers.abstract: Deep learning models in medical imaging are susceptible to shortcut learning, relying on confounding metadata (e.g., scanner model) that is often encoded in image embeddings. The crucial question is whether the model actively utilizes this encoded information for its final prediction. We introduce Weight Space Correlation Analysis, an interpretable methodology that quantifies feature utilization by measuring the alignment between the classification heads of a primary clinical task and auxiliary metadata tasks. We first validate our method by successfully detecting artificially induced shortcut learning. We then apply it to probe the feature utilization of an SA-SonoNet model trained for Spontaneous Preterm Birth (sPTB) prediction. Our analysis confirmed that while the embeddings contain substantial metadata, the sPTB classifier's weight vectors were highly correlated with clinically relevant factors (e.g., birth weight) but decoupled from clinically irrelevant acquisition factors (e.g. scanner). Our methodology provides a tool to verify model trustworthiness, demonstrating that, in the absence of induced bias, the clinical model selectively utilizes features related to the genuine clinical signal.

papers.title: Visual Interpretable and Explainable Deep Learning Models for Brain Tumor MRI and COVID-19 Chest X-ray Images
papers.research_question: What do deep learning models learn in medical images? The paper evaluates attribution methods for illuminating how deep neural networks analyze medical images.
papers.core_contribution: The paper evaluates adaptive path-based gradient integration attribution methods (Guided Integrated Gradients and XRAI) on CNN models for medical image analysis, demonstrating their ability to highlight salient features and improve model transparency for domain experts.
papers.conclusion: Different input attribution methods have varying degrees of explainability. A robust representation learner and the right attribution approach are crucial for obtaining interpretable saliency maps from deep CNNs in medical image analysis, which can help build trust for clinical adoption.
papers.key_findings:
DenseNet121 achieved the best test performance (98.10% accuracy) on the brain tumor MRI dataset, while InceptionResNetV2 performed best on the COVID-19 chest X-ray dataset (89.0% accuracy).
The XRAI attribution method provided the most interpretable saliency maps, highlighting regions of interest that corresponded well with expert tumor segmentations in the MRI dataset.
Vanilla Gradient and Guided Integrated Gradient methods produced noisier and less stable saliency maps compared to XRAI.
The choice of baseline (e.g., zero pixels) significantly affects the resulting saliency maps from gradient-based attribution methods.
Combining multiple attribution methods (e.g., XRAI and Blur IG) can improve model interpretability for domain experts by highlighting important features.
papers.limitation:
The COVID-19 chest X-ray dataset lacks ground truth segmentation masks, making it difficult to evaluate attribution maps against expert annotations.
CNNs have frequency, texture, and shape biases that differ from human visual processing, which may affect the interpretability of saliency maps.
future_direction: Research into volumetric medical imaging data
Quantification of explainability of visual attribution methods
Developing benchmarks for visual attribution methods
papers.abstract: Deep learning shows promise for medical image analysis but lacks interpretability, hindering adoption in healthcare. Attribution techniques that explain model reasoning may increase trust in deep learning among clinical stakeholders. This paper aimed to evaluate attribution methods for illuminating how deep neural networks analyze medical images. Using adaptive path-based gradient integration, we attributed predictions from brain tumor MRI and COVID-19 chest X-ray datasets made by recent deep convolutional neural network models. The technique highlighted possible biomarkers, exposed model biases, and offered insights into the links between input and prediction. Our analysis demonstrates the method's ability to elucidate model reasoning on these datasets. The resulting attributions show promise for improving deep learning transparency for domain experts by revealing the rationale behind predictions. This study advances model interpretability to increase trust in deep learning among healthcare stakeholders.

papers.title: What do neural networks learn in image classification? A frequency shortcut perspective
papers.research_question: What do neural networks learn in image classification from a frequency perspective, and how do frequency shortcuts based on data characteristics affect their learning and generalization?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks in image classification learn frequency shortcuts—specific frequency sets that simplify the objective—which can be texture- or shape-based depending on data characteristics, and these shortcuts impair generalization on out-of-distribution data.
papers.conclusion: Frequency shortcuts are prevalent in neural networks for image classification, driven by data characteristics and simplicity bias, and future research should focus on developing effective training schemes to mitigate this shortcut learning.
papers.key_findings:
NNs tend to learn simple solutions first during training, depending on the most distinctive frequency characteristics in the data, which can be low- or high-frequencies.
Frequency shortcuts are data-dependent and can be texture-based or shape-based, corresponding to specific frequency subsets that NNs exploit for classification.
Frequency shortcuts can be transferred across datasets and models, and their presence in OOD test sets can create an illusion of improved generalization.
Larger model capacity (e.g., ResNet50, ViT-B) and common data augmentation techniques (AutoAugment, AugMix, SIN) cannot fully avoid frequency shortcut learning.
Frequency shortcuts may prevent NNs from learning meaningful semantics, such as shape information, leading to poor generalization on similar-shaped objects with different textures.
future_direction: Focus on effective training schemes mitigating frequency shortcut learning.
Explore novel data augmentation strategies that explicitly target shortcut mitigation, e.g., leveraging dominant frequency maps.
papers.abstract: Frequency analysis is useful for understanding the mechanisms of representation learning in neural networks (NNs). Most research in this area focuses on the learning dynamics of NNs for regression tasks, while little for classification. This study empirically investigates the latter and expands the understanding of frequency shortcuts. First, we perform experiments on synthetic datasets, designed to have a bias in different frequency bands. Our results demonstrate that NNs tend to find simple solutions for classification, and what they learn first during training depends on the most distinctive frequency characteristics, which can be either low- or high-frequencies. Second, we confirm this phenomenon on natural images. We propose a metric to measure class-wise frequency characteristics and a method to identify frequency shortcuts. The results show that frequency shortcuts can be texture-based or shape-based, depending on what best simplifies the objective. Third, we validate the transferability of frequency shortcuts on out-of-distribution (OOD) test sets. Our results suggest that frequency shortcuts can be transferred across datasets and cannot be fully avoided by larger model capacity and data augmentation. We recommend that future research should focus on effective training schemes mitigating frequency shortcut learning.

papers.title: Leveraging CAM Algorithms for Explaining Medical Semantic Segmentation
papers.research_question: How can we improve the explainability of CNNs for semantic segmentation tasks, especially in medical imaging, by transferring a classification-based CAM method (HiRes CAM) to segmentation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes Seg-HiRes-Grad CAM, an extension of Seg-Grad CAM by combining it with HiRes CAM, to provide more accurate and explainable heatmaps for semantic segmentation, especially in medical imaging.
papers.conclusion: Seg-HiRes-Grad CAM provides more accurate and explainable results than Seg-Grad CAM, especially for medical images, by transferring the HiRes CAM approach to segmentation tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Seg-HiRes-Grad CAM highlights salient regions more precisely than Seg-Grad CAM, especially for medical images.
Seg-HiRes-Grad CAM avoids highlighting irrelevant regions (e.g., sky, trees) that Seg-Grad CAM sometimes includes.
The method is particularly effective for segmentations that are close together, such as teeth in dental images.
The success of the method depends on the input image resolution and the quality of the segmentation.
papers.limitation:
The runtime of segmentation-based CAM algorithms is higher than classification-based ones due to pixel-level computations.
The method fails for minimal image resolutions because too much detail is lost in the feature maps.
The CAM visualization depends on the segmentation result; false positives or negatives lead to less explainable results.
future_direction: Further transfers of classification-based CAM methods to segmentation tasks.
Using quantitative evaluation methods such as Remove and Retrain (ROAR) for enhanced comparisons.
papers.abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) achieve prevailing results in segmentation tasks nowadays and represent the state-of-the-art for image-based analysis. However, the under- standing of the accurate decision-making process of a CNN is rather unknown. The research area of explainable artificial intelligence (xAI) primarily revolves around understanding and interpreting this black-box behavior. One way of interpreting a CNN is the use of class ac- tivation maps (CAMs) that represent heatmaps to indicate the importance of image areas for the prediction of the CNN. For classification tasks, a variety of CAM algorithms exist. But for segmentation tasks, only one CAM algorithm for the interpretation of the output of a CNN exist. We propose a transfer between existing classification- and segmentation- based methods for more detailed, explainable, and consistent results which show salient pixels in semantic segmentation tasks. The resulting Seg-HiRes-Grad CAM is an exten- sion of the segmentation-based Seg-Grad CAM with the transfer to the classification-based HiRes CAM. Our method improves the previously-mentioned existing segmentation-based method by adjusting it to recently published classification-based methods. Especially for medical image segmentation, this transfer solves existing explainability disadvantages. The code is available at <a href='https://github.com/TillmannRheude/SegHiResGrad_CAM'>https://github.com/TillmannRheude/SegHiResGrad_CAM</a>

papers.title: Have We Learned to Explain?: How Interpretability Methods Can Learn to Encode Predictions in their Interpretations
papers.research_question: How do joint amortized explanation methods (JAMs) learn to encode predictions within their interpretations, and how can this issue be addressed?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REAL-X, an amortized explanation method that avoids encoding predictions in interpretations by learning a predictor model that approximates the true data distribution given any subset of inputs, and EVAL-X for evaluating interpretations.
papers.conclusion: REAL-X provides fast, high-fidelity explanations without encoding predictions, and EVAL-X is an effective method for evaluating interpretations, detecting encoded predictions.
papers.key_findings:
JAMs like L2X and INVASE can encode predictions within their interpretations, allowing high accuracy even with very few features.
JAMs omit control flow features that are important for the data generating process.
REAL-X selects control flow features and achieves higher fidelity upon evaluation with EVAL-X.
EVAL-X can detect when predictions are encoded in interpretations.
REAL-X explanations are ranked higher by expert radiologists for chest X-ray interpretation.
papers.limitation:
There is a trade-off between interpretability (number of features selected) and predictive accuracy.
REAL-X may have a higher false discovery rate (FDR) compared to other methods.
The method produces disjoint pixel selections for images rather than smooth saliency maps, which may be less interpretable.
future_direction: Producing feature attributions such as Shapley values using the evaluator model.
Tailoring the method for specific data modalities, e.g., smooth saliency maps for images.
Extending amortization to other interpretation techniques.
papers.abstract: While the need for interpretable machine learning has been established, many common approaches are slow, lack fidelity, or hard to evaluate.
