Amortized explanation methods reduce the cost of providing interpretations by learning a global selector model that returns feature importances for a single instance of data. The selector model is trained to optimize the fidelity of the interpretations, as evaluated by a predictor model for the target. Popular methods learn the selector and predictor model in concert, which we show allows predictions to be encoded within interpretations. We introduce EVAL-X as a method to quantitatively evaluate interpretations and REAL-X as an amortized explanation method, which learn a predictor model that approximates the true data generating distribution given any subset of the input. We show EVAL-X can detect when predictions are encoded in interpretations and show the advantages of REAL-X through quantitative and radiologist evaluation.

papers.title: Shape or Texture: Understanding Discriminative Features in CNNs
papers.research_question: What type of shape information is discriminative in CNNs, where is shape information encoded, and when does the network learn about object shape during training?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that CNNs learn shape information early in training, encode it primarily in the last few layers, and that shape encoding does not guarantee per-pixel semantic understanding.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides a systematic study of shape encoding in CNNs, revealing important mechanisms that characterize a network's ability to encode shape information, which can inform the design of more robust and trustworthy computer vision algorithms.
papers.key_findings:
CNNs learn the majority of shape information during the first few epochs of training.
Shape information is largely encoded in the last few layers of a CNN.
Biasing a CNN towards shape changes the number of shape encoding neurons in the last feature encoding stage.
Early layers also encode shape information, which can be combined with deeper layers for better shape extraction.
Encoding shape does not imply the encoding of localized per-pixel semantic information.
papers.abstract: Contrasting the previous evidence that neurons in the later layers of a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) respond to complex object shapes, recent studies have shown that CNNs actually exhibit a `texture bias': given an image with both texture and shape cues (e.g., a stylized image), a CNN is biased towards predicting the category corresponding to the texture. However, these previous studies conduct experiments on the final classification output of the network, and fail to robustly evaluate the bias contained (i) in the latent representations, and (ii) on a per-pixel level. In this paper, we design a series of experiments that overcome these issues. We do this with the goal of better understanding what type of shape information contained in the network is discriminative, where shape information is encoded, as well as when the network learns about object shape during training. We show that a network learns the majority of overall shape information at the first few epochs of training and that this information is largely encoded in the last few layers of a CNN. Finally, we show that the encoding of shape does not imply the encoding of localized per-pixel semantic information. The experimental results and findings provide a more accurate understanding of the behaviour of current CNNs, thus helping to inform future design choices.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformer Models
papers.research_question: How can we develop an interactive tool to explore learned representations and attentions in Transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool for exploring learned representations and attentions in Transformer models, enabling hypothesis formulation and replication of prior analyses.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is a tool that provides interactive insights into Transformer models' representations and attentions, facilitating hypothesis generation and analysis.
papers.key_findings:
EXBERT can replicate prior findings on BERT's attention heads learning linguistic dependencies such as AUX and POBJ.
BERT's embeddings encode linguistic information progressively across layers, with verbs becoming more prominent in later layers.
EXBERT detects gender bias in GPT-2 by showing that it predicts gendered pronouns based on stereotypical associations.
GPT-2's attention heads learn syntactic structures like AUX and DOBJ dependencies, similar to BERT.
The tool allows for interactive exploration and quick hypothesis testing of model behavior through attention visualization and corpus similarity search.
papers.limitation: EXBERT only presents statistics across a small number of neighbors for a single token at a time, which may not reveal global model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large Transformer-based language models can route and reshape complex information via their multi-headed attention mechanism. Although the attention never receives explicit supervision, it can exhibit recognizable patterns following linguistic or positional information. Analyzing the learned representations and attentions is paramount to furthering our understanding of the inner workings of these models. However, analyses have to catch up with the rapid release of new models and the growing diversity of investigation techniques. To support analysis for a wide variety of models, we introduce EXBERT, a tool to help humans conduct flexible, interactive investigations and formulate hypotheses for the model-internal reasoning process. EXBERT provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations and attention by matching a humanspecified input to similar contexts in large annotated datasets. By aggregating the annotations of the matched contexts, EXBERT can quickly replicate findings from literature and extend them to previously not analyzed models.

papers.title: Explainable multi-modal deep learning for transparent cancer diagnosis: integrating radiology, clinical features, and decision visualization
papers.research_question: How can radiological and clinical features be effectively integrated into a unified multi-modal deep learning framework for cancer diagnosis? Which explainable AI techniques can provide transparent, robust, and clinically coherent insights into multi-modal diagnostic decisions? Does the proposed explainable multi-modal framework enhance both diagnostic accuracy and interpretability when compared with uni-modal and non-explainable models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes an explainable multi-modal deep learning framework that integrates radiological imaging and structured clinical data using attention-based fusion, providing transparent and clinically coherent explanations for cancer diagnosis without compromising predictive accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The proposed explainable multi-modal deep learning framework achieves high diagnostic performance and provides clinically relevant explanations, demonstrating that explainable multi-modal learning can reconcile precision, resilience, and openness in oncological diagnosis.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed multi-modal model consistently outperforms uni-modal approaches and simple fusion baselines.
Attention-based fusion demonstrates superior performance compared to feature concatenation.
The integration of explainability does not compromise predictive accuracy.
The model provides clinically relevant explanations that align with radiologist annotations.
The model shows strong generalization across different cancer types and datasets.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation was based on retrospective, publicly available datasets, which might not account for the full extent of variations in real-world clinical scenarios.
The clinician assessment was qualitative and of a small scale, involving a limited number of experts.
Grad-CAM++ and SHAP are post-hoc methods and might not necessarily identify the true causal relationships in the model.
The present setup assumes that complete multi-modal data are available; missing or partially observed modalities are not addressed.
future_direction: Develop the framework for clinical trials and deployment in real-time scenarios.
Incorporate uncertainty estimation, causal explainability methods, and temporal clinical data.
Investigate approaches for resilient multi-modal learning when data is missing and broaden clinician-in-the-loop assessment.
papers.abstract: Introduction Although artificial intelligence–based cancer diagnostic models have demonstrated strong predictive performance, their lack of transparency and reliance on single-modality data continue to limit clinical trust and adoption. Effectively integrating multi-modal data with interpret-able decision-making remains a key challenge. Methods We propose an explainable multi-modal deep learning framework that integrates radiological imaging and structured clinical features using attention-based fusion. Image-level explanations are generated using Grad-CAM++, while SHAP is employed to quantify clinical feature contributions, enabling unified and cross-modal aligned interpretation rather than independent uni-modal explanations. The framework was evaluated on publicly available datasets, including CBIS-DDSM mammography, Duke Breast Cancer MRI, and TCGA cohorts (BRCA, LUAD, and GBM), comprising a total of 3,842 images from 2,917 patients. Results The proposed model consistently outperformed uni-modal approaches and simple fusion baselines, achieving an improved balance between sensitivity and specificity. Attention-based fusion demonstrated superior performance compared with feature concatenation, and the integration of explainability did not compromise predictive accuracy. Visual and clinical explanations highlighted diagnostically relevant tumor regions and established oncological risk factors. Stable performance across datasets indicates strong generalization capability. Discussion These results demonstrate that explainable multi-modal learning can effectively combine accuracy, interpret-ability, and robustness, supporting the development of reliable AI-based decision-support systems for cancer diagnosis.

papers.title: Interpretable AI in Radiology: Advancing Trust in X-ray Diagnostics with Explainability Techniques
papers.research_question: What is the role of explainable AI techniques in advancing trust and transparency in AI-driven radiology, specifically for X-ray diagnostics?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reviews explainable AI techniques in radiology, emphasizing the need for integrating XAI to ensure AI-driven systems are accurate, transparent, and trustworthy for clinical adoption.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that explainability in AI-driven radiology is essential for fostering trust and ensuring clinical adoption, and future research should refine XAI techniques to be more reliable and aligned with radiologists' needs.
papers.key_findings:
XAI techniques like Grad-CAM and SHAP provide visual and quantitative insights into model decisions, enhancing interpretability.
Challenges in AI-based radiology include model interpretability, bias, regulatory compliance, clinician trust, data quality, and generalizability.
Evaluation metrics such as IoU and fidelity score are crucial for assessing the effectiveness of explainability methods.
Explainability helps in detecting and mitigating biases in AI models, ensuring fair decision-making.
Integrating XAI into radiology is essential for bridging the gap between AI advancements and clinical implementation.
papers.limitation: Explainability methods such as gradient-based techniques suffer from noise sensitivity and may not be robust enough for clinical validation.
future_direction: Future research should aim to refine XAI techniques, making them more reliable, efficient, and aligned with radiologists’ needs.
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has significantly transformed radiology by enabling automated medical image classification, particularly for detecting abnormalities in chest X-rays and other imaging modalities. While deep learning models achieve remarkable accuracy, their black-box nature limits interpretability, raising concerns among clinicians and regulatory bodies [1]. Explainable AI (XAI) techniques aim to bridge this gap by providing insights into the decision-making processes of these models [2]. This paper comprehensively examines XAI methods applied to radiological image classification, focusing on chest X-ray datasets and pneumonia detection models [3]. A detailed exploration of model architectures, feature attribution techniques, and evaluation metrics is conducted to understand the role of explainability in medical AI [4]. Furthermore, key challenges in implementing explainability frameworks and future directions for research and clinical adoption are discussed [5]. This study emphasizes the need for integrating XAI into radiology to ensure AI-driven systems are not only accurate but also transparent and trustworthy.

papers.title: 3D ReX: Causal Explanations in 3D Neuroimaging Classification
papers.core_contribution: Introduces 3D-R EX, a causality-based post-hoc explainability tool for 3D models, generating responsibility maps to highlight regions crucial for model decisions in medical imaging.
papers.conclusion: 3D-R EX offers a causality-based approach for explaining 3D models in medical imaging, with potential to improve trust and provide biological insights.
papers.key_findings:
3D-R EX successfully generates causal responsibility maps for 3D MRI data.
Using 0-value occlusion produces explanations aligned with lesion locations, while healthy MRI occlusion highlights different regions.
The method reduces computational complexity by splitting on two axes instead of three.
Explanations can be visualized in 2D slices and 3D renderings for comprehensive insight.
The tool is model-agnostic and does not require access to internal model weights.
papers.limitation:
Computational complexity due to large search space in 3D data
Lack of comprehensive evaluation on a large-scale dataset
future_direction: Extend 3D-R EX to different medical imaging modalities.
Investigate explanations with different occlusion values on larger models.
Integrate with multi-modal data including genomic and patient history.
papers.abstract: Explainability remains a significant problem for AI models in medical imaging, making it challenging for clinicians to trust AI-driven predictions. We introduce 3D ReX, the first causality-based post-hoc explainability tool for 3D models. 3D ReX uses the theory of actual causality to generate responsibility maps which highlight the regions most crucial to the model's decision. We test 3D ReX on a stroke detection model, providing insight into the spatial distribution of features relevant to stroke.

papers.title: Interpretable breast cancer classification using CNNs on mammographic images
papers.research_question: How can we gain insights into the decision-making process of CNNs for mammogram classification? The paper compares three post-hoc interpretability techniques (LIME, Grad-CAM, Kernel SHAP) in terms of explanatory depth and computational efficiency.
papers.core_contribution: This paper compares three post-hoc interpretability techniques (LIME, Grad-CAM, Kernel SHAP) for CNN-based mammogram classification and finds that Grad-CAM provides the most comprehensive insights into the CNN's predictions, revealing distinctive patterns for normal, benign, and malignant tissue, while being computationally efficient and robust.
papers.conclusion: Grad-CAM is the preferred interpretation technique for the given dataset and model, providing insightful explanations in a time-efficient and stable way, and demonstrates the potential of explainable AI as a supplementary tool for radiologists in breast cancer diagnosis.
papers.key_findings:
The CNN model achieved an overall accuracy of 0.77 on the test set, with best performance on normal cases (F1=0.93) and worst on malignant cases (F1=0.44).
Grad-CAM was the most computationally efficient interpretability technique, with an average running time of 0.29 seconds per image.
Grad-CAM provided deterministic and robust explanations, unlike LIME and SHAP which showed variability across runs.
Grad-CAM's visual explanations aligned well with clinical intuition, showing round/oval shapes for benign predictions and irregular, scattered areas for malignant predictions.
LIME and Kernel SHAP were less accurate in identifying entire lesions and were less stable (especially LIME) and slower.
papers.limitation:
The dataset’s inherent limitations, including low image quality and the absence of a second breast view potentially negatively affected the performance of the CNN.
The reliance on manual ROI annotations and classification labels introduces potential biases.
The model showed a higher prevalence of misclassified malignant lumps (recall = 0.48), leaving more than half of true cancer cases undetected.
Training and evaluating the model on a single data split may have biased the results towards that specific split.
The interpretability evaluation is qualitative and may involve observer bias.
future_direction: Fine-tuning the trained ROI model on whole mammogram images to enable classification without ROI annotations.
Using datasets with higher resolution and two breast views (e.g., INBreast or DDSM) to improve performance.
Conducting human-subject experiments to assess how Grad-CAM enhances trust of radiologists.
papers.abstract: Deep learning models have achieved promising results in breast cancer classification, yet their 'black-box' nature raises interpretability concerns. This research addresses the crucial need to gain insights into the decision-making process of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for mammogram classification, specifically focusing on the underlying reasons for the CNN's predictions of breast cancer. For CNNs trained on the Mammographic Image Analysis Society (MIAS) dataset, we compared the post-hoc interpretability techniques LIME, Grad-CAM, and Kernel SHAP in terms of explanatory depth and computational efficiency. The results of this analysis indicate that Grad-CAM, in particular, provides comprehensive insights into the behavior of the CNN, revealing distinctive patterns in normal, benign, and malignant breast tissue. We discuss the implications of the current findings for the use of machine learning models and interpretation techniques in clinical practice.

papers.title: Improving Interpretability of Deep Neural Networks in Medical Diagnosis by Investigating the Individual Units
papers.research_question: How can attribution techniques like LRP and RAP improve the interpretability of DNNs in medical diagnosis by visualizing significant factors and revealing inconsistencies between human and DNN intentions?
papers.core_contribution: Attribution methods like LRP and RAP can effectively localize lesions in chest X-rays without bounding box supervision and reveal that DNNs may learn based on normal lung features rather than disease lesions, highlighting the need for interpretability in medical diagnosis.
papers.conclusion: Attribution techniques such as LRP and RAP offer efficient ways to interpret DNN decisions in medical diagnosis by localizing lesions and uncovering potential inconsistencies, underscoring the necessity of explainability for reliable adoption.
papers.key_findings:
LRP and RAP achieve higher IOU scores than CAM for localizing lesions in chest X-ray images, indicating better visualization accuracy.
Attribution methods provide detailed pixel-wise explanations compared to CAM's broad visualizations from resized feature maps.
DNNs trained for pneumonia classification may focus on normal lung features rather than pneumonia lesions, showing inconsistency with human intentions.
CheXNet, pretrained for multiple diseases, provides clear visual explanations aligned with lesion areas, unlike models trained only on pneumonia data.
The study emphasizes the importance of explainability to ensure DNNs' decision criteria align with clinical expectations.
papers.abstract: As interpretability has been pointed out as the obstacle to the adoption of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), there is an increasing interest in solving a transparency issue to guarantee the impressive performance. In this paper, we demonstrate the efficiency of recent attribution techniques to explain the diagnostic decision by visualizing the significant factors in the input image. By utilizing the characteristics of objectness that DNNs have learned, fully decomposing the network prediction visualizes clear localization of target lesion. To verify our work, we conduct our experiments on Chest X-ray diagnosis with publicly accessible datasets. As an intuitive assessment metric for explanations, we report the performance of intersection of Union between visual explanation and bounding box of lesions. Experiment results show that recently proposed attribution methods visualize the more accurate localization for the diagnostic decision compared to the traditionally used CAM. Furthermore, we analyze the inconsistency of intentions between humans and DNNs, which is easily obscured by high performance. By visualizing the relevant factors, it is possible to confirm that the criterion for decision is in line with the learning strategy. Our analysis of unmasking machine intelligence represents the necessity of explainability in the medical diagnostic decision.

papers.title: Does Circuit Analysis Interpretability Scale? Evidence from Multiple Choice Capabilities in Chinchilla
papers.research_question: Does circuit analysis interpretability scale to large language models, specifically for the algorithmic task of multiple-choice question answering?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that existing circuit analysis techniques (logit attribution, attention pattern visualization, activation patching) scale to a 70B parameter model, allowing identification and partial understanding of the circuit for multiple-choice question answering, particularly 'correct letter' heads.
papers.conclusion: Circuit analysis techniques can scale to large models, but the features used to implement algorithmic tasks can be messy in their semantics, even when limited to a distribution with little superposition.
papers.key_findings:
Identified 45 nodes (attention heads and MLPs) that are causally responsible for most of the model's performance on the multiple-choice task.
Categorized attention heads into four types: 'Correct Letter', 'Uniform', 'Single Letter', and 'Amplification'.
Found that 'correct letter' heads attend to the correct answer label and copy it to the output logits.
Used SVD to compress query/key/value subspaces of 'correct letter' heads, finding the query and key subspaces represent an 'Nth item in an enumeration' feature, but this is only a partial explanation for behavior on a more general distribution.
Showed that the algorithmic task of mapping the correct answer to its label is interpretable, but the specific features used are messy and only partially understood.
papers.limitation:
The effect of patching a node can be compensated by downstream nodes (backup behavior), potentially distorting results.
The analysis only finds a cross-section of the circuit (nodes separating ancestors and descendants) rather than the full set of relevant nodes.
Results are only applicable to the specific distribution tested (MMLU subset).
Focused on the net effect on the correct label, neglecting the part of the circuit that identifies the set of possible answer tokens.
future_direction: Investigating the rest of the circuit (nodes feeding into the correct letter heads).
Comparing different approaches to causal interventions (e.g., noising vs. denoising).
Automating circuit analysis to reduce labor intensity.
papers.abstract: \emph{Circuit analysis} is a promising technique for understanding the internal mechanisms of language models. However, existing analyses are done in small models far from the state of the art. To address this, we present a case study of circuit analysis in the 70B Chinchilla model, aiming to test the scalability of circuit analysis. In particular, we study multiple-choice question answering, and investigate Chinchilla's capability to identify the correct answer \emph{label} given knowledge of the correct answer \emph{text}. We find that the existing techniques of logit attribution, attention pattern visualization, and activation patching naturally scale to Chinchilla, allowing us to identify and categorize a small set of `output nodes' (attention heads and MLPs). We further study the `correct letter' category of attention heads aiming to understand the semantics of their features, with mixed results. For normal multiple-choice question answers, we significantly compress the query, key and value subspaces of the head without loss of performance when operating on the answer labels for multiple-choice questions, and we show that the query and key subspaces represent an `Nth item in an enumeration' feature to at least some extent. However, when we attempt to use this explanation to understand the heads' behaviour on a more general distribution including randomized answer labels, we find that it is only a partial explanation, suggesting there is more to learn about the operation of `correct letter' heads on multiple choice question answering.

papers.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: What does attention in protein Transformer language models capture about protein structure and function?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that attention in protein language models captures high-level structural and functional properties of proteins, and that attention focuses on progressively more complex properties with increasing layer depth.
papers.conclusion: Attention in protein Transformer models recovers structural and functional properties of proteins, and interpretability methods can aid scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Attention in deep layers aligns with contact maps, connecting amino acids that are spatially close in 3D structure but far in sequence.
Attention targets binding sites and post-translational modifications, key functional components.
Attention heads specialize in particular amino acids and their patterns are consistent with substitution matrices.
Deeper layers focus more on high-level properties (binding sites, contacts) while secondary structure is targeted more evenly across layers.
Knowledge in embeddings accumulates gradually over layers, while attention acquires knowledge primarily in final layers.
papers.limitation: The analyses are associative and do not establish causal links between attention and model behavior.
future_direction: Using attention and learned representations as tools for scientific discovery.
Developing contextual visualizations of learned representations for domain experts in scientific domains.
papers.abstract: Abstract Transformer architectures have proven to learn useful representations for protein classification and generation tasks. However, these representations present challenges in interpretability. Through the lens of attention, we analyze the inner workings of the Transformer and explore how the model discerns structural and functional properties of proteins. We show that attention (1) captures the folding structure of proteins, connecting amino acids that are far apart in the underlying sequence, but spatially close in the three-dimensional structure, (2) targets binding sites, a key functional component of proteins, and (3) focuses on progressively more complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth. We also present a three-dimensional visualization of the interaction between attention and protein structure. Our findings align with known biological processes and provide a tool to aid discovery in protein engineering and synthetic biology. The code for visualization and analysis is available at https://github.com/salesforce/provis .

papers.title: The Next Five Hurdles What is a Linear Representation? What is a Multidimensional Feature? The Dark Matter of Neural Networks? Attention Pivot Tables Measuring feature sensitivity using dataset filtering
papers.research_question: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement?
papers.core_contribution: This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering.
papers.conclusion: The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.
papers.key_findings:
Current sparse autoencoder methods may miss many rare features, suggesting a 'dark matter' of neural networks that is difficult to observe.
Linear representations can be mathematically linear even with multidimensional features, requiring a revised definition.
Attention pivot tables reveal interpretable skip-trigrams in one-layer transformers, but their clarity depends on training details and dataset.
Feature sensitivity measured via Claude-filtered datasets shows that individual features often have low sensitivity, and concepts are represented by multiple cooperating features.
Different versions of Claude agree well with each other and with human judgments when rating concept relevance in text snippets.
papers.limitation:
Dictionary learning may be unable to resolve extremely rare features, limiting comprehensiveness.
Features identified by sparse autoencoders often have imperfect sensitivity and specificity, with concepts distributed across multiple features.
Attention pivot table results are sensitive to training hyperparameters and dataset composition, making interpretation unreliable under suboptimal conditions.
future_direction: Developing more efficient dictionary learning algorithms to capture rare features.
Automating the discovery of complementary features that collectively represent concepts.
Further investigation into attention superposition and cross-layer superposition.
papers.abstract: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement? This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering. The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.

papers.title: Learning Interpretable Microscopic Features of Tumor by Multi-task Adversarial CNNs To Improve Generalization
papers.research_question: How can we improve the generalization and transparency of CNNs in histopathology by guiding training to focus on clinically relevant features and discard confounding factors?
papers.core_contribution: A novel CNN architecture combining multi-task learning and adversarial training to learn interpretable, clinically relevant features and improve generalization in histopathology image analysis.
papers.conclusion: Expert knowledge can be proactively used during CNN training via additional tasks to drive representation learning, improving robustness, generalization, and transparency for histopathology applications.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed multi-task adversarial architecture achieves improved generalization with an average AUC of 0.89 vs. 0.86 baseline on breast cancer detection.
Linear probing confirms that interpretable pathology features (e.g., nuclei density) are learned by the model.
Uncertainty-based loss weighting provides stable training and robust performance across data shifts compared to vanilla weighting.
The adversarial branch for acquisition center did not show marked improvement, possibly due to inaccurate center labels.
High-order combinations of auxiliary tasks do not automatically yield better generalization than low-order ones.
papers.limitation:
The uncertainty estimated is only homoscedastic (task-dependent) and does not correspond to data-dependent main task uncertainty.
The choice of auxiliary tasks requires prior knowledge to ensure they cooperate with the main task.
The adversarial branch for acquisition center did not show marked improvement, possibly due to inaccurate center labels in some datasets.
Auxiliary tasks become harder to learn when scaled up in number, with lower R2 for individual feature regression.
future_direction: Explore unsupervised domain adaptation methods (e.g., domain alignment layers) to handle latent domain information.
Investigate different loss weighting strategies for the adversarial task and include other undesired control targets (e.g., rotation, scale).
Extract additional features from unlabeled data and introduce them as weak supervision during training.
papers.abstract: Adopting Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) in the daily routine of primary diagnosis requires not only near-perfect precision, but also a sufficient degree of generalization to data acquisition shifts and transparency. Existing CNN models act as black boxes, not ensuring to the physicians that important diagnostic features are used by the model. Building on top of successfully existing techniques such as multi-task learning, domain adversarial training and concept-based interpretability, this paper addresses the challenge of introducing diagnostic factors in the training objectives. Here we show that our architecture, by learning end-to-end an uncertainty-based weighting combination of multi-task and adversarial losses, is encouraged to focus on pathology features such as density and pleomorphism of nuclei, e.g. variations in size and appearance, while discarding misleading features such as staining differences. Our results on breast lymph node tissue show significantly improved generalization in the detection of tumorous tissue, with best average AUC 0.89 (0.01) against the baseline AUC 0.86 (0.005). By applying the interpretability technique of linearly probing intermediate representations, we also demonstrate that interpretable pathology features such as nuclei density are learned by the proposed CNN architecture, confirming the increased transparency of this model. This result is a starting point towards building interpretable multi-task architectures that are robust to data heterogeneity. Our code is available at https://github.com/maragraziani/multitask_adversarial

papers.title: LADDER: Language-Driven Slice Discovery and Error Rectification in Vision Classifiers
papers.research_question: How can we use Large Language Models to discover and mitigate systematic biases in vision classifiers without relying on predefined attributes or annotations?
papers.core_contribution: LADDER introduces a method that uses Large Language Models to discover and mitigate systematic biases in vision classifiers by analyzing textual artifacts like captions and metadata, without requiring predefined attribute sets or annotations.
papers.conclusion: LADDER offers a robust framework for automated bias discovery and mitigation in vision classifiers, leveraging LLMs to handle complex biases without manual intervention.
papers.key_findings:
LADDER consistently outperforms current slice discovery methods, especially in medical imaging datasets.
It effectively uses LLMs' reasoning and domain knowledge to identify fine-grained biases, such as disease subtypes.
The method discovers similar biases across different model architectures and pretraining methods.
LADDER can mitigate multiple biases without annotations by generating pseudo-labels and fine-tuning the classifier head.
It can operate without captions by using instruction-tuned models and detect biases in metadata like DICOM headers.
papers.abstract: Slice discovery refers to identifying systematic biases in the mistakes of pre-trained vision models. Current slice discovery methods in computer vision rely on converting input images into sets of attributes and then testing hypotheses about configurations of these precomputed attributes associated with elevated error patterns. However, such methods face several limitations: 1) they are restricted by the predefined attribute bank; 2) they lack the common sense reasoning and domain-specific knowledge often required for specialized fields e.g., radiology; 3) at best, they can only identify biases in image attributes while overlooking those introduced during preprocessing or data preparation. We hypothesize that bias-inducing variables leave traces in the form of language (e.g., logs), which can be captured as unstructured text. Thus, we introduce LADDER, which leverages the reasoning capabilities and latent domain knowledge of Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate hypotheses about these mistakes. Specifically, we project the internal activations of a pre-trained model into text using a retrieval approach and prompt the LLM to propose potential bias hypotheses. To detect biases from preprocessing pipelines, we convert the preprocessing data into text and prompt the LLM. Finally, LADDER generates pseudo-labels for each identified bias, thereby mitigating all biases without requiring expensive attribute annotations. Rigorous evaluations on 3 natural and 3 medical imaging datasets, 200+ classifiers, and 4 LLMs with varied architectures and pretraining strategies - demonstrate that LADDER consistently outperforms current methods.

papers.title: Interpreting Deep Visual Representations via Network Dissection
papers.research_question: How can we quantify the interpretability of deep visual representations by aligning individual hidden units with visual semantic concepts, and what factors affect this interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Network Dissection, a method to quantify interpretability of deep visual representations by aligning individual units with visual concepts, and shows interpretability is axis-aligned and varies with architecture and training.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability is an important property of deep neural networks that provides new insights into their hierarchical structure.
papers.key_findings:
Deep visual representations are more interpretable than random bases of equivalent discriminative power.
Interpretability is an axis-aligned property that can be destroyed by rotating the representation.
Supervised training on large annotated datasets yields more object detectors than self-supervised training.
Batch normalization reduces interpretability while maintaining discriminative power.
Different network architectures and training conditions lead to varying levels of interpretability.
papers.limitation:
The method depends on the vocabulary of concepts in Broden; units detecting concepts not in Broden will not be counted.
The method measures alignment of individual units, so it may miss concepts represented by groups of units.
future_direction: Finding ways to capture the benefits of batch normalization without destroying interpretability.
Building more interpretable and explainable AI systems.
papers.abstract: The success of recent deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) depends on learning hidden representations that can summarize the important factors of variation behind the data. However, CNNs often criticized as being black boxes that lack interpretability, since they have millions of unexplained model parameters. In this work, we describe Network Dissection, a method that interprets networks by providing labels for the units of their deep visual representations. The proposed method quantifies the interpretability of CNN representations by evaluating the alignment between individual hidden units and a set of visual semantic concepts. By identifying the best alignments, units are given human interpretable labels across a range of objects, parts, scenes, textures, materials, and colors. The method reveals that deep representations are more transparent and interpretable than expected: we find that representations are significantly more interpretable than they would be under a random equivalently powerful basis. We apply the method to interpret and compare the latent representations of various network architectures trained to solve different supervised and self-supervised training tasks. We then examine factors affecting the network interpretability such as the number of the training iterations, regularizations, different initializations, and the network depth and width. Finally we show that the interpreted units can be used to provide explicit explanations of a prediction given by a CNN for an image. Our results highlight that interpretability is an important property of deep neural networks that provides new insights into their hierarchical structure.

papers.title: Explaining Predictions of Deep Neural Classifier via Activation Analysis
papers.research_question: How can we explain and support the interpretation of a deep convolutional neural network's decision-making process to a human expert by providing perceptually similar examples from an atlas?
papers.core_contribution: A novel explainability method for deep CNNs that encodes neuron activation statistics via Gaussian Mixture Models into a binary perceptual code, enabling retrieval of similar examples from an atlas to explain individual predictions.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method is viable for explaining CNN predictions in medical imaging by providing similar examples from an atlas, and analyzing the encoded atlas can help detect undesired model over-generalization.
papers.key_findings:
The method can retrieve activation-wise similar images from an atlas to serve as a prediction basis for explaining a CNN's decision.
Analysis of deeper network layers leads to higher average prediction basis accuracy.
The encoded atlas visualizations (via PCA) show clustering corresponding to different intra-classes, indicating the method can reveal distinct prediction strategies.
Less accurate prediction basis retrieval in some cases is attributed to similar neural activation patterns for different intra-classes learned during training, potentially indicating over-generalization.
The method's performance is associated with the relevance of input features (as shown by LRP analysis), where well-defined clusters correspond to high relevancy in textured areas.
papers.abstract: In many practical applications, deep neural networks have been typically deployed to operate as a black box predictor. Despite the high amount of work on interpretability and high demand on the reliability of these systems, they typically still have to include a human actor in the loop, to validate the decisions and handle unpredictable failures and unexpected corner cases. This is true in particular for failure-critical application domains, such as medical diagnosis. We present a novel approach to explain and support an interpretation of the decision-making process to a human expert operating a deep learning system based on Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). By modeling activation statistics on selected layers of a trained CNN via Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM), we develop a novel perceptual code in binary vector space that describes how the input sample is processed by the CNN. By measuring distances between pairs of samples in this perceptual encoding space, for any new input sample, we can now retrieve a set of most perceptually similar and dissimilar samples from an existing atlas of labeled samples, to support and clarify the decision made by the CNN model. Possible uses of this approach include for example Computer-Aided Diagnosis (CAD) systems working with medical imaging data, such as Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) or Computed Tomography (CT) scans. We demonstrate the viability of our method in the domain of medical imaging for patient condition diagnosis, as the proposed decision explanation method via similar ground truth domain examples (e.g. from existing diagnosis archives) will be interpretable by the operating medical personnel. Our results indicate that our method is capable of detecting distinct prediction strategies that enable us to identify the most similar predictions from an existing atlas.

papers.title: Interpreting Biomedical VLMs on High-Imbalance Out-of-Distributions: An Insight into BiomedCLIP on Radiology
papers.research_question: Can large, pretrained vision–language models accurately classify images in a multi-label, imbalanced, out-of-distribution biomedical dataset?
papers.core_contribution: This paper comprehensively evaluates the BiomedCLIP vision-language model on a highly imbalanced, out-of-distribution radiology dataset, comparing zero-shot, linear probing, and full fine-tuning adaptation strategies. It finds that linear probing offers a favorable trade-off, recovering much of the performance gains of full fine-tuning at a fraction of the computational cost while better preserving the model's inherent spatial interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Linear probing is an efficient adaptation strategy for biomedical VLMs on imbalanced OOD data, offering a good balance of performance, computational cost, and preserved interpretability, though challenges remain for rare disease detection.
papers.key_findings:
Zero-shot BiomedCLIP over-predicts all labels, leading to poor precision and low inter-class separability in the embedding space.
Full fine-tuning achieves the highest embedding separability and classification performance for abundant disease classes but generates less specific Grad-CAM heatmaps.
Linear probing achieves performance comparable to full fine-tuning for many classes at significantly lower computational cost and preserves the spatial fidelity of zero-shot Grad-CAM visualizations.
Both fine-tuning and linear probing struggle to classify extremely rare disease classes (e.g., Pneumothorax, Consolidation).
Shallower encoder layers yield more clinically meaningful and localized saliency maps compared to deeper layers after fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
IU-Xray is a single modality dataset with automated labels from CheXbert, limiting ground-truth fidelity and diversity.
Qualitative evaluation relies on a small set of 15 radiologist annotations, which may not generalize across institutions or imaging devices.
Only a single VLM (BiomedCLIP) and three adaptation strategies (zero-shot, linear probing, full fine-tuning) are evaluated; other models and parameter-efficient methods remain unexplored.
future_direction: Extend evaluation to additional biomedical datasets and modalities (e.g., histopathology, dermatology, neuroimaging) with manually curated labels.
Investigate class imbalance mitigation techniques (e.g., loss reweighting, synthetic augmentation) to boost rare-disease detection.
Explore lightweight adaptation methods such as soft prompts and adapter modules to balance accuracy, interpretability, and resource efficiency.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we construct two research objectives: i) explore the learned embedding space of BiomedCLIP, an open-source large vision language model, to analyse meaningful class separations, and ii) quantify the limitations of BiomedCLIP when applied to a highly imbalanced, out-of-distribution multi-label medical dataset. We experiment on IU-xray dataset, which exhibits the aforementioned criteria, and evaluate BiomedCLIP in classifying images (radiographs) in three contexts: zero-shot inference, full finetuning, and linear probing. The results show that the model under zero-shot settings over-predicts all labels, leading to poor precision and inter-class separability. Full fine-tuning improves classification of distinct diseases, while linear probing detects overlapping features. We demonstrate visual understanding of the model using Grad-CAM heatmaps and compare with 15 annotations by a radiologist. We highlight the need for careful adaptations of the models to foster reliability and applicability in a real-world setting. The code for the experiments in this work is available and maintained on GitHub.

papers.title: Peering into the Heart: A Comprehensive Exploration of Semantic Segmentation and Explainable AI on the MnMs-2 Cardiac MRI Dataset
papers.research_question: How can semantic segmentation and explainable AI techniques be integrated for accurate and interpretable analysis of cardiac MRI images?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a segmentation model combining nnU-Net with Vision Transformer and residual blocks, achieving competitive performance on the MnMs-2 dataset, and uses Grad-CAM and Feature Ablation to provide interpretable visualizations of the model's decision-making process.
papers.conclusion: The proposed approach effectively segments cardiac MRI images and provides interpretable visualizations, enhancing transparency and confidence for potential clinical use.
papers.key_findings:
Integration of Vision Transformer and residual blocks improved Dice scores for 2D long-axis images but decreased performance for 3D short-axis images.
PReLU activation improved performance for 3D short-axis segmentation but not for 2D long-axis segmentation.
Grad-CAM and Feature Ablation visualizations showed the model focused on the target class (e.g., right ventricle) and aligned with clinical expectations regarding cardiac phases.
The model achieved competitive segmentation accuracy, particularly for the challenging right ventricle segmentation task.
The study demonstrates the value of explainable AI techniques for building trust in medical image segmentation models.
papers.limitation:
The medical imaging dataset is small compared to datasets used to train Vision Transformers in other domains, which may hinder the ViT components from learning meaningful representations.
Zero-padding pre-processing for 3D short-axis images may have negatively impacted the extraction of spatial context and model performance.
future_direction: Investigate the generalizability of the methodology by applying it to various medical imaging datasets and diverse segmentation tasks.
Explore more advanced explainable AI techniques to gain richer insights into the model's reasoning and decision-making processes.
Integrate explainable AI into clinical workflows to facilitate a collaborative environment between human expertise and AI capabilities.
papers.abstract: Abstract Accurate and interpretable segmentation of medical images is crucial for computer-aided diagnosis and image-guided interventions. This study explores the integration of semantic segmentation and explainable AI techniques on the MnMs-2 Cardiac MRI dataset. We propose a segmentation model that achieves competitive dice scores (nearly 90 %) and Hausdorff distance (less than 70), demonstrating its effectiveness for cardiac MRI analysis. Furthermore, we leverage Grad-CAM, and Feature Ablation, explainable AI techniques, to visualise the regions of interest guiding the model predictions for a target class. This integration enhances interpretability, allowing us to gain insights into the model decision-making process and build trust in its predictions.

papers.title: Decoding Decision Reasoning: A Counterfactual-Powered Model for Knowledge Discovery
papers.research_question: How to discern the rationale behind AI model's predictions in medical imaging for early disease detection and prognosis?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes PrognosisEx, an explainable prognostic model that decodes decision reasoning by identifying class-specific features and generating counterfactual explanations for medical image classification.
papers.conclusion: This work presents an innovative, explainable prognostic model that provides insight into its decision process and identifies features used for decisions, improving the safety of AI in healthcare and demonstrating promise for biomarker discovery.
papers.key_findings:
PrognosisEx achieves comparable prognostic performance to state-of-the-art deep learning models while providing explainability.
The model identifies class-specific features that drive predictions, such as ground-glass opacities and vascularisation for mortality risk.
Counterfactual examples generated by manipulating features reveal semantic meanings, like increased GGOs and reduced lung area indicating higher mortality.
Identified features align with existing prognostic knowledge, validating the model's decision-making.
PrognosisEx offers a cost-effective tool for biomarker discovery in diseases with limited prognostic understanding.
future_direction: Broader validation with different imaging modalities and medical scenarios using public datasets.
papers.abstract: In medical imaging, particularly in early disease detection and prognosis tasks, discerning the rationale behind an AI model's predictions is crucial for evaluating the reliability of its decisions. Conventional explanation methods face challenges in identifying discernible decisive features in medical image classifications, where discriminative features are subtle or not immediately apparent. To bridge this gap, we propose an explainable model that is equipped with both decision reasoning and feature identification capabilities. Our approach not only detects influential image patterns but also uncovers the decisive features that drive the model's final predictions. By implementing our method, we can efficiently identify and visualise class-specific features leveraged by the data-driven model, providing insights into the decision-making processes of deep learning models. We validated our model in the demanding realm of medical prognosis task, demonstrating its efficacy and potential in enhancing the reliability of AI in healthcare and in discovering new knowledge in diseases where prognostic understanding is limited.

papers.title: Randomized-MLP Regularization Improves Domain Adaptation and Interpretability in DINOv2
papers.research_question: How can randomized MLP regularization improve domain adaptation and interpretability in Vision Transformers like DINOv2?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Randomized-MLP (RMLP) regularization, a method that improves interpretability and domain adaptation in Vision Transformers by encouraging semantically aligned representations and reducing attention artifacts.
papers.conclusion: RMLP regularization enhances interpretability and robustness of ViT representations across natural and ophthalmological domains, producing more structured embeddings and mitigating attention artifacts.
papers.key_findings:
RMLP regularization improves or maintains downstream performance on natural and medical image tasks.
RMLP produces more interpretable attention maps by reducing first- and second-order artifacts.
Fine-tuning with RMLP improves segmentation performance on medical images, achieving state-of-the-art on OCT segmentation.
RMLP generalizes to other self-supervised models like SwAV, improving their performance.
The method is lightweight and requires no retraining of the representation heads.
papers.limitation:
Optimal regularization strength depends on data modality and ViT latent space dimensionality, and no principled selection method is proposed.
Experiments are limited to small- and mid-scale datasets.
future_direction: Investigate performance at larger scales and across a broader range of domains.
papers.abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs), such as DINOv2, achieve strong performance across domains but often repurpose low-informative patch tokens in ways that reduce the interpretability of attention and feature maps. This challenge is especially evident in medical imaging, where domain shifts can degrade both performance and transparency. In this paper, we introduce Randomized-MLP (RMLP) regularization, a contrastive learning-based method that encourages more semantically aligned representations. We use RMLPs when fine-tuning DINOv2 to both medical and natural image modalities, showing that it improves or maintains downstream performance while producing more interpretable attention maps. We also provide a mathematical analysis of RMLPs, offering insights into its role in enhancing ViT-based models and advancing our understanding of contrastive learning.

papers.title: Transcoders Find Interpretable LLM Feature Circuits
papers.research_question: How can we perform fine-grained circuit analysis through MLP sublayers in transformers, given the polysemanticity of neurons? The paper proposes transcoders as a solution to enable input-invariant circuit analysis.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces transcoders, a method for approximating MLP sublayers with sparse, interpretable features, enabling input-invariant circuit analysis through MLPs.
papers.conclusion: Transcoders are an effective tool for decomposing model computations involving MLPs into interpretable circuits, enabling scalable and interpretable circuit analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Transcoders are as interpretable as SAEs and perform similarly or better in terms of sparsity and faithfulness.
Transcoders enable circuit analysis that factorizes into input-invariant and input-dependent terms, allowing for general claims about model behavior.
Blind case studies demonstrate that transcoders can reverse-engineer features without looking at activating examples.
Analysis of the GPT2-small greater-than circuit reveals new insights, such as the role of the MLP0 layer.
papers.limitation:
Transcoders may not capture all nuances of the original MLP, as seen in the 'caught' feature example where the transcoder did not accurately model the difference between 'was caught' and 'caught the ball'.
Blind case studies had some failures, indicating that circuit analysis with transcoders is not always perfect.
future_direction: Scaling transcoders to larger models.
Applying transcoders to more tasks and models.
papers.abstract: A key goal in mechanistic interpretability is circuit analysis: finding sparse subgraphs of models corresponding to specific behaviors or capabilities. However, MLP sublayers make fine-grained circuit analysis on transformer-based language models difficult. In particular, interpretable features -- such as those found by sparse autoencoders (SAEs) -- are typically linear combinations of extremely many neurons, each with its own nonlinearity to account for. Circuit analysis in this setting thus either yields intractably large circuits or fails to disentangle local and global behavior. To address this we explore transcoders, which seek to faithfully approximate a densely activating MLP layer with a wider, sparsely-activating MLP layer. We introduce a novel method for using transcoders to perform weights-based circuit analysis through MLP sublayers. The resulting circuits neatly factorize into input-dependent and input-invariant terms. We then successfully train transcoders on language models with 120M, 410M, and 1.4B parameters, and find them to perform at least on par with SAEs in terms of sparsity, faithfulness, and human-interpretability. Finally, we apply transcoders to reverse-engineer unknown circuits in the model, and we obtain novel insights regarding the "greater-than circuit" in GPT2-small. Our results suggest that transcoders can prove effective in decomposing model computations involving MLPs into interpretable circuits. Code is available at https://github.com/jacobdunefsky/transcoder_circuits/.

papers.title: Beyond the Black Box: Interpretability of LLMs in Finance
papers.research_question: How can mechanistic interpretability techniques be applied to understand and control the behavior of Large Language Models (LLMs) in financial applications to improve transparency and reliability?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates the application of mechanistic interpretability techniques—Logit Lens, Attribution Patching, and Sparse Autoencoders—to financial use cases, showing how they can be used to understand, debug, and steer model behavior for tasks like sentiment analysis, bias detection, and hallucination reduction.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability offers a promising path to dissect and guide AI-driven financial decisions with greater transparency and control, though challenges in scalability, generalization, and mapping abstract features to human-understandable concepts remain.
papers.key_findings:
Logit Lens analysis reveals how token prediction probabilities evolve across transformer layers in response to financial prompts, showing refinement of predictions in deeper layers.
Attribution Patching identifies specific attention heads in layers 8 and 10 of GPT-2 as causally significant for correct financial predictions.
Sparse Autoencoders can extract interpretable, monosemantic features from model activations relevant to financial concepts like credit risk.
Feature steering via Sparse Autoencoders can modify model outputs, such as improving sentiment classification accuracy for credit risk analysis without fine-tuning.
A feature-activation-thresholded Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) approach can reduce hallucinations in financial question-answering by ensuring external factual data is incorporated when internal feature activations are low.
papers.limitation:
Scalability is a major concern, as manual circuit analysis becomes infeasible for very large models, and automated interpretability tools are still in early development.
Many techniques fail to generalize effectively to real-world financial applications, as models often rely on abstract representations not directly mappable to human-understandable financial concepts.
The evolving nature of financial markets and regulations means models trained on historical data may struggle to adapt, requiring dynamic interpretability pipelines.
Identifying a particular neuron or attention head does not always clarify the exact influence of features such as credit score or volatility on the final decision.
future_direction: Integrating mechanistic interpretability with feature-level attributions to ensure AI decisions are explainable in terms of real-world financial indicators.
Developing a hybrid approach that integrates traditional statistical modeling techniques using financial time series data with unstructured data processed by LLMs.
Building fully integrated interpretability tooling that combines techniques from various research efforts to streamline analysis workflows for financial professionals.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable capabilities across a spectrum of tasks in financial services, including report generation, chatbots, sentiment analysis, regulatory compliance, investment advisory, financial knowledge retrieval, and summarization. However, their intrinsic complexity and lack of transparency pose significant challenges, especially in the highly regulated financial sector, where interpretability, fairness, and accountability are critical. As far as we are aware, this paper presents the first application in the finance domain of understanding and utilizing the inner workings of LLMs through mechanistic interpretability, addressing the pressing need for transparency and control in AI systems. Mechanistic interpretability is the most intuitive and transparent way to understand LLM behavior by reverse-engineering their internal workings. By dissecting the activations and circuits within these models, it provides insights into how specific features or components influence predictions - making it possible not only to observe but also to modify model behavior. In this paper, we explore the theoretical aspects of mechanistic interpretability and demonstrate its practical relevance through a range of financial use cases and experiments, including applications in trading strategies, sentiment analysis, bias, and hallucination detection. While not yet widely adopted, mechanistic interpretability is expected to become increasingly vital as adoption of LLMs increases. Advanced interpretability tools can ensure AI systems remain ethical, transparent, and aligned with evolving financial regulations. In this paper, we have put special emphasis on how these techniques can help unlock interpretability requirements for regulatory and compliance purposes - addressing both current needs and anticipating future expectations from financial regulators globally.

papers.title: Identifying and Controlling Important Neurons in Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How important are individual neurons for obtaining high-quality translations? Do individual neurons in NMT models contain interpretable linguistic information? Can we control MT output by intervening in the representation at the individual neuron level?
papers.core_contribution: Develops unsupervised methods (MaxCorr, MinCorr, LinReg, SVCCA) for discovering important neurons in NMT models, shows these neurons impact translation quality and capture linguistic phenomena, and demonstrates translation control by modifying individual neuron activations.
papers.conclusion: The work indicates that not all information is distributed in NMT models, and many human-interpretable grammatical and structural properties are captured by individual neurons. Modifying neuron activations allows for controlling translation output according to specified linguistic properties.
papers.key_findings:
Erasing top-ranked neurons (by the proposed methods) hurts translation quality more than erasing bottom-ranked neurons.
Individual neurons capture interpretable linguistic properties such as parentheses, tense, number, gender, and noun phrase segmentation.
Translation output can be controlled (e.g., tense, number, gender) by modifying the activations of specific neurons, though success varies by property.
Different ranking methods capture different types of information: MaxCorr and MinCorr tend to find position information, while LinReg and SVCCA find token identity information.
The methods are task-independent and can be applied to other neural networks.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is applied only to LSTM-based NMT models; application to other architectures like the Transformer is left for future work.
Controlling some properties (e.g., gender) is more difficult, possibly because they are more distributed than others (e.g., tense).
future_direction: Apply the analysis to other NMT components (e.g., the decoder) and architectures (e.g., Transformer, convolutional sequence-to-sequence).
Develop more sophisticated ways to control translation output, for example by modifying representations in variational NMT architectures.
Analyze the spectrum of localized vs. distributed information in neural language representations more broadly.
papers.abstract: Neural machine translation (NMT) models learn representations containing substantial linguistic information. However, it is not clear if such information is fully distributed or if some of it can be attributed to individual neurons. We develop unsupervised methods for discovering important neurons in NMT models. Our methods rely on the intuition that different models learn similar properties, and do not require any costly external supervision. We show experimentally that translation quality depends on the discovered neurons, and find that many of them capture common linguistic phenomena. Finally, we show how to control NMT translations in predictable ways, by modifying activations of individual neurons.

papers.title: Concept Bottleneck Models
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether concept bottleneck models can achieve competitive task accuracy with standard end-to-end models while enabling interpretation and intervention via high-level concepts, and explores the trade-offs involved.
papers.core_contribution: Concept bottleneck models achieve competitive task accuracy with standard end-to-end models while enabling interpretation and test-time intervention via human-specified concepts, leading to improved accuracy when concepts are corrected.
papers.conclusion: Concept bottleneck models are promising for settings like medicine where human experts can collaborate with models using high-level concepts, as they achieve competitive accuracy while supporting interpretation and intervention.
papers.key_findings:
Concept bottleneck models achieve competitive task accuracy with standard end-to-end models on both x-ray grading and bird identification tasks.
Bottleneck models have high concept accuracy, whereas linear probes on standard models have lower concept accuracy, making post-hoc interpretation difficult.
Test-time intervention by correcting concept predictions significantly improves task accuracy.
Different training schemes (independent, sequential, joint) lead to different trade-offs between task accuracy and intervention effectiveness.
Concept bottleneck models can be more robust to covariate shifts when concepts are less correlated with spurious features, as demonstrated on the TravelingBirds dataset.
papers.limitation:
Requires annotated concepts at training time
Assumes that concepts are correctly specified and complete; performance may degrade with incomplete concepts
For CUB, the use of denoised class-level concepts may not reflect instance-level variations
future_direction: Learning concepts by interactively querying humans.
Accounting for incomplete concepts by adding a direct side channel from input to target.
Applying concept bottleneck models to other domains like medicine and science.
papers.abstract: We seek to learn models that we can interact with using high-level concepts: if the model did not think there was a bone spur in the x-ray, would it still predict severe arthritis? State-of-the-art models today do not typically support the manipulation of concepts like "the existence of bone spurs", as they are trained end-to-end to go directly from raw input (e.g., pixels) to output (e.g., arthritis severity). We revisit the classic idea of first predicting concepts that are provided at training time, and then using these concepts to predict the label. By construction, we can intervene on these concept bottleneck models by editing their predicted concept values and propagating these changes to the final prediction. On x-ray grading and bird identification, concept bottleneck models achieve competitive accuracy with standard end-to-end models, while enabling interpretation in terms of high-level clinical concepts ("bone spurs") or bird attributes ("wing color"). These models also allow for richer human-model interaction: accuracy improves significantly if we can correct model mistakes on concepts at test time.

papers.title: Identifying Interpretable Subspaces in Image Representations
papers.research_question: How can we automatically explain features in image representations using natural language concepts? Also, which features in the representation space are explainable?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces FALCON, an automatic framework for explaining image representation features using natural language concepts. It also shows that interpretable subspaces are often composed of feature groups rather than individual features.
papers.conclusion: FALCON provides an effective way to automatically explain features in image representations. The study reveals that interpretable subspaces often consist of feature groups, and the extracted concepts can be used for debugging and transfer.
papers.key_findings:
FALCON can automatically extract human-understandable concepts for features without human intervention.
Individual features are often not interpretable, but groups of features are more interpretable.
FALCON concepts are validated by human evaluation with high precision and recall.
Concepts can be used to explain failures in downstream tasks.
Concepts can be transferred across representation spaces via a linear transformation.
papers.limitation:
The quality of explanations is dependent on the captioning dataset and the vision-language model.
The method may not capture very high-level abstract concepts that are not well-represented in the captioning data.
future_direction: Extending FALCON to other modalities like text and audio.
Improving the concept extraction to handle more abstract features.
Exploring the use of FALCON for model editing and improving model robustness.
papers.abstract: We propose Automatic Feature Explanation using Contrasting Concepts (FALCON), an interpretability framework to explain features of image representations. For a target feature, FALCON captions its highly activating cropped images using a large captioning dataset (like LAION-400m) and a pre-trained vision-language model like CLIP. Each word among the captions is scored and ranked leading to a small number of shared, human-understandable concepts that closely describe the target feature. FALCON also applies contrastive interpretation using lowly activating (counterfactual) images, to eliminate spurious concepts. Although many existing approaches interpret features independently, we observe in state-of-the-art self-supervised and supervised models, that less than 20% of the representation space can be explained by individual features. We show that features in larger spaces become more interpretable when studied in groups and can be explained with high-order scoring concepts through FALCON. We discuss how extracted concepts can be used to explain and debug failures in downstream tasks. Finally, we present a technique to transfer concepts from one (explainable) representation space to another unseen representation space by learning a simple linear transformation. Code available at https://github.com/NehaKalibhat/falcon-explain.

papers.title: TS-CNN: A Three-Tier Self-Interpretable CNN for Multi-Region Medical Image Classification
papers.research_question: How to improve the interpretability and accuracy of deep convolutional neural networks for medical image classification, particularly for images with multiple, scattered regions of interest?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a novel three-tier self-interpretable CNN architecture (TS-CNN) that improves classification accuracy and provides inherent interpretability for medical images with multiple, scattered regions of interest by integrating global, attention, and local branches.
papers.conclusion: The proposed TS-CNN architecture offers a flexible solution that improves classification metrics and provides interpretable visualizations, balancing accuracy and transparency for medical image classification tasks.
papers.key_findings:
The fusion branch of TS-CNN consistently improves classification accuracy over the global branch alone across multiple backbone models and datasets.
The architecture is flexible and works with various backbone CNNs (e.g., DenseNet-121, ResNet-50) and post-hoc interpretability methods (GradCAM, Saliency maps).
TS-CNN outperforms the backbone models on both a synthetic blob dataset and the real-world PAD-UFES-20 skin lesion dataset.
The model's performance is vulnerable to input image noise and heavily relies on the effectiveness of the global branch for accurate attention localization.
papers.limitation:
The model is vulnerable to noise in input images, with performance degrading as noise levels increase.
The fusion model's performance heavily relies on the accurate attention localization of the global branch.
future_direction: Investigate techniques to enhance the model's robustness to noise, such as data augmentation or noise reduction algorithms.
Explore alternative architectures or modifications to the existing model.
papers.abstract: Medical image classification is critical, where reliability and transparency are crucial for the safe and accurate diagnosis of diseases. Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs) are widely used in medical image classification due to their high performance. However, they are often considered black-boxes because they offer little insight into decision-making. Therefore, improving the interpretability of DCNNs is crucial for their adoption in medical diagnoses. This paper proposes a novel three-tier self-interpretable DCNN (TS-CNN) architecture for multi-region medical image classification, which improves classification performance while being inherently interpretable. The proposed TS-CNN architecture is well-suited for medical images with multiple regions, such as images with scattered and randomly shaped lesions. The proposed architecture has three branches: a global branch that learns the relevant patterns from the raw input image; an attention branch that selects the important regions and discards the irrelevant parts for the local branch to learn; and a fusion branch that distills knowledge from both the global and local branches for classification. The proposed architecture is flexible in terms of the backbone CNNs used for classification and post-hoc interpretability methods used for attention capture.We demonstrate the flexibility and generalization of the architecture through a series of experiments involving multiple state-of-the-artCNN architectures such as DenseNet-121, Inception, Xception, and ResNet-50 as the global/local branches, each paired with GradCAM and Saliency maps as attention modules. The proposed architecture outperformed the backbone model in classification tasks on two datasets: a custom-made blob dataset and a publicly available skin lesion PAD-UFES-20 dataset, demonstrating its potential for improving accuracy in medical image classification tasks. The code related to this work can be found at: https://github.com/sikha2552/TS-CNN-A-Three-Tier-Self-Interpretable-CNN-for-Medical-Image-Classification-Empowered-with-Post-hoc.git.

papers.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language\n Models
papers.research_question: How does attention in protein Transformer models capture structural and functional properties of proteins?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that attention in protein Transformer models captures the folding structure of proteins, targets binding sites, and focuses on progressively more complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that attention in protein Transformer models recovers structural and functional properties of proteins, and that such interpretability methods can potentially aid scientific discovery in biology.
papers.key_findings:
Attention in protein Transformers captures tertiary structure (contact maps).
Attention targets functional sites like binding sites and post-translational modifications.
Deeper layers focus on more complex properties (e.g., binding sites, contacts) while secondary structure is targeted more evenly across layers.
Attention heads specialize in particular amino acids and their attention patterns correlate with substitution matrices.
The findings are consistent across multiple Transformer architectures (BERT, ALBERT, XLNet) and datasets.
papers.limitation: The analyses are associative and do not establish causal links between attention and model behavior.
