papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an interpretable neuron editing method that effectively reduces gender bias in LLMs while preserving their original capabilities, supported by a new dataset and a detailed analysis of bias mechanisms at the neuron level.
papers.conclusion: The proposed interpretable neuron editing method successfully addresses the challenges of understanding and mitigating gender bias in LLMs, achieving a strong balance between fairness and functionality without compromising the models' original capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Gender bias is pervasive across multiple LLMs, as evidenced by non-zero entropy differences and skewed proportions in the CommonWords dataset.
Specific neuron circuits, including 'gender neurons' activated by stereotypical words and 'general neurons' activated by the <start> token, are responsible for gender bias.
Editing even a small number of general neurons can significantly degrade the model's performance on common tasks due to hierarchical neuron interactions.
The proposed interpretable neuron editing method, combining logit-based and causal-based strategies, effectively reduces gender bias (e.g., improving ICAT scores) while maintaining performance on tasks like reading comprehension and arithmetic.
The method outperforms existing fine-tuning and neuron editing approaches in balancing bias reduction with capability preservation.
papers.limitation:
The method relies on the CommonWords dataset for neuron selection, and results may vary for tasks or datasets not covered in the study.
Experiments are conducted on five decoder-only LLMs, requiring potential adaptations for other architectures.
The evaluation metrics (ICAT, entropy difference, accuracy) may not fully capture fairness or real-world performance.
The interpretability insights guiding neuron selection rely on assumptions (e.g., projecting neurons into vocabulary space) that may only be approximations.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit gender bias, posing challenges for their safe deployment. Existing methods to mitigate bias lack a comprehensive understanding of its mechanisms or compromise the model's core capabilities. To address these issues, we propose the CommonWords dataset, to systematically evaluate gender bias in LLMs. Our analysis reveals pervasive bias across models and identifies specific neuron circuits, including gender neurons and general neurons, responsible for this behavior. Notably, editing even a small number of general neurons can disrupt the model's overall capabilities due to hierarchical neuron interactions. Based on these insights, we propose an interpretable neuron editing method that combines logit-based and causal-based strategies to selectively target biased neurons. Experiments on five LLMs demonstrate that our method effectively reduces gender bias while preserving the model's original capabilities, outperforming existing fine-tuning and editing approaches. Our findings contribute a novel dataset, a detailed analysis of bias mechanisms, and a practical solution for mitigating gender bias in LLMs.

papers.title: Deep Image Segmentation Using Explainable Attention Mechanisms: Applications in Biomedical Imaging
papers.research_question: How can we overcome the lack of interpretability in deep learning models for medical image segmentation by introducing an explainable framework that combines CNNs and transformers with attention mechanisms and XAI tools?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces an explainable hybrid deep learning model for biomedical image segmentation that combines a CNN encoder with a Transformer decoder, integrates CBAM attention modules, and embeds XAI tools (Grad-CAM++ and SHAP) to achieve high segmentation accuracy and interpretability in a unified architecture.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework successfully improves segmentation accuracy and provides inherent interpretability, addressing the trust gap and forming a solid basis for clinical adoption of AI-aided diagnostic tools.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed model outperforms baseline models (U-Net, Attention U-Net, TransUNet) on ISIC 2018 and BraTS 2021 datasets, achieving Dice scores of 0.902 and 0.895 respectively.
The integrated explainability tools (Grad-CAM++ and SHAP) produce visual explanations that align with clinical landmarks, validated by expert assessments with over 85% clinical relevance.
Ablation studies confirm the importance of attention modules (CBAM) and explainability components for both performance and clinical trust.
papers.limitation:
The computational cost is significantly larger than lightweight CNN models due to transformer modules and attention methods, which may hinder real-time deployment in resource-limited clinical settings.
The model requires detailed preprocessing and augmentation optimization for best performance and assumes clean and annotated datasets, which may not align with noisy or incomplete real-world clinical data.
Explainability methods like SHAP are computationally expensive and may not be fitting to all use cases.
future_direction: Applying the same pipeline to other medical imaging modalities (e.g., chest X-rays, CT scans, retinal fundus images) with domain-specific adjustments.
Addressing task-specific problems like modality-dependent noise, data scarcity, or label variability via transfer learning, weak supervision, or synthetic data generation.
Meeting emerging ethical and regulatory requirements for AI-driven diagnostic systems, focusing on accountability, fairness, and decision-making transparency.
papers.abstract: Correct and discernible segmentation of an image is an important part of biomedical imaging, especially when anatomical structures and pathological regions are identified. Although deep learning architectures, like U-Net and its variants, have performed well, their lack of interpretability, transparency and contextual reasoning has limited their clinical adoption. This research helps to overcome the most important issue of high-performance medical segmentation by introducing a new explainable framework that combines convolutional encoders with transformer-based decoders and dual attention mechanisms. There are three aspects of this work, based on the following objectives. (1) To boost the performance of segmentation by means of hybrid local-global feature modelling; (2) To bring about clarity through visual explanation tools; and (3) To conduct clinical viability checks through expert assessments. The architecture proposed includes CBAM for fine spatial and channel attention and combines Grad-CAM++ and SHAP for local and global explainability. Such modules make it possible for clinicians to view the decision paths of models and establish trust in automated outputs. Experiments in two datasets, which were publicly available, were performed: ISIC 2018 for skin lesion segmentation and BraTS 2021 for brain tumor segmentation. The quantitative results show that the suggested method is better than several strong baseline models, such as U-Net, Attention U-Net, and TransUNet, delivering Dice scores of 0.902 and 0.895 on ISIC and BraTS datasets, respectively. Visual comparisons and expert confirmation validate the clinical plausibility of the predicted masks and demonstrate the potential worth of the explainability in high-stakes healthcare conditions. On the whole, this work provides a prudent, precise and explainable deep learning approach toward medical image segmentation and offers ample room for scientific integration and trust-conscious implementation in diagnostics workflows.

papers.title: Interpreting Arithmetic Mechanism in Large Language Models through Comparative Neuron Analysis
papers.research_question: How is arithmetic ability implemented in large language models, specifically the role of attention heads and FFN neurons, and what is the internal logic chain from input to prediction? Additionally, how does the LoRA fine-tuning method work?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Comparative Neuron Analysis (CNA) method to interpret arithmetic mechanisms in LLMs, identifying an internal logic chain of four stages, and applies it to understand LoRA and for model pruning and bias reduction.
papers.conclusion: The paper identifies important attention heads and FFN neurons for arithmetic, proposes the CNA method to construct the internal logic chain, finds LoRA amplifies important FFN neurons, and applies CNA to model pruning and editing.
papers.key_findings:
Arithmetic ability is localized in a few attention heads (arithmetic heads), each specializing in distinct operations.
The internal logic chain from input to prediction consists of four stages: feature enhancing, feature transferring, feature predicting, and prediction enhancing.
LoRA enhances prediction probabilities by amplifying the coefficient scores of important FFN neurons related to the final prediction.
Model pruning retaining only 5% of deep FFN neurons identified by CNA maintains performance on arithmetic tasks.
Model editing by zeroing 18 FFN neurons identified by CNA reduces gender bias by 35.7%.
papers.limitation:
The case studies rely on projecting vectors in vocabulary space, which is empirically interpretable but lacks complete theoretical foundation.
There is a lack of standardization across various studies regarding attribution methods (e.g., different intervention methods).
A potential risk is that attackers can identify and edit important neurons to change model behavior maliciously.
future_direction: Further investigation of the multiplication heads which do not significantly impact accuracy.
Explorations on different datasets for gender bias reduction.
Distinguishing whether a model has been edited to prevent malicious use.

papers.title: LLM Circuit Analyses Are Consistent Across Training and Scale
papers.research_question: Do circuit analyses of LLMs generalize across training time and model scale?
papers.core_contribution: Circuit analyses are consistent across training and scale: task abilities and supporting functional components emerge at similar token counts across model sizes, and the overarching algorithms implemented by circuits remain stable even when individual components change.
papers.conclusion: Circuit analyses generalize well over both training and scale, suggesting that studies on small models at the end of pre-training can inform understanding of larger models and models with longer training.
papers.key_findings:
Task abilities and functional components (e.g., induction heads, name-mover heads) emerge consistently at similar token counts across different model scales.
The algorithm implemented by a circuit remains stable over training even when the specific attention heads implementing it change.
Circuit size correlates with model size and can fluctuate over time while the algorithm remains the same.
Components like induction heads emerge around 2B tokens across scales, paralleling task learning curves.
Circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training provide insights that generalize to larger models and longer training runs.
papers.limitation:
The study does not include fine-tuning or other post-training techniques.
Circuit completeness is challenging to verify.
The findings need validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
future_direction: Validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
Investigating the load-balancing mechanism that maintains task performance when components change.
papers.abstract: Most currently deployed large language models (LLMs) undergo continuous training or additional finetuning. By contrast, most research into LLMs' internal mechanisms focuses on models at one snapshot in time (the end of pre-training), raising the question of whether their results generalize to real-world settings. Existing studies of mechanisms over time focus on encoder-only or toy models, which differ significantly from most deployed models. In this study, we track how model mechanisms, operationalized as circuits, emerge and evolve across 300 billion tokens of training in decoder-only LLMs, in models ranging from 70 million to 2.8 billion parameters. We find that task abilities and the functional components that support them emerge consistently at similar token counts across scale. Moreover, although such components may be implemented by different attention heads over time, the overarching algorithm that they implement remains. Surprisingly, both these algorithms and the types of components involved therein can replicate across model scale. These results suggest that circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training can provide insights that still apply after additional pre-training and over model scale.

papers.title: An Interpretable CNN for the Segmentation of the Left Ventricle in Cardiac MRI by Real-Time Visualization
papers.research_question: How can an interpretable convolutional neural network be created for left ventricle segmentation in cardiac MRI, balancing accuracy and interpretability without relying on transfer learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel interpretable CNN for left ventricle segmentation in cardiac MRI, trained from scratch without transfer learning, using global average pooling for interpretability and real-time visualization of gradient changes and layer features.
papers.conclusion: The proposed interpretable CNN method is feasible and efficient for left ventricle segmentation in cardiac MRI, providing a balance of accuracy and interpretability without the need for transfer learning.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed model achieved a Dice coefficient of 94.48% and an accuracy of 99.7% on the Sunnybrook dataset.
The model, trained from scratch, performed comparably to standard ImageNet transfer learning models for the medical imaging task.
The use of global average pooling improved interpretability and reduced parameters, helping avoid overfitting.
Real-time visualization of gradient changes and layer features allowed for monitoring and analysis during training.
The model is lightweight and suitable for deployment on mobile devices.
papers.abstract: The interpretability of deep learning models has emerged as a compelling area in artificial intelligence research. The safety criteria for medical imaging are highly stringent, and models are required for an explanation. However, existing convolutional neural network solutions for left ventricular segmentation are viewed in terms of inputs and outputs. Thus, the interpretability of CNNs has come into the spotlight. Since medical imaging data are limited, many methods to fine-tune medical imaging models that are popular in transfer models have been built using massive public ImageNet datasets by the transfer learning method. Unfortunately, this generates many unreliable parameters and makes it difficult to generate plausible explanations from these models. In this study, we trained from scratch rather than relying on transfer learning, creating a novel interpretable approach for autonomously segmenting the left ventricle with a cardiac MRI. Our enhanced GPU training system implemented interpretable global average pooling for graphics using deep learning. The deep learning tasks were simplified. Simplification included data management, neural network architecture, and training. Our system monitored and analyzed the gradient changes of different layers with dynamic visualizations in real-time and selected the optimal deployment model. Our results demonstrated that the proposed method was feasible and efficient: the Dice coefficient reached 94.48%, and the accuracy reached 99.7%. It was found that no current transfer learning models could perform comparably to the ImageNet transfer learning architectures. This model is lightweight and more convenient to deploy on mobile devices than transfer learning models.

papers.title: Towards interpretable-by-design deep learning algorithms
papers.research_question: How can deep learning models be made interpretable by design using prototypes, and how does this approach perform in terms of accuracy, computational efficiency, and resistance to confounding without requiring finetuning of the backbone model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the IDEAL framework, which transforms standard deep learning models into interpretable, prototype-based models without necessarily requiring finetuning, achieving competitive performance, especially with Vision Transformer backbones, while offering inherent interpretability and robustness to confounding.
papers.conclusion: The IDEAL framework offers an interpretable-by-design alternative to standard deep learning that can match the performance of opaque models, especially when using modern architectures like ViT, without the need for computationally expensive finetuning, and is effective for lifelong learning and mitigating confounding biases.
papers.key_findings:
The IDEAL framework without finetuning achieves performance competitive with finetuned models, with the gap being especially small for Vision Transformer (ViT) architectures.
The framework provides interpretability through real-image prototypes, allowing users to see which training examples a prediction is based on.
IDEAL circumvents catastrophic forgetting and enables efficient class-incremental learning, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines on benchmarks like iCIFAR-100.
Without finetuning, IDEAL improves performance on confounded data compared to finetuned counterparts by avoiding overfitting to spurious correlations.
The choice of prototype selection method (e.g., k-means) is crucial for performance when the backbone is not finetuned, but becomes less significant when the backbone is finetuned.
papers.abstract: The proposed framework named IDEAL (Interpretable-by-design DEep learning ALgorithms) recasts the standard supervised classification problem into a function of similarity to a set of prototypes derived from the training data, while taking advantage of existing latent spaces of large neural networks forming so-called Foundation Models (FM). This addresses the issue of explainability (stage B) while retaining the benefits from the tremendous achievements offered by DL models (e.g., visual transformers, ViT) pre-trained on huge data sets such as IG-3.6B + ImageNet-1K or LVD-142M (stage A). We show that one can turn such DL models into conceptually simpler, explainable-through-prototypes ones. The key findings can be summarized as follows: (1) the proposed models are interpretable through prototypes, mitigating the issue of confounded interpretations, (2) the proposed IDEAL framework circumvents the issue of catastrophic forgetting allowing efficient class-incremental learning, and (3) the proposed IDEAL approach demonstrates that ViT architectures narrow the gap between finetuned and non-finetuned models allowing for transfer learning in a fraction of time \textbf{without} finetuning of the feature space on a target dataset with iterative supervised methods.

papers.title: Have Faith in Faithfulness: Going Beyond Circuit Overlap When Finding Model Mechanisms
papers.research_question: How faithful are circuits found by edge attribution patching (EAP), and what is the relationship between overlap and faithfulness? The paper also introduces a new method, EAP-IG, to improve faithfulness.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces EAP-IG, a gradient-based circuit finding method that produces more faithful circuits than EAP, and shows that overlap metrics are insufficient for evaluating circuit faithfulness.
papers.conclusion: When comparing circuits, measuring overlap is no substitute for measuring faithfulness; EAP-IG provides a more faithful alternative to EAP for circuit finding.
papers.key_findings:
EAP-IG circuits are more faithful than EAP circuits on many tasks, though activation patching circuits sometimes outperform both.
Overlap (node or edge) does not always imply faithfulness; moderate overlap does not predict faithfulness well.
EAP-IG scores have higher correlation with activation patching scores for important edges, leading to more faithful circuits.
EAP-IG requires few steps (e.g., m=5) to achieve high faithfulness, making it efficient.
Cross-task faithfulness analysis reveals that circuit mechanisms can be shared across related tasks (e.g., Greater-Than variants) but not always.
papers.limitation:
Testing circuit completeness is challenging, and manually-found 'ground-truth' circuits may be unreliable.
EAP-IG does not always match the performance of activation patching (e.g., on the IOI task).
future_direction: Developing more efficient algorithms for computing faithfulness.
Investigating weighted graph edit distance as a metric that accounts for edge importance.
Exploring methods to ensure circuit completeness in addition to faithfulness.
papers.abstract: Many recent language model (LM) interpretability studies have adopted the circuits framework, which aims to find the minimal computational subgraph, or circuit, that explains LM behavior on a given task. Most studies determine which edges belong in a LM's circuit by performing causal interventions on each edge independently, but this scales poorly with model size. Edge attribution patching (EAP), gradient-based approximation to interventions, has emerged as a scalable but imperfect solution to this problem. In this paper, we introduce a new method - EAP with integrated gradients (EAP-IG) - that aims to better maintain a core property of circuits: faithfulness. A circuit is faithful if all model edges outside the circuit can be ablated without changing the model's performance on the task; faithfulness is what justifies studying circuits, rather than the full model. Our experiments demonstrate that circuits found using EAP are less faithful than those found using EAP-IG, even though both have high node overlap with circuits found previously using causal interventions. We conclude more generally that when using circuits to compare the mechanisms models use to solve tasks, faithfulness, not overlap, is what should be measured.

papers.title: X-VMamba: Explainable Vision Mamba
papers.research_question: How can we understand what State Space Models (SSMs) have learned and how they process information, given the lack of transparent attention mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a controllability-based interpretability framework for State Space Models (SSMs) that quantifies how input patches influence internal state dynamics, with two formulations (Jacobian-based and Gramian-based) that operate in a single forward pass with linear complexity.
papers.conclusion: Controllability analysis establishes a principled, mathematically rigorous interpretability paradigm for SSMs, providing unprecedented visibility into their internal dynamics and hierarchical processing across domains.
papers.key_findings:
SSMs naturally implement hierarchical feature refinement, with early layers capturing diffuse low-level textures and deeper layers focusing on semantically meaningful, clinically relevant patterns.
Influence scores become progressively more focused in deeper layers, with fewer patches having high influence, indicating a hierarchical filtering mechanism.
The choice of image scanning strategy (e.g., forward, backward, transposed) substantially modulates the distribution of influence scores across patches.
The proposed controllability framework provides domain-specific signatures aligned with diagnostic criteria, such as lesion boundaries in dermatology and high-density areas in mammography.
papers.limitation:
The Gramian formulation assumes local linearity of the SSM dynamics and does not account for non-linearities between layers (e.g., activation functions, normalization).
The current analysis computes controllability independently at each layer and does not provide an end-to-end attribution map from raw inputs to final outputs.
For sequential data, the method provides static, per-time-step influence scores and does not capture temporal causal influence (how inputs at time t affect outputs at future times t+τ).
future_direction: Extending the controllability framework to account for non-linear transformations between SSM layers.
Developing methods for end-to-end attribution by propagating influence scores through the entire network depth.
Enabling temporal causal analysis for sequential data to capture how inputs influence future outputs over finite horizons.
papers.abstract: State Space Models (SSMs), particularly the Mamba architecture, have recently emerged as powerful alternatives to Transformers for sequence modeling, offering linear computational complexity while achieving competitive performance. Yet, despite their effectiveness, understanding how these Vision SSMs process spatial information remains challenging due to the lack of transparent, attention-like mechanisms. To address this gap, we introduce a controllability-based interpretability framework that quantifies how different parts of the input sequence (tokens or patches) influence the internal state dynamics of SSMs. We propose two complementary formulations: a Jacobian-based method applicable to any SSM architecture that measures influence through the full chain of state propagation, and a Gramian-based approach for diagonal SSMs that achieves superior speed through closed-form analytical solutions. Both methods operate in a single forward pass with linear complexity, requiring no architectural modifications or hyperparameter tuning. We validate our framework through experiments on three diverse medical imaging modalities, demonstrating that SSMs naturally implement hierarchical feature refinement from diffuse low-level textures in early layers to focused, clinically meaningful patterns in deeper layers. Our analysis reveals domain-specific controllability signatures aligned with diagnostic criteria, progressive spatial selectivity across the network hierarchy, and the substantial influence of scanning strategies on attention patterns. Beyond medical imaging, we articulate applications spanning computer vision, natural language processing, and cross-domain tasks. Our framework establishes controllability analysis as a unified, foundational interpretability paradigm for SSMs across all domains. Code and analysis tools will be made available upon publication

papers.title: Contrastive Integrated Gradients: A Feature Attribution-Based Method for Explaining Whole Slide Image Classification
papers.research_question: How to improve feature attribution for whole slide image classification to better highlight class-discriminative regions and provide more interpretable explanations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Contrastive Integrated Gradients (CIG), a feature attribution method that computes contrastive gradients in logit space to highlight class-discriminative regions, and proposes two new metrics (MIL-AIC and MIL-SIC) for evaluating attribution in weakly supervised settings.
papers.conclusion: CIG consistently produces more informative and stable attributions than existing methods, both quantitatively and qualitatively, improving interpretability and supporting more explainable AI systems in computational pathology.
papers.key_findings:
CIG achieves higher MIL-AIC and MIL-SIC scores than baseline attribution methods (Vanilla Gradient, IG, EG, IDG) across multiple cancer datasets and model architectures.
CIG produces more focused and accurate attributions that align closely with tumor regions, as shown in qualitative visualizations.
CIG satisfies the axioms of integrated attribution methods (completeness, sensitivity, implementation invariance).
CIG works reliably across different cancer subtypes (breast, renal, lung) and model types (MLP, CLAM).
The proposed evaluation metrics (MIL-AIC, MIL-SIC) are adapted for weakly supervised WSI classification and capture how model predictions evolve as salient regions are introduced.
papers.limitation:
The evaluation is best suited for tumor-positive slides and may be less meaningful for normal slides.
Lack of human-subject evaluation.
future_direction: Incorporate rigorous human-subject evaluations of interpretability.
papers.abstract: Interpretability is essential in Whole Slide Image (WSI) analysis for computational pathology, where understanding model predictions helps build trust in AI-assisted diagnostics. While Integrated Gradients (IG) and related attribution methods have shown promise, applying them directly to WSIs introduces challenges due to their high-resolution nature. These methods capture model decision patterns but may overlook class-discriminative signals that are crucial for distinguishing between tumor subtypes. In this work, we introduce Contrastive Integrated Gradients (CIG), a novel attribution method that enhances interpretability by computing contrastive gradients in logit space. First, CIG highlights class-discriminative regions by comparing feature importance relative to a reference class, offering sharper differentiation between tumor and non-tumor areas. Second, CIG satisfies the axioms of integrated attribution, ensuring consistency and theoretical soundness. Third, we propose two attribution quality metrics, MIL-AIC and MIL-SIC, which measure how predictive information and model confidence evolve with access to salient regions, particularly under weak supervision. We validate CIG across three datasets spanning distinct cancer types: CAMELYON16 (breast cancer metastasis in lymph nodes), TCGA-RCC (renal cell carcinoma), and TCGA-Lung (lung cancer). Experimental results demonstrate that CIG yields more informative attributions both quantitatively, using MIL-AIC and MIL-SIC, and qualitatively, through visualizations that align closely with ground truth tumor regions, underscoring its potential for interpretable and trustworthy WSI-based diagnostics

papers.title: High resolution weakly supervised localization architectures for medical images
papers.research_question: How can the localization accuracy of Class-Activation Maps (CAM) be improved for weakly-supervised medical image analysis by designing a network architecture that avoids components harmful to shift-equivariance?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes PYLON, a high-resolution weakly-supervised localization network that avoids Global Average Pooling and Group Normalization to preserve shift-equivariance, achieving state-of-the-art point localization accuracy on the Chest X-Ray 14 dataset without sacrificing classification performance.
papers.conclusion: Shift-equivariance is crucial for accurate weakly-supervised localization, and avoiding GAP and Group Normalization leads to better performance. PYLON demonstrates high localization accuracy without compromising classification ability.
papers.key_findings:
Segmentation models (e.g., DeeplabV3+, FPN, PAN) perform poorly for weakly-supervised localization due to task mismatch.
Global Average Pooling (GAP) and Group Normalization are identified as components that significantly degrade localization accuracy in weakly-supervised settings.
Removing GAP and replacing Group Normalization with Batch Normalization improves localization accuracy in segmentation models.
PYLON, which removes GAP and uses a redesigned decoder, achieves the highest point localization accuracy, especially for small objects like nodules.
Higher resolution feature maps improve localization accuracy, with diminishing returns beyond a certain point.
papers.limitation: The reason why Group Normalization hinders localization accuracy is not determined, leaving an open question for future work.
future_direction: Investigate why Group Normalization hinders localization in weakly-supervised settings.
papers.abstract: In medical imaging, Class-Activation Map (CAM) serves as the main explainability tool by pointing to the region of interest. Since the localization accuracy from CAM is constrained by the resolution of the model's feature map, one may expect that segmentation models, which generally have large feature maps, would produce more accurate CAMs. However, we have found that this is not the case due to task mismatch. While segmentation models are developed for datasets with pixel-level annotation, only image-level annotation is available in most medical imaging datasets. Our experiments suggest that Global Average Pooling (GAP) and Group Normalization are the main culprits that worsen the localization accuracy of CAM. To address this issue, we propose Pyramid Localization Network (PYLON), a model for high-accuracy weakly-supervised localization that achieved 0.62 average point localization accuracy on NIH's Chest X-Ray 14 dataset, compared to 0.45 for a traditional CAM model. Source code and extended results are available at https://github.com/cmb-chula/pylon.

papers.title: Mask-Free Neuron Concept Annotation for Interpreting Neural Networks in Medical Domain
papers.research_question: How can neural networks be interpreted in medical domains without requiring pixel-wise annotated datasets for neuron concept annotation?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes MAMMI, a mask-free neuron concept annotation method for medical image models that uses vision-language models and adaptive selection to handle class imbalance, outperforming previous methods.
papers.conclusion: MAMMI is an effective mask-free method for neuron concept annotation in medical vision models, addressing limitations of previous approaches and demonstrating superior performance.
papers.key_findings:
MAMMI achieves superior performance in neuron concept annotation compared to mask-based and other vision-language methods in medical settings.
Using a medical-specific concept set extracted from MIMIC-CXR reports significantly improves interpretability over general concept sets.
Adaptive neuron representative image selection effectively handles class-imbalanced data distributions and improves concept matching.
MedCLIP outperforms other CLIP models for medical concept annotation in MAMMI.
MAMMI accurately identifies neuron concepts at penultimate layers, whereas baselines like TSI and CLIP Dissect fail to do so.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in deep neural networks have shown promise in aiding disease diagnosis and medical decision-making. However, ensuring transparent decision-making processes of AI models in compliance with regulations requires a comprehensive understanding of the model's internal workings. However, previous methods heavily rely on expensive pixel-wise annotated datasets for interpreting the model, presenting a significant drawback in medical domains. In this paper, we propose a novel medical neuron concept annotation method, named Mask-free Medical Model Interpretation (MAMMI), addresses these challenges. By using a vision-language model, our method relaxes the need for pixel-level masks for neuron concept annotation. MAMMI achieves superior performance compared to other interpretation methods, demonstrating its efficacy in providing rich representations for neurons in medical image analysis. Our experiments on a model trained on NIH chest X-rays validate the effectiveness of MAMMI, showcasing its potential for transparent clinical decision-making in the medical domain. The code is available at https://github.com/ailab-kyunghee/MAMMI.

papers.title: Unlocking the Heart Using Adaptive Locked Agnostic Networks
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ALAN, a self-supervised method that produces interpretable parcels for medical images, enabling simple downstream models with limited labeled data.
papers.conclusion: ALAN provides interpretable latent features that enable simple downstream models, reducing the need for labeled data and facilitating regulatory approval and expert incorporation in medical imaging applications.
papers.key_findings:
The self-supervised backbone (DINO ViT) robustly identifies anatomical subregions (parcels) of the heart in echocardiogram images.
The parcel-to-segment downstream model can segment cardiac regions (left ventricle and left atrium) with reasonable DICE scores, though performance varies with region size.
A DINO model pretrained on ImageNet performs almost as well as one trained on echocardiogram data, indicating generalization across imaging modalities.
Increasing the number of parcel classes (K) improves segmentation of small anatomical regions, but can be kept below 100 for good results.
The ALAN approach achieves competitive accuracy for echocardiogram view classification using a simple kNN classifier on the backbone features.
papers.limitation:
The EchoNet-Dynamic dataset lacks diversity, primarily consisting of apical chamber views, which may limit generalization to other views.
Self-supervised methods still require more work to match the performance of supervised methods in real-life medical applications.
Manual annotations of the left atrium sometimes do not cover the full surface, affecting DICE score evaluation.
future_direction: Investigate training the backbone model on datasets with other medical imaging modalities to further explore generalization.
papers.abstract: Supervised training of deep learning models for medical imaging applications requires a significant amount of labeled data. This is posing a challenge as the images are required to be annotated by medical professionals. To address this limitation, we introduce the Adaptive Locked Agnostic Network (ALAN), a concept involving self-supervised visual feature extraction using a large backbone model to produce anatomically robust semantic self-segmentation. In the ALAN methodology, this self-supervised training occurs only once on a large and diverse dataset. Due to the intuitive interpretability of the segmentation, downstream models tailored for specific tasks can be easily designed using white-box models with few parameters. This, in turn, opens up the possibility of communicating the inner workings of a model with domain experts and introducing prior knowledge into it. It also means that the downstream models become less data-hungry compared to fully supervised approaches. These characteristics make ALAN particularly well-suited for resource-scarce scenarios, such as costly clinical trials and rare diseases. In this paper, we apply the ALAN approach to three publicly available echocardiography datasets: EchoNet-Dynamic, CAMUS, and TMED-2. Our findings demonstrate that the self-supervised backbone model robustly identifies anatomical subregions of the heart in an apical four-chamber view. Building upon this, we design two downstream models, one for segmenting a target anatomical region, and a second for echocardiogram view classification.

papers.title: An Efficient Explainability of Deep Models on Medical Images
papers.research_question: How can the results obtained by deep learning models applied to the classification of chest X-rays be explained in a clear and comprehensible way to physicians?
papers.core_contribution: This paper applies and compares visual explainability methods (GradCAM, LIME, Vanilla Gradient, etc.) to deep learning models for chest X-ray classification, finding that GradCAM, LIME, and Vanilla Gradient are the most effective and doctor-validated methods for providing understandable explanations.
papers.conclusion: GradCAM was the most effective visual explainability method, closely followed by LIME and Vanilla Gradient, providing clear and interpretable explanations that are validated by medical professionals.
papers.key_findings:
MobileNetV2 was the best-performing model on the first dataset (COVID-19 Radiography Dataset), while VGG16 performed best on the second dataset (COVID CXR Image Dataset Research).
Doctors rated GradCAM, LIME, and Vanilla Gradient as the most effective explainability methods based on criteria like understanding, satisfaction, and accuracy.
SmoothGrad and Integrated Gradient methods received lower scores from doctors in the evaluation.
The application of explainability methods provides clear visualizations of the regions in chest X-rays that influence the model's classification decisions.
Explainability boosts doctors' confidence in deep learning models and facilitates their adoption in critical medical applications.
future_direction: Identifying and correcting biases in deep learning models to ensure more accurate and fair results.
Exploring alternative methods of explainability such as text-based explanation through examples.
Using larger datasets to evaluate the performance of deep learning models and explainability methods on a larger scale.
papers.abstract: Nowadays, Artificial Intelligence (AI) has revolutionized many fields and the medical field is no exception. Thanks to technological advancements and the emergence of Deep Learning (DL) techniques AI has brought new possibilities and significant improvements to medical practice. Despite the excellent results of DL models in terms of accuracy and performance, they remain black boxes as they do not provide meaningful insights into their internal functioning. This is where the field of Explainable AI (XAI) comes in, aiming to provide insights into the underlying workings of these black box models. In this present paper the visual explainability of deep models on chest radiography images are addressed. This research uses two datasets, the first on COVID-19, viral pneumonia, normality (healthy patients) and the second on pulmonary opacities. Initially the pretrained CNN models (VGG16, VGG19, ResNet50, MobileNetV2, Mixnet and EfficientNetB7) are used to classify chest radiography images. Then, the visual explainability methods (GradCAM, LIME, Vanilla Gradient, Gradient Integrated Gradient and SmoothGrad) are performed to understand and explain the decisions made by these models. The obtained results show that MobileNetV2 and VGG16 are the best models for the first and second datasets, respectively. As for the explainability methods, the results were subjected to doctors and were validated by calculating the mean opinion score. The doctors deemed GradCAM, LIME and Vanilla Gradient as the most effective methods, providing understandable and accurate explanations.

papers.title: XAI-MeD: Explainable Knowledge Guided Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Domain Generalization and Rare Class Detection in Medical Imaging
papers.research_question: How to improve robustness under distribution shift, enhance rare-class sensitivity, and provide transparent interpretations in medical AI by integrating expert knowledge with deep learning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces XAI-MeD, a neuro-symbolic framework that integrates clinical expert knowledge with deep learning to improve domain generalization, rare-class detection, and provide interpretable explanations in medical imaging.
papers.conclusion: XAI-MeD represents a significant step toward human-centered AI by integrating neural and symbolic paradigms, ensuring robustness, interpretability, and clinical alignment in medical AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
XAI-MeD achieves 84.6% accuracy and 89.7% sensitivity in SOZ localization, outperforming standalone DL and knowledge baselines.
The framework reduces manual expert review effort by 84.2% in SOZ localization.
In DR grading, XAI-MeD improves F1-scores for rare classes by over 10% compared to standalone DL.
XAI-MeD demonstrates robust cross-domain generalization, with 6% gain in accuracy on unseen datasets.
Ablation studies show that neuro-symbolic fusion achieves the best generalization performance.
papers.limitation:
Dependence on auxiliary supervised models (e.g., YOLO lesion detectors and U-Net anatomical segmenters) which require manually annotated data.
Finite clinical knowledge coverage due to reliance on expert-defined rule sets, unable to capture rare or edge cases not in training.
future_direction: Exploring weakly supervised or self-supervised lesion discovery to reduce dependency on manual annotations.
Investigating rule induction from large medical corpora using large language models to expand knowledge coverage.
papers.abstract: Explainability domain generalization and rare class reliability are critical challenges in medical AI where deep models often fail under real world distribution shifts and exhibit bias against infrequent clinical conditions This paper introduces XAIMeD an explainable medical AI framework that integrates clinically accurate expert knowledge into deep learning through a unified neuro symbolic architecture XAIMeD is designed to improve robustness under distribution shift enhance rare class sensitivity and deliver transparent clinically aligned interpretations The framework encodes clinical expertise as logical connectives over atomic medical propositions transforming them into machine checkable class specific rules Their diagnostic utility is quantified through weighted feature satisfaction scores enabling a symbolic reasoning branch that complements neural predictions A confidence weighted fusion integrates symbolic and deep outputs while a Hunt inspired adaptive routing mechanism guided by Entropy Imbalance Gain EIG and Rare Class Gini mitigates class imbalance high intra class variability and uncertainty We evaluate XAIMeD across diverse modalities on four challenging tasks i Seizure Onset Zone SOZ localization from rs fMRI ii Diabetic Retinopathy grading across 6 multicenter datasets demonstrate substantial performance improvements including 6 percent gains in cross domain generalization and a 10 percent improved rare class F1 score far outperforming state of the art deep learning baselines Ablation studies confirm that the clinically grounded symbolic components act as effective regularizers ensuring robustness to distribution shifts XAIMeD thus provides a principled clinically faithful and interpretable approach to multimodal medical AI.

papers.title: Provable concept learning for interpretable predictions using\n variational autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we provably identify high-level, previously unknown ground-truth concepts for interpretable predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CLAP, a VAE-based framework that provably identifies ground-truth concepts and achieves optimal classification accuracy for interpretable predictions.
papers.conclusion: CLAP provides a framework for interpretable predictions with theoretical guarantees for concept learning and optimal prediction accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
CLAP provably identifies ground-truth concepts in synthetic data and achieves optimal classification accuracy.
CLAP learns distinct, interpretable concepts on real medical data (e.g., heart shape, lung shape) for disease prediction.
CLAP provides both global and local feature importance for interpretable predictions.
CLAP outperforms baselines like SENN and CCVAE in learning disentangled concepts.
The framework is robust to over-parameterized latent spaces via sparsity regularization.
papers.limitation:
VAE visualizations are not as sharp as GANs
May not perform well in small data regimes
future_direction: Replace VAE with GAN for sharper visualizations while maintaining provable concept learning.
Develop solutions for small data regimes, e.g., via transfer learning.
papers.abstract:
In safety-critical applications, practitioners are reluctant to trust neural
networks when no interpretable explanations are available. Many attempts to
provide such explanations revolve around pixel-based attributions or use
previously known concepts. In this paper we aim to provide explanations by
provably identifying \emph{high-level, previously unknown ground-truth
concepts}. To this end, we propose a probabilistic modeling framework to derive
(C)oncept (L)earning and (P)rediction (CLAP) -- a VAE-based classifier that
uses visually interpretable concepts as predictors for a simple classifier.
Assuming a generative model for the ground-truth concepts, we prove that CLAP
is able to identify them while attaining optimal classification accuracy. Our
experiments on synthetic datasets verify that CLAP identifies distinct
ground-truth concepts on synthetic datasets and yields promising results on the
medical Chest X-Ray dataset.

papers.title: Can Subnetwork Structure be the Key to Out-of-Distribution Generalization?
papers.research_question: Can models with particular structure avoid being biased towards spurious correlation in out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization? The paper investigates whether subnetworks within biased models can achieve better OOD performance.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that biased models contain unbiased functional subnetworks, proposes the functional lottery ticket hypothesis, and introduces Modular Risk Minimization (MRM) to improve OOD generalization by learning subnetwork structures.
papers.conclusion: Subnetwork structure is a key factor for out-of-distribution generalization, and the proposed Modular Risk Minimization method effectively learns such structures to improve OOD performance.
papers.key_findings:
Even biased models that exploit spurious correlations contain subnetworks that are less susceptible to these shortcuts.
The functional lottery ticket hypothesis: a full network contains a subnetwork that can achieve better OOD performance when trained in isolation.
Modular Risk Minimization (MRM) effectively learns subnetworks that improve OOD generalization and can be combined with other OOD methods.
Sparsity constraints alone are insufficient for OOD generalization; the structure of the subnetwork is key.
MRM and its variants consistently improve OOD performance across multiple biased datasets.
papers.limitation:
The work has not considered data settings where group attribution information is available (e.g., as in Sagawa et al., 2019).
The experiments use a label noise-free setting, which may not reflect scenarios where spurious features have higher correlation than invariant features.
future_direction: Explore combinations of MRM with different loss designs for subnetwork and model learning.
Extend the approach to data settings with group attribution available.
Investigate the relationship between the structure of digit modules and subsets found by methods like 'and mask' under more domains.
papers.abstract: Can models with particular structure avoid being biased towards spurious correlation in out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization? Peters et al. (2016) provides a positive answer for linear cases. In this paper, we use a functional modular probing method to analyze deep model structures under OOD setting. We demonstrate that even in biased models (which focus on spurious correlation) there still exist unbiased functional subnetworks. Furthermore, we articulate and demonstrate the functional lottery ticket hypothesis: full network contains a subnetwork that can achieve better OOD performance. We then propose Modular Risk Minimization to solve the subnetwork selection problem. Our algorithm learns the subnetwork structure from a given dataset, and can be combined with any other OOD regularization methods. Experiments on various OOD generalization tasks corroborate the effectiveness of our method.

papers.title: Query Circuits: Explaining How Language Models Answer User Prompts
papers.research_question: How can we explain why a language model produces a particular output for a specific input query by tracing the information flow inside the model?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces query circuit discovery for local, input-level explanations of LLMs, proposes a robust evaluation metric (NDF) and sampling-based methods (BoN) to efficiently identify sparse, faithful circuits.
papers.conclusion: Query circuit discovery, aided by BoN sampling and NDF, demonstrates that compact sub-networks can explain much of an LLM's behavior on individual queries, offering a promising path for scalable, faithful explanations of LLM decisions.
papers.key_findings:
Extremely sparse query circuits (e.g., 1.3% of edges) can recover a large portion (e.g., 60%) of model performance on individual queries.
Best-of-N (BoN) sampling effectively discovers faithful query circuits, outperforming baseline methods.
Normalized Deviation Faithfulness (NDF) is a more robust evaluation metric for query circuits compared to Normalized Faithfulness Score (NFS).
Query circuits enable local, prompt-level explanations of LLM decisions, offering a step towards scalable interpretability.
papers.limitation:
The method neglects combinatorial interactions among edges, which is a fundamental limitation of using indirect effects as edge scores.
The work focuses on queries with single-token outputs (e.g., option IDs) and does not address multi-token generations.
There is no automated method for interpreting the functionalities of identified edges and nodes; manual investigation is not scalable.
future_direction: Develop methods to account for combinatorial interactions among edges in circuit discovery.
Extend query circuit discovery to multi-token generations.
Integrate automated interpretability methods to explain the functionalities of discovered circuits.
papers.abstract: Explaining why a language model produces a particular output requires local, input-level explanations. Existing methods uncover global capability circuits (e.g., indirect object identification), but not why the model answers a specific input query in a particular way. We introduce query circuits, which directly trace the information flow inside a model that maps a specific input to the output. Unlike surrogate-based approaches (e.g., sparse autoencoders), query circuits are identified within the model itself, resulting in more faithful and computationally accessible explanations. To make query circuits practical, we address two challenges. First, we introduce Normalized Deviation Faithfulness (NDF), a robust metric to evaluate how well a discovered circuit recovers the model's decision for a specific input, and is broadly applicable to circuit discovery beyond our setting. Second, we develop sampling-based methods to efficiently identify circuits that are sparse yet faithfully describe the model's behavior. Across benchmarks (IOI, arithmetic, MMLU, and ARC), we find that there exist extremely sparse query circuits within the model that can recover much of its performance on single queries. For example, a circuit covering only 1.3% of model connections can recover about 60% of performance on an MMLU questions. Overall, query circuits provide a step towards faithful, scalable explanations of how language models process individual inputs.

papers.title: Explainability in Generative Medical Diffusion Models: A Faithfulness-Based Analysis on MRI Synthesis
papers.research_question: How can prototype-based explainability methods link the relationship between generated and training features in diffusion models for MRI synthesis, and which method provides the most faithful explanations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a faithfulness-based explainability framework that integrates prototype-based reasoning with diffusion models for MRI synthesis, demonstrating that Enhanced ProtoPNet (EPPNet) achieves the highest faithfulness score, making diffusion models more transparent and trustworthy.
papers.conclusion: Diffusion models can generate realistic and anatomically accurate breast MRI images while being explainable through prototype-based methods, with EPPNet providing the most faithful explanations, advancing trustworthy AI for medical imaging.
papers.key_findings:
EPPNet achieves the highest faithfulness score (0.1534) among prototype-based methods for explaining diffusion-generated MRI images.
The diffusion model generates high-fidelity breast MRI images with PSNR of 19.37, SSIM of 0.6530, and LPIPS of 0.2893.
The denoising trajectory provides visual explainability by showing how anatomical features emerge from noise over time.
Prototype-based methods can effectively link generated image features to training data, improving interpretability.
The framework balances image quality and explainability, contributing to trustworthy generative AI in healthcare.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to single-class medical imaging tasks, which may not generalize to multiclass scenarios.
future_direction: Extend the approach to multiclass tasks and multiple imaging modalities, such as MRI and CT scans.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the explainability of generative diffusion models in the context of medical imaging, focusing on Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) synthesis. Although diffusion models have shown strong performance in generating realistic medical images, their internal decision making process remains largely opaque. We present a faithfulness-based explainability framework that analyzes how prototype-based explainability methods like ProtoPNet (PPNet), Enhanced ProtoPNet (EPPNet), and ProtoPool can link the relationship between generated and training features. Our study focuses on understanding the reasoning behind image formation through denoising trajectory of diffusion model and subsequently prototype explainability with faithfulness analysis. Experimental analysis shows that EPPNet achieves the highest faithfulness (with score 0.1534), offering more reliable insights, and explainability into the generative process. The results highlight that diffusion models can be made more transparent and trustworthy through faithfulness-based explanations, contributing to safer and more interpretable applications of generative AI in healthcare.

papers.title: Visual interpretability of image-based classification models by generative latent space disentanglement applied to in vitro fertilization
papers.research_question: How to discover the underlying visual properties driving image-based classification models in a human-interpretable way?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DISCOVER, a generative model that learns disentangled latent representations to discover and visualize the image properties driving classification decisions, enabling human-interpretable counterfactual explanations.
papers.conclusion: DISCOVER enables human-interpretable visual explanations for image classification models, discovers new image properties, and provides transparency for individual predictions, with potential for biological discovery.
papers.key_findings:
DISCOVER successfully identifies known blastocyst quality properties (size and trophectoderm) as classification-driving features.
DISCOVER discovers new properties (blastocoel density) that were not explicitly annotated.
DISCOVER provides instance-specific interpretation, ranking the importance of each property for individual predictions.
DISCOVER generalizes to other domains (natural images and Alzheimer's disease MRI).
DISCOVER outperforms existing interpretability methods (GradCAM, SHAP, LIME) in providing disentangled visual explanations.
papers.limitation:
One latent feature may encode multiple independent semantic image properties (entanglement).
DISCOVER may miss semantic image properties that are associated with the classification task (e.g., inner cell mass was not identified).
The method requires training a generative model, which can be computationally expensive.
papers.abstract: The success of deep learning in identifying complex patterns exceeding human intuition comes at the cost of interpretability. Non-linear entanglement of image features makes deep learning a "black box" lacking human meaningful explanations for the models' decision. We present DISCOVER, a generative model designed to discover the underlying visual properties driving image-based classification models. DISCOVER learns disentangled latent representations, where each latent feature encodes a unique classification-driving visual property. This design enables "human-in-the-loop" interpretation by generating disentangled exaggerated counterfactual explanations. We apply DISCOVER to interpret classification of in vitro fertilization embryo morphology quality. We quantitatively and systematically confirm the interpretation of known embryo properties, discover properties without previous explicit measurements, and quantitatively determine and empirically verify the classification decision of specific embryo instances. We show that DISCOVER provides human-interpretable understanding of "black box" classification models, proposes hypotheses to decipher underlying biomedical mechanisms, and provides transparency for the classification of individual predictions.

papers.title: Decompose the model: Mechanistic interpretability in image models with Generalized Integrated Gradients (GIG)
papers.research_question: How can mechanistic interpretability be achieved in image models by systematically tracing the pathway from input to output across an entire dataset, moving beyond class-specific explanations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a novel approach for mechanistic interpretability in image models, using Pointwise Feature Vectors (PFVs) and Effective Receptive Fields (ERFs) to decompose model embeddings into interpretable Concept Vectors, and a new Generalized Integrated Gradients (GIG) method to trace their causal contributions across layers for a dataset-wide analysis.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a novel approach for extracting and attributing concepts within image models, enabling a comprehensive layer-wise analysis that advances mechanistic interpretability by moving from class-specific to dataset-wide explanations.
papers.key_findings:
The method can extract and attribute 'shared concepts' that are common across similar classes, unlike class-specific explanation methods.
The proposed concept extraction method using bisecting k-means clustering outperforms other methods (like Sparse AutoEncoder and dictionary learning) in fidelity metrics (C-Deletion and C-Insertion) across most layers.
The Generalized Integrated Gradients (GIG) method effectively quantifies the causal relationships between concept vectors across different layers, validated by inter-layer deletion/insertion experiments.
The approach provides a holistic, dataset-wide understanding of model behavior, tracing how concepts are constructed and aggregated from lower to higher layers.
future_direction: Extending the method to other deep learning architectures, such as Transformer models.
More thoroughly investigating the implications of analyzing entire datasets rather than focusing solely on class-specific explanations.
papers.abstract: In the field of eXplainable AI (XAI) in language models, the progression from local explanations of individual decisions to global explanations with high-level concepts has laid the groundwork for mechanistic interpretability, which aims to decode the exact operations. However, this paradigm has not been adequately explored in image models, where existing methods have primarily focused on class-specific interpretations. This paper introduces a novel approach to systematically trace the entire pathway from input through all intermediate layers to the final output within the whole dataset. We utilize Pointwise Feature Vectors (PFVs) and Effective Receptive Fields (ERFs) to decompose model embeddings into interpretable Concept Vectors. Then, we calculate the relevance between concept vectors with our Generalized Integrated Gradients (GIG), enabling a comprehensive, dataset-wide analysis of model behavior. We validate our method of concept extraction and concept attribution in both qualitative and quantitative evaluations. Our approach advances the understanding of semantic significance within image models, offering a holistic view of their operational mechanics.

papers.title: Fine-Tuning is Subgraph Search: A New Lens on Learning Dynamics
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how fine-tuning works from a mechanistic interpretability perspective, viewing fine-tuning as a search for and optimization of a subgraph within the model's computational graph.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit-tuning, a fine-tuning method that dynamically localizes and optimizes subgraphs (circuits) within a model's computational graph, enabling analysis of learning dynamics and balancing task performance with general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Circuit-tuning provides a new method for studying learning dynamics from a mechanistic interpretability perspective, offering insights into how fine-tuning works and enabling more precise fine-tuning that balances task performance and general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit-tuning provides better training stability and preserves language modeling ability better than full fine-tuning.
The functionality of specific attention heads (Subject Attribute Heads) can reverse during fine-tuning to adapt to new tasks.
Some attention heads (Subject Identification Heads) preserve their functions and are shared before and after fine-tuning.
Nodes within a circuit cooperate through division of labor and indirect interactions to complete tasks.
Edges in the computational graph exhibit strengthening and weakening akin to Hebbian learning during fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: The study of mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse-engineer a model to explain its behaviors. While recent studies have focused on the static mechanism of a certain behavior, the learning dynamics inside a model remain to be explored. In this work, we develop a fine-tuning method for analyzing the mechanism behind learning. Inspired by the concept of intrinsic dimension, we view a model as a computational graph with redundancy for a specific task, and treat the fine-tuning process as a search for and optimization of a subgraph within this graph. Based on this hypothesis, we propose circuit-tuning, an algorithm that iteratively builds the subgraph for a specific task and updates the relevant parameters in a heuristic way. We first validate our hypothesis through a carefully designed experiment and provide a detailed analysis of the learning dynamics during fine-tuning. Subsequently, we conduct experiments on more complex tasks, demonstrating that circuit-tuning could strike a balance between the performance on the target task and the general capabilities. Our work offers a new analytical method for the dynamics of fine-tuning, provides new findings on the mechanisms behind the training process, and inspires the design of superior algorithms for the training of neural networks.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Enable Scalable and Reliable Circuit Identification in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently and robustly discover interpretable circuits in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method for circuit identification using discrete sparse autoencoders trained on attention head outputs, which is more efficient and robust than existing techniques.
papers.conclusion: Discrete sparse autoencoders offer a scalable, efficient, and robust approach for circuit identification in large language models, providing a promising direction for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The method outperforms or matches state-of-the-art circuit identification techniques (ACDC, HISP, SP) in precision and recall on three tasks (IOI, Greater-than, Docstring).
The method is robust to hyperparameter choices and requires only 5-10 text examples per task to learn robust representations.
The identified circuits can match or even outperform the full model's performance on the specific tasks with fewer components.
The method can identify negative components in circuits (e.g., negative name-mover heads in IOI) that other algorithms struggle to find.
The process is significantly faster, reducing runtime from hours to seconds compared to existing methods.
papers.limitation: The method currently only analyzes attention heads and not other components like MLP layers, which may be important for some circuits (e.g., Greater-than).
future_direction: Extending the method to analyze MLP layers and other model components.
Applying the method to larger models and more complex tasks.
Exploring the use of vector-quantized variational autoencoders (VQ-VAEs) as an alternative to sparse autoencoders.
papers.abstract: This paper introduces an efficient and robust method for discovering interpretable circuits in large language models using discrete sparse autoencoders. Our approach addresses key limitations of existing techniques, namely computational complexity and sensitivity to hyperparameters. We propose training sparse autoencoders on carefully designed positive and negative examples, where the model can only correctly predict the next token for the positive examples. We hypothesise that learned representations of attention head outputs will signal when a head is engaged in specific computations. By discretising the learned representations into integer codes and measuring the overlap between codes unique to positive examples for each head, we enable direct identification of attention heads involved in circuits without the need for expensive ablations or architectural modifications. On three well-studied tasks - indirect object identification, greater-than comparisons, and docstring completion - the proposed method achieves higher precision and recall in recovering ground-truth circuits compared to state-of-the-art baselines, while reducing runtime from hours to seconds. Notably, we require only 5-10 text examples for each task to learn robust representations. Our findings highlight the promise of discrete sparse autoencoders for scalable and efficient mechanistic interpretability, offering a new direction for analysing the inner workings of large language models.

papers.title: Self-Ablating Transformers: More Interpretability, Less Sparsity
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between sparsity and interpretability in transformers? Does inducing sparsity during training via a self-ablation mechanism enhance interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a self-ablation mechanism that enforces selective activation (k-winner-takes-all) during training, leading to improved interpretability (more localized circuits, specialized neurons) without necessarily increasing overall sparsity.
papers.conclusion: Self-ablation improves transformer interpretability across multiple indicators (circuit localization, feature disentanglement, neuron explainability) by promoting functional specialization and localized computation, challenging the simple intuition that sparsity alone leads to interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Self-ablation reduces circuit complexity, as shown by fewer edges in ACDC circuits for the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task.
Self-ablation leads to sparser feature representations (lower L0 norm in Sparse Autoencoders) and better reconstruction fidelity (higher CE score).
Self-ablation improves neuron explainability, with ablated models achieving higher automated explanation scores.
Self-ablation results in more focused neuron activation patterns, evidenced by lower graph density, lower transitivity, and increased specialization metrics in Neuron-to-Graph analysis.
Self-ablation incurs only a modest increase in validation perplexity, indicating a manageable trade-off between interpretability and language modeling performance.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation was conducted on the linguistically simple TinyStories dataset, which lacks complex syntax, diverse vocabulary, and abstract reasoning, limiting generalizability to real-world language.
Experiments were conducted on relatively small models; it is unknown how the self-ablation mechanism scales to much larger architectures.
future_direction: Evaluating self-ablation on linguistically diverse datasets to test scalability to complex linguistic phenomena.
Investigating the impact of model scale on the self-ablation mechanism's effects.
Exploring the application of self-ablation within a fine-tuning paradigm to improve interpretability of existing large language models.
papers.abstract: A growing intuition in machine learning suggests a link between sparsity and interpretability. We introduce a novel self-ablation mechanism to investigate this connection ante-hoc in the context of language transformers. Our approach dynamically enforces a k-winner-takes-all constraint, forcing the model to demonstrate selective activation across neuron and attention units. Unlike post-hoc methods that analyze already-trained models, our approach integrates interpretability directly into model training, promoting feature localization from inception. Training small models on the TinyStories dataset and employing interpretability tests, we find that self-ablation leads to more localized circuits, concentrated feature representations, and increased neuron specialization without compromising language modelling performance. Surprisingly, our method also decreased overall sparsity, indicating that self-ablation promotes specialization rather than widespread inactivity. This reveals a complex interplay between sparsity and interpretability, where decreased global sparsity can coexist with increased local specialization, leading to enhanced interpretability. To facilitate reproducibility, we make our code available at https://github.com/keenanpepper/self-ablating-transformers.

papers.title: S-Chain: Structured Visual Chain-of-Thought For Medicine
papers.research_question: How can expert-annotated structured visual chain-of-thought (SV-CoT) improve faithful reasoning, interpretability, and visual grounding in medical vision-language models compared to synthetic CoTs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces S-Chain, the first large-scale expert-annotated dataset with structured visual chain-of-thought (SV-CoT) for medical VQA, and demonstrates that SV-CoT supervision significantly improves model interpretability, grounding fidelity, and robustness compared to synthetic CoTs.
papers.conclusion: S-Chain establishes a new benchmark for grounded medical reasoning and paves the way toward more trustworthy and explainable medical vision-language models.
papers.key_findings:
S-Chain supervision consistently outperforms baseline (Q4-only) and synthetic GPT-4.1-generated CoTs across medical and general-purpose VLMs.
Expert-verified SV-CoT annotations reduce hallucinations and improve visual grounding compared to auto-generated rationales.
Combining SV-CoT with retrieval-augmented generation (MedRAG) yields further performance improvements, though SV-CoT is the dominant driver.
Models trained with SV-CoT show better alignment between reasoning steps and visual evidence, leading to more clinically trustworthy outputs.
Closed-source API models (e.g., GPT-4.1) under few-shot prompting still fall short of the reliability achieved by models fine-tuned with expert-grounded SV-CoT.
papers.abstract: Faithful reasoning in medical vision-language models (VLMs) requires not only accurate predictions but also transparent alignment between textual rationales and visual evidence. While Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has shown promise in medical visual question answering (VQA), no large-scale expert-level dataset has captured stepwise reasoning with precise visual grounding. We introduce S-Chain, the first large-scale dataset of 12,000 expert-annotated medical images with bounding boxes and structured visual CoT (SV-CoT), explicitly linking visual regions to reasoning steps. The dataset further supports 16 languages, totaling over 700k VQA pairs for broad multilingual applicability. Using S-Chain, we benchmark state-of-the-art medical VLMs (ExGra-Med, LLaVA-Med) and general-purpose VLMs (Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL2.5), showing that SV-CoT supervision significantly improves interpretability, grounding fidelity, and robustness. Beyond benchmarking, we study its synergy with retrieval-augmented generation, revealing how domain knowledge and visual grounding interact during autoregressive reasoning. Finally, we propose a new mechanism that strengthens the alignment between visual evidence and reasoning, improving both reliability and efficiency. S-Chain establishes a new benchmark for grounded medical reasoning and paves the way toward more trustworthy and explainable medical VLMs.

papers.title: Mechanistic Anomaly Detection for "Quirky" Language Models
papers.research_question: Can internal model features be used to detect anomalous training signals (when models use faulty heuristics) in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Mechanistic anomaly detectors can achieve high discrimination on some tasks but are not effective across all models and tasks; MAD may be effective in low-stakes applications but requires advances for high-stakes settings.
papers.conclusion: Anomaly detection results are inconsistent across models and tasks; while sometimes highly discriminative, performance degrades to chance in some cases, indicating that more work is needed for reliable real-world application.
papers.key_findings:
Anomaly detector performance varies significantly between models (model-dependent detection).
Detection efficacy is strongly task-dependent (e.g., arithmetic tasks yield higher performance).
Larger deviations in behavior generally make anomalies easier to detect, though not universally.
Anomaly detection performance is closely related to the linear separability of features between normal and anomalous classes.
Detectors that depend on different features (activations vs. attribution) offer somewhat independent signals, but naive combination did not improve performance.
papers.limitation: The manipulations in the datasets are artificial, and real-world tasks will differ systematically, likely with systematic changes in detector performance.
future_direction: Conduct additional experiments to assess whether models trained on more tokens make anomaly detection harder.
Develop benchmarks more closely aligned with intended real-world tasks.
Advances in both detection and evaluation are needed for high-stakes settings.
papers.abstract: As LLMs grow in capability, the task of supervising LLMs becomes more challenging. Supervision failures can occur if LLMs are sensitive to factors that supervisors are unaware of. We investigate Mechanistic Anomaly Detection (MAD) as a technique to augment supervision of capable models; we use internal model features to identify anomalous training signals so they can be investigated or discarded. We train detectors to flag points from the test environment that differ substantially from the training environment, and experiment with a large variety of detector features and scoring rules to detect anomalies in a set of ``quirky'' language models. We find that detectors can achieve high discrimination on some tasks, but no detector is effective across all models and tasks. MAD techniques may be effective in low-stakes applications, but advances in both detection and evaluation are likely needed if they are to be used in high stakes settings.

papers.title: Rank-1 LoRAs Encode Interpretable Reasoning Signals
papers.research_question: How can minimal parameter changes, specifically rank-1 LoRAs, be used to understand and interpret the mechanisms behind reasoning capabilities in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Minimal parameter changes via a rank-1 LoRA can recover most reasoning performance and provide interpretable insights, enabling targeted analysis of model behavior.
